title: Payment Methods and Convenience Fees
bodyText:
Since January 1, 2025, you may not charge a tenant a convenience fee on a rent payment unless you also accept at least one way of paying rent that carries no convenience fee. So if tenants can pay by card or through a portal that adds a fee, also accept a fee-free method (for example check, money order or a no-fee bank transfer) and list it in the lease.

A fee you do pass through is a fee beyond rent: disclose it in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); an undisclosed fee can be recovered by the tenant.

Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to accept cash, barring you from requiring electronic payment, or banning card surcharges generally. Rent is payable without demand at the time and place the lease sets; if the lease sets no place, it is payable at the dwelling unit.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic or revenue-management pricing software, and none on sharing rent or occupancy data with other landlords; no 2025 or 2026 act adds one. Rhode Island's general antitrust act still applies: every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade is unlawful (R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-36-4). Whether using a shared pricing tool with competing landlords amounts to such an agreement is a question for case law and federal antitrust law, which this library does not cover; take advice before adopting one.

title: No Application Fees; Background and Credit Check Costs
bodyText: Since January 1, 2024, neither you nor your broker, property manager or anyone acting for you may require or demand that a prospective tenant pay a rental application fee. You may require an official state criminal background check (from the BCI at the Department of Attorney General, the state police, or the local police department where the applicant lives) and a credit check, with these limits: if the applicant supplies a background check or credit report issued within 90 days of the application, you may not charge for one; if not, you may charge no more than the actual cost of obtaining it, and you must give the applicant a copy of any report you charged for. The section allows a charge only for those two reports, so don't charge for any other screening product (for example a private eviction-history search) or bundle a processing margin into the cost. You may always get your own report at your own expense. Rhode Island has no other application-fee rule, such as a refund rule or a fee cap formula.

title: No Statutory Order for Applying Payments
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute fixing the order in which you apply a tenant's payments, so the lease's order controls (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Applying each payment to rent first is the safer choice: Rhode Island's nonpayment eviction and cure rules turn on unpaid rent, not unpaid fees. Accepting a partial payment of rent does not waive the balance due. But accepting rent while knowing of a default, or accepting performance that differs from the lease, waives your right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give the tenant written notice within ten days; you keep your other remedies for the default.

title: Collection Fees
bodyText: Municipal ordinances and case law were not). If you refer the debt to a collection agency, Rhode Island's debt-collection law bars the agency from collecting any interest, fee, charge or expense on top of the debt unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or the law permits it, so without a lease term no collection fee can be collected at all. (You, collecting your own debt in your own name, and an agent who collects only for landlords are outside that law's definition of debt collector.) What the landlord-tenant act itself lets you recover: after the tenancy ends, use-and-occupation, actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees; in a nonpayment case, attorney's fees only if the tenant received a demand notice in the prior six months and the nonpayment was willful. A lease term making the tenant pay your attorney's fees beyond what the act allows is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to the tenant's actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Take advice before adding a collection-fee term.

title: What You May Collect Before Move-In
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no single list of what you may collect before a tenancy starts; several rules combine.

A security deposit, however you label it (damage, pet or any other deposit, refundable or not), may not exceed one month's periodic rent in total. A furnished apartment whose furniture has a replacement value of $5,000 or more when the lease is signed may also carry a separate furniture deposit of up to one month's rent.

You may not charge an application fee; you may pass on only the actual cost of an official state criminal background check or credit report the applicant doesn't supply.

Any other fee beyond rent must be listed in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. No statute bars a move-in fee as such (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not).

The act treats prepaid rent separately from the security deposit, so first month's rent is not part of the deposit limit; see the last-month's-rent row before collecting more rent in advance.

title: Disclosing Fees Beyond Rent
bodyText:
If any fee beyond rent applies to renting the unit, the lease must list those fees in the same section as the rent and must say that additional fees may apply. With no written lease, give the tenant a written list of every fee beyond rent. Any change in required fees must be disclosed in writing at least 30 days before it takes effect; that sentence sits in the no-written-lease paragraph, but follow it for every tenancy. If you don't disclose a fee as required, the tenant may recover the undisclosed fees paid.

The placement rule does not apply where the tenant or unit receives a state or federal subsidy that requires a different lease format. The same subsection requires the lease to say which utilities are in the rent and to state any renters-insurance requirement (covered in their own rows). Rhode Island has no all-in pricing rule for rental advertising and no first-page fee box.

title: No Specific Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute that specifically bars charging a fee for a service you don't provide (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Related rules still apply. Every fee beyond rent must be disclosed in the rent section of the lease (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format; with no written lease, in writing), and a tenant can recover fees paid that weren't disclosed as required. If you willfully cut off or reduce heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the tenancy and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Charge only for services the lease names and you actually provide.

title: Fees Are Not Rent
bodyText: Rhode Island defines rent as the payment or consideration a tenant pays you for the use of the premises. No statute says that late fees, utility charges or other fees are rent, and none says a lease can make a fee rent by calling it "additional rent" (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). This matters at the eviction stage: the nonpayment process (rent 15 days in arrears, then a five-day demand notice) is built on the stipulated rent, and the demand notice states the amount of rent in arrears. Put only rent in that notice and pursue fees separately. One statutory exception: if a tenant fails to fix a maintenance breach that materially affects health and safety within 20 days after your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may have the work done properly and bill its actual and reasonable cost as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the tenancy has ended. Whether recurring charges such as pet rent or parking count as rent is for the courts.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Municipal ordinances and case law were not), such as a registration, inspection or certificate fee, and the library does not offer such a clause. State-level obligations sit with you: you must register every unit with the Department of Health's statewide rental registry (the statute sets no registration fee, but missing registration brings civil fines of at least $50 a month, or $125 a month for missing pre-1978 lead certificate information, and blocks a nonpayment eviction filing), and a $100 state fire marshal fee per inspection involving a residential use (waived if no violation is found) is payable by the property owner. In Providence and Warwick you must also register with the city clerk. If you nonetheless pass a fee on, it is a fee beyond rent: list it in the rent section of the lease (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant may recover it.

title: How Late Fees Work in Rhode Island
bodyText:
Rhode Island lets you charge a late fee only as the lease provides, and sets no grace period or cap for ordinary residential tenancies (see the late-fee-limit row). Three rules shape how you charge it.

First, a late fee is a fee beyond rent: list it in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it.

Second, it is not rent. Rhode Island defines rent as payment for the use of the premises, and the nonpayment process (rent 15 days in arrears, then the five-day demand notice) is built on rent, so leave late fees out of the demand and collect them separately.

Third, accepting rent while knowing the tenant is in default waives your right to end the tenancy for that default unless you give written notice within ten days; a partial payment never waives the balance.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText:
Rhode Island sets no maximum late fee and no grace period for ordinary residential tenancies (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not); the amount and timing are whatever the lease states. Keep the fee a reasonable estimate of what late payment costs you: a court may refuse to enforce a fee it sees as a penalty.

Two kinds of housing have their own rules. A mobile and manufactured home park lease may not allow a late charge before a seven-day grace period ends or above 5% of the monthly rent due. A licensed assisted living residence may charge only reasonable late fees, under a written schedule it gave the resident at or before admission or signing.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring the same rent or terms for a month-to-month tenancy and a fixed-term lease, and no cap on the rent difference between them (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). The law still treats them differently. Unless the lease fixes a definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer who pays weekly). A periodic tenancy ends by written notice in the statutory form: at least 10 days for week-to-week, 30 days for month-to-month (and any period between a month and a year), and three months before the end of the occupation year for year-to-year; a fixed term ends on its own date. A rent increase needs 60 days' written notice for every tenancy, but 120 days for a month-to-month tenant over 62 (independent living, assisted living and congregate care facilities excluded). If a tenant stays on with your consent after the term and no new term is agreed, the tenancy becomes week to week (weekly payers) or month to month.

title: No Rule on Notice Fees
bodyText: Municipal ordinances and case law were not), and the library does not offer a notice-fee clause. Rhode Island's pre-eviction notices are sent by you, not served by an officer: the five-day demand for rent 15 days in arrears and the 20-day noncompliance notice are mailed, in the statutory forms. What you can recover is set by the act: in a nonpayment case, actual damages, plus reasonable attorney's fees only if the tenant got an earlier demand notice within the six months before you filed and the nonpayment was willful; a tenant who cures at the hearing pays court costs; for other breaches, attorney's fees only if the noncompliance was willful. A lease term making the tenant pay your attorney's fees beyond what the act allows is unenforceable, so don't dress a lawyer's notice-drafting charge up as a notice fee.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: You may not raise the rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant complained to a building or housing code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you about your maintenance duties, organized or joined a tenants' union or similar group, or used any other lawful right or remedy. If the tenant complained within six months before your action, the court must presume it was retaliation unless you produce evidence otherwise; there is no presumption if the complaint came after you gave notice of a rent increase or service cut. A retaliating landlord faces the tenant's choice of recovering possession or ending the lease, plus up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, and attorney's fees, and the tenant has a defense to eviction. You may still evict if the tenant is behind in rent, if the tenant's own lack of care mainly caused the code violation, or if code compliance or a public taking requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit and the city or town has met its relocation requirements. Separately, you may not evict, end the tenancy, raise rent or cut services because a tenant in good faith petitions to pay rent into court over lead hazards, or retaliate over enforcement of the lead laws, whether or not there is a written lease. While a code enforcement notice of violation, conference, hearing or appeal is pending you may not evict without just cause. The older trespass-and-possession chapter also requires judgment for a tenant whose tenancy was ended as a penalty for justified lawful acts. The rule covers every tenancy type.

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText:
Municipal ordinances and case law were not). If you give one, state it in the lease (the library's rent-concession clause does this) with its amount and the rental periods it covers, so the rent and what the tenant actually owes are clear.

Two statutes limit taking a concession back when a tenant leaves early. A servicemember who ends the lease under the military-orders rule can't be charged an early termination charge, and since July 1, 2026 a tenant who ends the lease because of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking owes no penalty, early-termination fee or future rent, only rent through the termination date or the move-out date, whichever is later. Clawing back a concession from either tenant risks being treated as the charge the statute forbids. Whether a general recapture-on-default term is an unenforceable penalty is a question for case law, so the library does not offer one.

title: No Rent Control or Rent Cap
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statewide rent control and no limit on how much you may raise the rent, and no state statute either authorizes or forbids local rent control. What state law does regulate is timing: you must give written notice of an increase at least 60 days before it takes effect, or 120 days for a month-to-month tenant over 62 (independent living, assisted living and congregate care facilities are excluded), and during a fixed term you can raise the rent only if the lease allows it. Two narrow rules can reach the amount. On leased land under a home owned by someone, the homeowner may send an excessive lot-rent increase to binding arbitration. And during a declared state of emergency, the price-gouging law bars unconscionably high prices for essential commodities, defined to include services; the statute doesn't say whether that reaches rent, so avoid sharp increases in a declared emergency area.

title: Raising Rent During the Term
bodyText:
No Rhode Island statute addresses a general lease term that raises the rent during a fixed term (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not), with one exception: a term making the tenant pay an increase in real estate tax levied during the term is void unless it states the tenant's exact percentage, limits the tenant to the unit's proportionate share of the increase and refunds a proportionate share of any abatement (see the tax-escalation clause).

Otherwise the act lets you and the tenant agree on rent terms that no law prohibits. Without such a term, the rent in a fixed-term lease stays the same until the term ends; the library's optional mid-term increase clause is the way to reserve one.

Any increase, scheduled or not, should get written notice at least 60 days before it takes effect, or 120 days for a month-to-month tenant over 62 (the statute excludes independent living, assisted living and congregate care facilities); the statute doesn't say whether an increase already written into the lease needs a separate notice, so send one.

Rhode Island's retaliation rule has no safe harbor for increases written into the lease: an increase in retaliation for the tenant complaining to a code agency or to you about repairs, joining a tenants' union or using another legal right is prohibited, and an increase within six months after such a complaint is presumed retaliatory, unless the complaint came after your notice of the increase. Raising rent in response to lead-law enforcement is also unlawful.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText:
Before any rent increase takes effect, give the tenant written notice at least 60 days ahead. For a month-to-month tenant over age 62, the notice must be at least 120 days. These periods apply to every kind of residential tenancy (week-to-week, month-to-month, year-to-year and fixed term), but not to independent living, assisted living or congregate care facilities. If a state or federal housing program sets a shorter notice period for the unit, the statute doesn't require more than that program's period.

Keep proof of when you delivered it. During a fixed term you also need a lease term allowing the increase (see the mid-term increase clause).

An increase in retaliation for the tenant complaining to a code agency or to you about repairs, joining a tenants' union or using another legal right is prohibited, and the tenant may defend an eviction and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. An increase within six months after such a complaint is presumed retaliatory, unless the tenant complained only after receiving notice of the increase.

title: Rent Installments and Partial Payments
bodyText:
Rhode Island lets you and the tenant agree on when and where rent is paid, so a lease may split the monthly rent into scheduled installments (the library's installment clause does this). If the lease says nothing, rent is due at the unit, at the start of each term for tenancies of a month or less, and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the start of each month, and it is apportioned day by day.

Partial payments are a separate thing: if the tenant pays only part of what is due, taking it doesn't waive the balance. But if you accept rent knowing of any default by the tenant, or accept performance that varies from the lease, you waive the right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days (you keep your other remedies for the default).

The nonpayment demand can be sent once any part of the rent that is due has been unpaid for 15 days, so a scheduled installment that goes unpaid starts its own 15 days from its due date. No statute says this about installments in so many words, so count from each installment's own due date and never send the demand before 15 full days have passed.

title: No Rent Receipt Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to give a receipt for rent, even rent paid in cash, or to keep a rent ledger for the tenant. Giving a written receipt for every cash payment, and a statement of payments when asked, is still good practice. Tenants who claim the state's property tax relief credit for renters must give the Division of Taxation reasonable proof of rent paid and your name and address, so expect requests for a year-end statement. Records also matter to you: a nonpayment demand must state the amount of rent 15 days in arrears, and if the tenant disputes it, your payment records are your proof. Check local ordinances, which we did not search.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to a credit bureau, regulates whether you report rent payments, or bars you from requiring a tenant to join a rent-reporting program. If you do report payment data, federal credit reporting law applies to what you furnish, so keep it accurate and correct disputed entries; we did not review that law here. Any fee you charge the tenant for a reporting service is a fee beyond the rent, so it must be listed in the lease's rent section with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); an undisclosed fee can be recovered by the tenant.

title: Sales and Hotel Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Rhode Island taxes rent only for living quarters in hotels, rooming houses and tourist camps; no statute names an ordinary apartment or house lease as taxable, but the rooming-house definition is broad. State sales tax (7%) applies to rentals of living quarters in hotels, rooming houses and tourist camps, but only on the first 30 consecutive days of each rental, and not where the occupant has a written lease of 12 months or more. A hotel includes a house, condo or apartment used or advertised for transient lodging of 30 days or less; a home rented under a documented arrangement for more than 30 consecutive days, or for a calendar month, is outside that definition. A rooming house is any structure held out as a place where living quarters are supplied for pay to transient or permanent guests or tenants, so if you rent rooms, or rent any unit on a lease shorter than 12 months, ask the Division of Taxation whether your rentals are taxable. If you do rent short-term, the hotel taxes also apply: a 2% local hotel tax, plus either the 5% state hotel tax or, for a whole house, condo or other dwelling rented in its entirety, the 5% whole-home short-term rental tax (since January 1, 2026). Short-term and vacation rentals are outside this library; talk to the Division of Taxation before offering one.

title: Bounced Checks and Returned Payments
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute capping a returned-payment fee you set in the lease, and none on failed electronic payments. If you charge one, it is a fee beyond rent, so state it with its amount in the lease's rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); a tenant can recover a fee you didn't disclose.

For a bounced check, draft or similar instrument, the dishonored-check law gives you a separate remedy: if it isn't paid within 10 days, you may send a notice of dishonor in the statutory form by certified mail, return receipt requested (or regular mail backed by an affidavit of mailing). If the tenant still hasn't paid 30 days after mailing, you may sue in district court, or under small-claims procedure, for the check amount, a $25 collection fee and three times the check amount (at least $200, at most $1,000). It is a defense that payment was stopped justifiably or the account was attached. Keep any fee separate from rent in a nonpayment demand.

title: No Government Shutdown Protection
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute gives tenants who are federal or state workers extra time to pay rent, protection from late fees or a defense to eviction during a government shutdown. The usual rules apply: once rent is 15 days in arrears you may send the five-day demand notice, and the tenant can cure by paying in full before you file suit (and in some cases at the hearing). Taking a partial payment doesn't waive the balance, so a written payment plan with an affected tenant can avoid the cost of an eviction without giving up your claim.

title: Rhode Island's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Rhode Island sets these money limits, whatever the lease says. Security deposit: no more than one month's rent, whatever you call it; for a furnished unit whose furniture is worth $5,000 or more, a separate furniture deposit of up to one more month's rent. Application fee: none; you may charge only the actual cost of a state criminal background check or credit report if the applicant hasn't supplied one issued within 90 days, and you must give them a copy. Payment method: no convenience fee on rent unless you also accept a fee-free way to pay. Attorney's fees: only as the landlord-tenant act allows. Early termination: no charge to a servicemember ending the lease under the military-orders rule, and since July 1, 2026 no fee, penalty or future rent for a tenant ending it because of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Lock change for such a tenant: no more than the community's customary price. Rhode Island caps neither rent, rent increases (60 days' notice, 120 for month-to-month tenants over 62) nor late fees, and a returned-check fee set in the lease has no cap; the dishonored-check law adds a $25 collection fee and $200 to $1,000 in damages after its notice process.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute bars or limits a late fee on the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays, and Rhode Island sets no late-fee cap for ordinary tenancies. Even so, charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share and only when the tenant's share is late; when a housing agency pays its share late, collect from the agency under your contract with it. Federal programs such as Housing Choice Vouchers have their own lease addenda and contract rules on fees and tenant rent, which we did not review; follow them where they apply. Units in the state's rental assistance program have their own rules: the tenant pays 30% of adjusted income, and you may end the tenancy only for serious or repeated lease violations, a violation of law or other good and substantial cause.

title: Passing On Real Estate Tax Increases
bodyText:
A Rhode Island lease may make the tenant pay part of a real estate tax increase during the term, but only if the clause expressly states three things: that the tenant pays only the share of the increase that the unit bears to the whole taxed property, the exact percentage the tenant pays, and that if you win a tax abatement on the whole property you will refund the tenant a proportionate share, less reasonable attorney's fees. A clause missing any of these is void.

If the percentage you set turns out to exceed the unit's true share, you must refund the excess with 5% interest a year from the date you collected it. The library's optional tax-increase clause meets these terms. Give the tenant written notice of each payment at least 60 days before it is due, since a pass-through may count as a rent increase, and list the charge in the lease's rent section with your other fees (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format).

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText: No Rhode Island landlord-tenant statute sets interest on unpaid rent or damages, and the library offers no lease interest clause. You don't need one: when a court awards you money damages, such as rent or the cost of repairing damage beyond the security deposit, the clerk adds interest at 12% a year from the date your claim arose, and the judgment then carries 12% a year until paid. That automatic prejudgment interest does not apply to a contract obligation where interest is already provided, so a lease clause with a lower rate could cost you interest. A higher contract rate raises usury questions: the usury cap (the greater of 21% or prime plus 9 points) is written for loans, and the statute doesn't say whether it reaches interest under a lease, so take advice before setting a high rate.

title: Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Rhode Island has no program or tax credit that pays landlords for renting to veterans; the state's veteran property-tax exemptions apply to a veteran's own home. Veteran and servicemember status are protected under Rhode Island's fair housing law: you may not ask about an applicant's honorable-discharge veteran status or service in the armed forces, refuse to rent because of it, treat the tenant differently in the terms of the tenancy, or run an ad that indicates a preference based on it. That last rule cuts both ways, so be careful advertising a veterans-only special; the statute doesn't say whether a voluntary veteran discount is allowed, so take advice first. Servicemembers also have a statutory right to end a lease on military orders.

title: Accepting Rent After a Breach
bodyText: If you accept rent knowing the tenant is in default, or accept performance that differs from the lease (for example, a payment made late or in a different way), you give up the right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give the tenant written notice within 10 days. The notice should say you are accepting the payment without waiving the breach. Accepting a partial payment never waives the unpaid balance, and acceptance never waives your other remedies, such as damages. Don't rely on a general no-waiver sentence in the lease to do this job: the act bars lease terms that take away tenants' rights under it, so send the 10-day notice each time. Once an eviction is under way, payments a tenant makes while execution is stayed or while an appeal is pending don't waive your right to possession or reinstate the tenancy.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require a move-in inspection, condition checklist, inventory or move-out walk-through, and the library's existing-condition clause is all the lease needs. Document the unit's condition anyway, with a dated checklist and photos signed by you and the tenant at move-in and again at move-out. At the end of the tenancy you may deduct from the deposit only for physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant's breach of their duties (plus unpaid rent and reasonable cleaning and trash disposal), itemized in a written notice delivered with any refund within 20 days after the latest of the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession or the tenant's giving you a forwarding address. If you withhold wrongly, the tenant can recover the amount due plus damages of twice the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney's fees, and a move-in record is your best evidence of what changed.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute lets a lease fix in advance the amounts you will take from the security deposit for cleaning, carpets or repairs, and the library does not offer such a schedule. What you may keep is set by statute: unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning expenses, reasonable trash disposal expenses, and the damage you actually suffered from the tenant's breach of their duties, other than ordinary wear and tear, each itemized in a written notice. A lease can't waive these limits. A preset charge is safe only if it is no more than the actual, reasonable cost when the tenancy ends, so itemize what you actually spent or would reasonably spend. Withholding more risks paying the tenant twice the amount wrongly withheld plus attorney's fees.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A security deposit refund you owe a former tenant but can't deliver, for example because the check was never cashed or the tenant can't be found, does not become yours. Rhode Island's unclaimed property act lists security deposits and refunds expressly. If you hold the money in the ordinary course of your rental business and it stays unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable, it is presumed abandoned, whether or not the tenant ever asked for it. You must then report it to the General Treasurer before November 1 each year, as of the previous June 30, and pay it over. For a refund of $50 or more, first send the tenant written notice at their last known address no more than 120 days before you file. Don't put a lease term saying an unclaimed deposit becomes yours: the deposit statute bars waivers. Keep records showing you sent the refund within 20 days.

title: Paying the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no right to pay the security deposit in installments, so you may require it in full before move-in. You may agree to installments; if you do, put the schedule in writing. Every installment is part of the security deposit: the total of all installments can't exceed one month's rent, whatever you call the payments, and at the end of the tenancy the refund and 20-day itemization rules apply to everything the tenant paid toward it.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses collecting the last month's rent in advance, or a tenant using the security deposit as the last month's rent. The act treats prepaid rent and the security deposit as separate things: a security deposit is money given at the start of the tenancy as a deposit against physical damage to the unit, capped at one month's rent however you label it, while prepaid rent is rent paid ahead of time. If you collect last month's rent up front, call it prepaid rent in the lease, apply it to the last month, and don't hold it back for damage; money that works as security could be counted toward the deposit cap. Prepaid rent must be returned when the tenancy ends early in the statute's listed cases: your failure to deliver possession, termination for your noncompliance, fire or casualty, unlawful ouster or cut-off of services, a servicemember's termination (within 30 days), and, since July 1, 2026, termination by a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Nothing in the act lets a tenant skip the last month's rent because you hold a deposit.

title: No Conditions on the Deposit Refund
bodyText: Rhode Island does not let you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, and the deposit statute bars lease terms that waive its rules. The refund clock starts on the latest of three dates: the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession, or the tenant's giving you a forwarding address for the refund. Within 20 days after that date, deliver the refund with a written itemized notice of any deductions. A tenant who hasn't given a forwarding address delays the deadline but doesn't lose the deposit. Failing to comply exposes you to twice the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees. A periodic tenant still owes you the statutory notice to end the tenancy, but that is a separate duty, and a missing notice can't forfeit the deposit. The deposit law lets you deduct unpaid accrued rent. Whether rent for the rest of a notice period the tenant didn't give counts as accrued rent isn't settled by statute, and court decisions weren't searched, so deduct only rent that had come due and gone unpaid, and pursue any other claim separately, which the deposit law allows.

title: Deposit After a Survivor Termination
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, a tenant who ends the lease early because they or a household member were a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking (with the written verification the statute requires) gets a deposit refund under the normal deposit rules, plus any rent prepaid for the period after termination, as long as they turn over full possession without damage. The tenant must move out within 30 days of the notice unless you agree on another time, and owes rent only through the termination date or the move-out date, whichever is later; you may deduct that unpaid rent and the usual deposit items. Within 20 days after the tenancy ends, give the tenant a full and specific written statement of the basis for keeping any of the deposit or prepaid rent, with any refund. The deposit deductions don't include fees, so don't deduct a lock-change fee. If co-tenants stay, the statute doesn't say when this tenant's tenancy concludes; get advice before holding the departing tenant's share. These rights can't be waived.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: Rhode Island has no expedited security deposit procedure. Your deadline is 20 days after the latest of the end of the tenancy, the tenant's delivery of possession, or the tenant's forwarding address, and you may always return the deposit sooner. You may not charge an administrative, processing or accounting fee for doing so, or deduct one from the deposit: the statute lists the only deductions (unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear), and a lease can't add to them.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute authorizes or regulates a monthly fee, surety bond or insurance product that a tenant pays instead of a security deposit, and the library does not offer one. If you use such a program, two rules apply. Any fee the tenant pays is a fee beyond rent, so it must be listed in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. And money that works as security for damage, whatever you call it, can count as a security deposit, which is capped at one month's rent in total. Deposit-replacement products sold by third parties may be insurance; check that the provider is properly licensed before offering one.

title: Holding Deposits
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses a holding deposit or other money taken from an applicant before the lease is signed. Two rules shape what is safe. You may not require an applicant to pay a rental application fee; you may charge only the actual cost of a state criminal background check or credit report the applicant doesn't supply. A nonrefundable payment to apply for or hold a unit risks being treated as the application fee the statute bans, so the library offers no holding-fee clause. If you take a refundable holding deposit, put in writing how long you will hold the unit and that you will refund it in full if you or the applicant don't go ahead. Once the lease is signed, money you keep as security counts toward the one-month deposit cap, and money applied to rent is rent.

title: No Inspection Notice Penalty
bodyText: Rhode Island has no inspection-notice duty, so there is no penalty, such as losing the right to deduct for damage, for not offering a move-in or move-out inspection or not telling the tenant about one. The deposit penalty that does apply is tied to the refund itself: if you don't deliver the itemized notice and any refund within 20 days after the latest of the end of the tenancy, delivery of possession or the tenant's forwarding address, or you withhold more than the law allows, the tenant can recover the amount due plus twice the amount wrongfully withheld and attorney's fees. Separately, where the unit's water service line is found to contain lead and you decline or don't respond to the tenant's request to replace it, then refuse or fail to respond within 60 days to a second request, the tenant may end the lease, and you can't withhold the deposit because the tenant used that right.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: Rhode Island has no notice procedure for a nonrefundable deposit, because the law leaves no room for one. Any money you take as security, whatever you call it, counts toward the one-month deposit cap, and at the end of the tenancy the tenant is owed the entire amount minus only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant's breach of their duties, itemized in writing within 20 days. A lease cannot waive these rules, and wrongfully keeping deposit money costs you the amount plus twice what you withheld and the tenant's attorney fees. A separately stated fee is a different thing: no statute bars a nonrefundable move-in or pet fee as such, but every fee beyond rent must be listed in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. You may not charge an application fee at all.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring a separate written notice, at the time you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. That is because no part of a Rhode Island security deposit can be made nonrefundable: whatever you call the money, it counts toward the one-month cap and must be returned within 20 days minus only the deductions the deposit law lists, and a lease cannot waive that. Don't hand a tenant a notice or receipt calling any part of a deposit nonrefundable. If you charge a separate fee, the notice that matters is in the lease itself: list every fee beyond rent in the rent section, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText:
You may not ask for or accept a security deposit of more than one month's rent. The limit covers every deposit together, whatever you call it (damage, pet, key or anything else, refundable or not), and a lease cannot waive it. The cap is stated in months, not rental periods, so for a week-to-week roomer it is a month's worth of rent, not one week's.

Two exceptions: if you rent a furnished unit whose furniture has a replacement value of $5,000 or more when the lease is signed, you may also take a separate furniture deposit of up to one month's rent; and a restoration escrow you negotiate with a tenant with a disability for a reasonable modification does not count toward the cap.

You may not charge a tenant with a disability extra, such as a pet deposit, for a guide dog or other trained personal assistive animal (the tenant remains liable for damage it causes); other assistance animals approved as a reasonable accommodation should not carry a pet deposit either (see the assistance-animal row).

When a tenant dies and an adult resident or live-in caregiver continues the tenancy for the post-death grace period, you may not require that person to pay an additional deposit. The statute does not say whether you may top up a deposit after a rent increase. Mobile home rentals by a licensed park have their own one-month limit.

title: Where to Keep the Deposit
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant act does not tell you where to keep a security deposit: it requires no escrow, trust or separate account, no particular bank, and no notice to the tenant of where the money is held. What it does require is that you return the full deposit, minus the listed deductions, within 20 days, and whoever owns the property when the tenancy ends is bound by that, so keeping the money separate and traceable is the sensible course. Three narrower rules apply. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson receives the deposit, it must go into the firm's escrow account at a federally insured institution in Rhode Island, kept apart from the broker's own funds. A mobile home park licensee renting a mobile home must keep deposits in an earmarked savings account. A restoration deposit you negotiate with a tenant with a disability for a reasonable modification goes into an interest-bearing escrow account, with the interest belonging to the tenant. Since June 19, 2026 a bank account may be set up as a 'special deposit' for tenant security deposits, but this is optional.

title: No Interest on Deposits
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to pay interest on a residential security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing account. At the end of the tenancy you owe back the amount the tenant gave you, minus the deductions the deposit law lists. Two exceptions. A mobile home park licensee that rents a mobile home and takes a security deposit must pay the resident 3% interest a year, annually or when the rental ends, and is liable for up to three times the interest due if it doesn't. And if you negotiate a restoration deposit with a tenant with a disability as a condition of a reasonable modification, it goes into an interest-bearing escrow account and the interest belongs to the tenant. A lease may promise interest if you choose, but nothing requires it.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: No Rhode Island lease may waive any part of the security deposit law: the one-month cap, the separate furniture deposit limit, the closed list of deductions, the 20-day itemized refund, the tenant's right to twice the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney fees, and the rule that a new owner is bound. A lease term that tries is unenforceable, so terms such as "the deposit is forfeited if Tenant leaves early", "a cleaning charge of $X will be deducted in every case" or "Tenant waives the 20-day deadline" won't hold. Using such a term can also cost you: if you deliberately use a lease containing provisions you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. You and a tenant can still agree after move-out on how a disputed deduction is settled.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: If you transfer your interest in a rented property, whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by Rhode Island's deposit rules, so a buyer should expect to owe the full refund and 20-day itemization even if the seller never handed the money over. No statute requires the seller to transfer deposits to the buyer, so transfer them, or credit them at closing, and tell the tenant who now holds the deposit. As seller, you are released from liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act only for events after you give the tenant written notice of a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, never earlier than the conveyance itself. The notice must give the buyer's name, address and telephone number and certify that you complied with the housing code rule requiring outstanding violations to be corrected, or violation notices passed to the buyer and the enforcing officer, before a sale. A departing manager is released the same way after written notice naming who takes over. In a building of four or fewer units, a buyer (other than a third-party bona fide purchaser) or a successor to a mortgagor takes title with the same duties to the tenant the seller had.

title: Penalty for Mishandling the Deposit
bodyText: If you don't return the deposit, minus only the deductions the law allows, with a written itemized notice within 20 days after the later of the end of the tenancy, the tenant's return of possession, or the tenant giving you a forwarding address, the tenant can sue for the amount due plus damages equal to twice the amount you wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney fees. So withholding $500 you weren't entitled to keep can cost you $1,500 plus the tenant's lawyer. The statute requires no showing of bad faith, and it can apply to a late or missing itemized notice, not only to an improper deduction. A lease term that waives any of this is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with terms you know are prohibited adds actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. You keep your own claims: if the damage exceeds the deposit, you may sue for the rest. Mobile home park licensees renting a mobile home face a different penalty: up to twice the deposit and three times the interest due.

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText:
When the tenancy ends, return the deposit with a written notice itemizing every deduction within 20 days after the latest of three dates: the end of the tenancy, the tenant's return of possession, or the tenant giving you a forwarding address for the refund. You may deduct only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal, and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant's breach of their maintenance duties.

A furniture deposit is returned on the same 20-day schedule, minus reasonable cleaning and repair and damage to the furniture beyond ordinary wear and tear.

Deliver the notice by hand or first-class mail to the address the tenant gave you, or their last known residence, and keep proof. Late or improper handling exposes you to twice the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney fees.

Special cases: if a tenant dies and an adult resident or caregiver continues under the post-death grace period, the balance goes to that person if the grace period runs more than one month and otherwise to the tenant's estate; and from July 1, 2026, a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking who ends the lease early under the survivor-termination law must get the refund and a full and specific statement of any amount kept within 20 days of the end of the tenancy, a clock that does not wait for a forwarding address.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits. Two limits still apply. Every deposit, however you label it, is capped at one month's rent (plus a separate furniture deposit of up to one month for furniture worth $5,000 or more). And Rhode Island's fair housing law bars discriminating in the terms or conditions of a rental, which includes the deposit you ask for, because of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, veteran or servicemember status, country of ancestral origin, disability, age, familial status, or a tenant's status as a victim of domestic abuse. Keep a written, neutral deposit policy and apply it the same way to everyone.

title: What the Deposit Can Cover
bodyText:
Rhode Island gives you a closed list of what you may keep from the deposit when the tenancy ends: unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning expenses, reasonable trash disposal expenses, and physical damage to the premises beyond ordinary wear and tear that you suffered because the tenant broke their maintenance duties. A lease cannot add to the list. Late fees, attorney's fees, utility charges and other fees are not on it, so pursue them separately rather than deducting them, unless a charge is genuinely rent for the use of the unit.

Ordinary wear and tear includes deterioration caused by your own failure to prepare for expected conditions or to meet your obligations. The statute speaks only of applying the deposit when the tenancy ends; it does not provide for drawing on it, or requiring the tenant to top it up, during the tenancy.

Special cases: during a post-death grace period you may deduct damage caused by the deceased tenant or the person continuing the tenancy; and if a tenant ends the lease because you refused, or failed to respond within 60 days to, a second request to replace a water service line found to contain lead, you may not withhold the deposit because of that termination.

title: No Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule for a separate utility deposit held by a landlord, and the library offers none. Money you hold to secure the tenant's payments is a security deposit however you label it, so a "utility deposit" counts toward the one-month cap together with the security deposit. At the end of the tenancy the deposit law lets you keep only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning, reasonable trash disposal and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear; unpaid utility charges the tenant owes you are not on that list unless they are part of the rent, so bill and collect them separately. If the tenant pays a utility company directly, any deposit the utility takes is between the tenant and the utility. Whatever the arrangement, the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which the tenant pays.

title: Alterations Tenants May Make Without Your Consent
bodyText:
Your lease may require your written consent before a tenant alters the unit, and a tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises.

But Rhode Island gives tenants some rights a lease can't take away. You may not refuse a tenant with a disability reasonable modifications, at the tenant's expense, needed for full enjoyment of the unit; where reasonable you may require restoration of the interior at move-out, and negotiate payments into an interest-bearing restoration escrow.

A tenant may have repairs costing under $500 a year done and deduct the cost from rent if you fail to fix a code, habitability, facilities, trash or water and heat problem within 20 days of written notice.

From July 1, 2026, if all tenants in possession (or a court order) ask you to change the locks because a tenant or adult household member reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking at the premises, and you don't within two business days, the tenant or household member may change them, in a workmanlike way with locks of similar or better quality (otherwise you may replace the lock or seek reimbursement).

In a multiple dwelling, a tenant may choose their own cable, phone or internet provider, which may install its facilities at no cost to you; you can't charge tenants differently for their choice. A tenant may take on alterations or remodeling only by a signed written agreement for adequate consideration, and never work needed to cure a code violation.

title: Who Handles Bed Bugs and Other Pests
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute specific to bed bugs. The state housing code divides responsibility for extermination of insects, rodents and other pests, and tenants must comply with code duties placed on them.

The tenant is responsible in a single-unit dwelling, and in a multi-unit building when theirs is the only unit infested. You are responsible when two or more units, or the shared or public areas, are infested, and whenever the infestation comes from your failure to keep the building rodent-proof or reasonably insect-proof. You must also keep the premises fit and habitable, and you may not rent out a vacant unit that isn't clean and sanitary.

A tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect and treat, but give at least two days' notice except in an emergency or where that's impracticable, and enter only at reasonable times.

A tenant who complains to code officials about a code violation affecting health and safety, such as an infestation, or complains to you that you aren't meeting your code and repair duties, is protected from retaliation, though you may still seek possession if the tenant's own lack of care mainly caused the violation or the tenant is behind on rent. Local codes may be stricter.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather. What the law does allow is a lease term requiring the tenant to notify you of any anticipated absence of more than ten days, no later than the first day of the absence; the library's extended-absence clause uses it, and it protects pipes in winter as well as at any other time. During an absence of more than seven days you may enter without the tenant's consent if reasonably necessary to protect the property, for example to keep heat on or check for frozen pipes. If the tenant has actually moved out, the abandonment rules apply instead.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: Rhode Island's housing code requires every dwelling unit and all public and common areas to have properly installed, working electric service, outlets and fixtures where power lines are within 300 feet, and every public hall must have at least one ceiling or wall light fixture, with switches placed so the area ahead can be lit. In a building with four or more units, every public hall and stairway must be lit, by daylight or electric light, at all times, to at least six footcandles at floor or tread level. In a building with three or fewer units, switch-controlled lighting that can be turned on when needed is enough. You must also keep all common areas clean and safe. No state statute addresses common-area lights wired to a tenant's meter, but the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which the tenant pays, so disclose any such arrangement there or the tenant may recover the undisclosed charges. Local codes may be stricter.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText:
In Rhode Island, when a tenant orders construction, alterations or repairs, the contractors' and suppliers' mechanic's liens reach the tenant's interest in the building and land, but not yours, unless you first gave written consent assenting to that work. That makes your written approval of a tenant's alteration risky: it may be the very consent that lets a contractor lien your property if the tenant doesn't pay.

Before approving work in writing, require proof that the tenant has paid or will pay the contractor, a lien waiver, or a separate written statement that you do not assent to liens on your interest; the library's optional no-liens clause adds a lease promise along those lines, but the statute doesn't say what effect such a promise has. A contractor dealing directly with a tenant must give the tenant a written notice of possible mechanic's lien before starting work, or lose its own lien right. Work you order yourself, including repairs you make on a tenant's request, can lien your interest in the ordinary way.

title: Enforcing Against Disturbances
bodyText:
Every Rhode Island tenant must behave, and make anyone on the premises with their consent behave, so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises; that duty applies whether or not the lease repeats it. The termination process below is open for a material breach of the lease, or for a breach of the statutory duty that materially affects health and safety, so keep the lease's no-disturbance term: it lets you act on a material disturbance that doesn't threaten health or safety.

To enforce it, give a written demand notice in the statutory form describing the conduct and what will cure it; if the tenant doesn't cure within 20 days of mailing, the tenancy ends on the date you name, at least 21 days after mailing, and you may file for eviction the next day.

If substantially the same disturbance recurs within six months of a good-faith notice, you may terminate on at least 20 days' written notice with no chance to cure.

For a seasonal tenant under a written lease within the statute's summer (May 1 to October 15) or academic-year (September 1 to June 1) windows with no renewal right, who has been charged with a municipal ordinance violation or has broken a lease term on excessive noise or disturbance of the peace, you may file for eviction immediately without a notice. You may also recover actual damages and seek an injunction, plus attorney's fees if the breach is willful.

title: Move-In Condition and Your Repair Duties
bodyText:
A tenant's signed acknowledgment that the unit is in good order is useful evidence, especially in a later deposit dispute, but in Rhode Island it cannot relieve you of your repair duties. You must comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable throughout the tenancy, and no lease may let you collect rent free of those obligations or have the tenant waive them. You may not rent out a vacant unit unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy and code-compliant.

Before signing any lease, tell the prospective tenant about any outstanding minimum housing code violations on the building, and note them in the lease's exceptions. If you are cited later, give each affected tenant a copy of the violation notice within 30 days unless you correct everything within that time. Rhode Island does not require a move-in inspection or checklist, but a dated, itemized condition record with photos is your best proof when you deduct for damage.

title: Tenant Absences
bodyText:
Rhode Island lets your lease require a tenant to tell you about any anticipated absence of more than ten days, no later than the first day of the absence; the library's extended-absence clause does this. The statute sets no penalty if the tenant doesn't, so the lease term is enforced like any other lease breach.

Separately, during any absence of more than seven days you may enter without the tenant's consent if it is reasonably necessary to protect the property, whether or not the tenant gave notice; otherwise you need the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold. Either way, give at least two days' notice unless there is an emergency or notice is impracticable, and enter only at reasonable times.

An absence is not abandonment. A unit is abandoned only when the tenant has left without notice, has no intention of returning, has not paid rent for more than 15 days and has removed substantially all possessions. Even then, send a certified letter, return receipt requested, saying you will re-rent unless the tenant replies within seven days, and then make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in your rental, and sets no lease conditions (such as insurance or liability terms) for one. Unless your lease says otherwise, a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling, so whether a child care business is allowed is up to the lease; say so expressly if you want to permit or forbid it. Recent zoning changes limit what cities and towns can do to licensed family child care providers, but they don't bind you as a landlord. If you permit child care, require the tenant to keep the state license in force and to carry liability insurance that covers it, and check your own insurance. Don't refuse or condition a rental because the applicant has children: familial status is protected under fair housing law.

title: No Home Business Right
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no statutory right to run a business from a rental, so the lease decides. By law a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unless you agree otherwise, so if you want to allow quiet home offices, remote work or a small business, or to forbid customer traffic, signage or stored inventory, say so in the lease. Zoning law treats remote work and home occupations as residential uses in many cases, but zoning rules bind towns, not your lease. Whatever you allow, the tenant still may not disturb neighbors, and you may want proof of business insurance if clients visit. Running a business can also trigger local licensing or zoning limits the tenant must meet.

title: Co-Tenants and Joint Liability
bodyText:
No Rhode Island statute sets general rules for co-tenants, so a lease term making everyone who signs jointly and severally liable is enforced as written: you may collect the full rent, or full damages, from any one of them.

Several statutes change the result in specific cases. From July 1, 2026, a tenant who ends the lease under the survivor-termination law because they or a household member are a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking owes rent only through the later of the termination date or the date they actually move out, even if they were jointly liable; you can still proceed in good faith against the remaining tenants without a retaliation claim. A servicemember's lawful termination also ends any obligation of the servicemember's dependents under the lease. When a tenant dies, past-due rent is a claim against the estate, and adults who elect to stay on for the post-death grace period are jointly and severally liable for the rent during that period.

title: Yard Work and Landscaping
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute assigns lawn, landscaping or irrigation work to either side. Grounds and areas held out for tenants generally are part of the premises, and you must keep all common areas clean and safe, so in a multi-unit building shared yards stay your responsibility. You may have a tenant take on yard work, but Rhode Island allows a tenant to perform specified maintenance tasks only under a writing signed by both of you, made in good faith and supported by adequate consideration; the work may not be something needed to bring the property into code compliance, and the arrangement may not reduce what you owe other tenants. Put the tasks in the signed lease or a signed addendum, list them specifically, and make the consideration clear (for example, that the rent reflects the tenant's yard work). Report leaks and watering problems promptly so you can meet your own repair duties.

title: Tenant Water Bills Can Become a Lien
bodyText: In Rhode Island, you as owner are liable for the water rates set by a city, town, fire district or water district for water furnished to your building, whether the owner or a tenant used it, and unpaid charges are a lien on the property collected the same way as real estate taxes. No statute lets a lease clause or a notice to the water supplier shift that liability to the tenant or keep the lien off your property. So if the tenant pays the water bill, watch for nonpayment (ask for proof of payment or arrange for the supplier to copy you on delinquency notices), and say in the lease that the tenant must pay the bill and reimburse you for any amount charged to you. Sewer, refuse and other district charges are often set by local or special acts with their own lien rules; check with your municipality. The lease must still disclose which utilities the tenant pays.

title: Occupancy Limits and Listing Occupants
bodyText:
Your lease may list who will live in the unit and require the tenant to tell you about new occupants.

Two sets of rules limit what you can do. The state housing code caps occupancy by floor space: at least 150 square feet of habitable room space for the first occupant and 130 for each additional one; each bedroom needs 70 square feet for the first sleeper and 50 for each additional one; usable closet space counts too. It also bars more than one family plus two unrelated occupants (guests and domestic employees aside), or one household of unrelated people, without a rooming house permit. You may not rent a unit for more occupants than the code allows.

Fair housing law bars limits based on familial status or other protected traits, so set any occupancy limit by space and safety, apply it to everyone, and don't use it to exclude families with children. Since July 1, 2026, a person living with the tenant as an authorized occupant is a household member with rights under the survivor-protection laws, so keep your occupant list current.

title: Acts the Law Bars Tenants From
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant act lists what every tenant must refrain from, whether or not the lease repeats it. A tenant may not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so; may not disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment, or let people there with the tenant's consent do so; may not use any part of the premises in a way that maintains a narcotics nuisance; may not use the premises or adjacent public property to manufacture, sell or deliver a controlled substance, or possess one there with intent to do so (schedule I or II); and may not commit a crime of violence on the premises or adjacent public property. For damage or disturbance you must generally give a 20-day cure notice before ending the tenancy, but a repeat of substantially the same breach within six months of that notice lets you terminate on 20 days' notice without a chance to cure, and for a seasonal tenant under the statute's summer or academic-year lease, an ordinance charge or a breach of the lease's occupancy or noise terms lets you file without notice. For the drug and violent-crime breaches, cure doesn't save the tenancy and you may file for eviction without a notice of noncompliance. You may also recover actual damages and, for willful breaches, attorney's fees.

title: No Special Remedy for Misuse of the Unit
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general statute giving you a special remedy when a tenant uses the property for a purpose other than the one the lease states (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Two old criminal-law sections are exceptions: a lease of a place used as a gambling house is void, and the occupant can be ejected after a demand for possession (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-19-23); and a tenant's use of the premises for a purpose the nuisance chapter lists (such as lewdness, assignation or prostitution, a house of ill fame, illegal gaming, or unlicensed liquor sales) annuls the lease and lets the owner re-enter without process of law (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-30-6; see the nuisance row). Take advice before relying on either, since the landlord-tenant act bars self-help and its eviction procedure may still apply. The act's default rule is that, unless you agree otherwise, a tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling, and a lease use restriction is enforced like any other term. If the misuse is a material breach of the lease, give the statutory 20-day cure notice; if the tenant doesn't stop, the tenancy ends on the date you name (at least 21 days after mailing) and you may file for eviction. A repeat of substantially the same breach within six months needs only 20 days' notice with no cure. Drug dealing, a narcotics nuisance or a crime of violence on the premises is different: those breaches can't be cured and you may file without a noncompliance notice. You may also recover actual damages and seek an injunction.

title: Smoking, Vaping and Cannabis Rules
bodyText:
Your lease may ban smoking and vaping of tobacco and cannabis anywhere on the property, and Rhode Island law already bans smoking, including electronic cigarettes, in lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multi-unit residential buildings with more than four units; those buildings must post "No smoking" signs. The units themselves, as private residences, are not covered by the smoke-free law, so a ban inside units comes only from your lease.

Cannabis has two limits. You may not prohibit a tenant from consuming cannabis by means other than smoking or vaping (edibles, for example), or from transferring cannabis without payment, as long as the tenant stays within the legal possession and transfer limits. And you may not refuse to rent to, or penalize, a medical marijuana cardholder solely for being a cardholder, although you may decline to lease, or to continue leasing, to a cardholder who cultivates, manufactures, processes, smokes or vaporizes medical marijuana in the unit.

title: Subletting and Assignment
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute on residential subletting or assignment, so the lease decides: you may require your prior written consent, in your sole discretion, and treat an unauthorized sublease as a breach, enforced through the usual 20-day cure notice. No statute requires you to be reasonable or to answer a sublet request within a set time. A tenant who does sublet becomes a landlord under the act toward the subtenant, with all of a landlord's duties, and stays liable to you unless you release them.

Short-term rentals add a state rule: no one may list a residence on a hosting platform for stays of up to 30 nights without the property's current state registration number, and the registration records whether the registrant owns or rents. A tenant who lists your unit without your consent breaches a lease ban, but the registration rule doesn't itself require your permission, so keep the lease ban explicit.

title: No Statutory Duty to Forward Legal Papers
bodyText: Rhode Island law does not require a tenant to tell you about, or hand over, papers in a lawsuit or other proceeding to recover the property, and it has no rule on a tenant attorning to (recognizing as landlord) someone who claims the property. If you want tenants to pass such papers along promptly, the duty has to come from the lease; the library's notice-of-proceedings clause does this. Keep your own address current with tenants (the act requires you to disclose who manages the property and who receives notices for you), so papers reach you directly, and watch for foreclosure postings at your buildings.

title: Tenant's Insurance and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute says whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renters insurance. You may require renters insurance, but only if the lease states the requirement (or, without a written lease, you tell the tenant in writing). Two rules limit how far you can go. Your repair and habitability duties stay with you: no lease may let you collect rent free of them, so you can't make a tenant's insurance claim a condition of repairs you owe. And a lease may not make the tenant indemnify you, or limit your liability, for liability that arises under law, so a clause shifting your own losses to the tenant's insurer through the tenant is unenforceable, and using a term you know is prohibited can cost up to three months' rent plus attorney's fees. For damage the tenant caused, you may recover your actual damages from the tenant, whom their insurer may then cover.

title: Shifting Repairs and Chores to the Tenant
bodyText:
Every tenant must keep the unit clean and safe and use its facilities reasonably, but the repair and habitability duties are yours. Rhode Island lets you and a tenant agree that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling only if the agreement is made in good faith, is in a writing signed by both of you, and is supported by adequate consideration; the work must not be something needed to bring the property up to the building and housing codes, and the deal must not reduce what you owe other tenants. There is no single-family exception. List the tasks specifically and state what the tenant gets for them.

If a tenant breaches their own maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety and doesn't fix it within 20 days after your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, have the work done properly and bill the actual and reasonable cost as rent on the next rent due date, or for immediate payment if the tenancy has ended.

title: Tenant Duties Set by Law
bodyText: Rhode Island puts these duties on every tenant, whether or not the lease repeats them: comply with building and housing code obligations primarily imposed on tenants that materially affect health and safety; keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as its condition permits; dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste cleanly and safely; keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits; and use electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, reasonably. The state housing code adds occupant duties, including: furnishing garbage containers in one- to three-family buildings (you supply them in buildings of four or more units); maintaining and replacing screens and storm doors and windows once installed for the season, unless you agree otherwise; replacing shades or other privacy devices you first installed; and extermination when the tenant's unit is the only one infested and you didn't cause it. Tenants must also not unreasonably refuse you access and, unless agreed otherwise, use the unit only as a dwelling. The acts a tenant must refrain from are covered separately.

title: Who Pays Which Utilities
bodyText:
Every Rhode Island lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which are the tenant's responsibility; with no written lease, give the tenant that information in writing. If you don't, the tenant can recover fees paid that weren't properly disclosed.

Whoever pays, you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, as the housing code requires, unless the building isn't required to have them or the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with a direct utility connection.

If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service that the lease or the law makes yours, the tenant may, after notice, buy the service and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages for reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing rent-free (and recover its cost up to one rental period's rent), plus attorney's fees. These remedies don't apply if the tenant or their household or guests caused the problem.

title: No Utility Cutoffs for Submetered Service
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special rules letting a landlord who submeters or bills tenants for electricity, gas or water interrupt the service for nonpayment.
