The general rules control: you may not interrupt, or cause the interruption of, heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or any other essential service, whether to recover possession or to collect a charge; a tenant whose service you willfully cut off may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. If a tenant doesn't pay a utility charge you bill under the lease, pursue it as a debt or a lease breach, not by shutting anything off. Two other rules matter if you meter electricity yourself: apartment buildings with more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977 may not use master meters for electricity, and each unit must have its own meter (publicly financed elderly or disabled housing may elect a single meter). And the lease must say which utilities are included in rent and which the tenant pays.

title: Keeping Utilities On
bodyText:
Neither side may cut off essential services as a pressure tactic. You may not interrupt, or cause the interruption of, heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential service to get a tenant out, and if you willfully or negligently fail to supply a service the lease or the law makes yours, the tenant may, after notice, buy it and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages, or move to substitute housing rent-free, plus attorney's fees.

If Woonsocket (under its ordinance) or the Narragansett Bay Commission shuts off, or is about to shut off, water for unpaid sewer fees, a tenant may pay those charges and deduct them from rent by giving you the receipt.

A lease term making the tenant keep the services in their name on and paid is a contract term you can enforce as a lease breach.

When service is in the tenant's name, the utility's own shutoff rules protect some households: a regulated electric, gas or water utility must follow Public Utilities Commission rules before terminating a household where all adults are 65 or older, or where a resident is disabled or seriously ill, and some low-income households have added protection. A utility may not refuse service to a new occupant because the previous occupant left without paying, unless the service benefits that previous occupant.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Rhode Island's smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules live in the state Fire Safety Code, not in the landlord-tenant act. The code is the national Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101), 2021 editions, as amended by the state Fire Safety Code Board's regulations. In one-, two- and three-family homes the code covers only smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and the statute requires three-family dwellings to have both. What a home needs depends on when it was built or converted: some older homes may use battery alarms, while newer ones need hardwired, interconnected alarms placed under the national alarm standard in effect when they were built. Three-family buildings also need interconnected smoke alarms on common stair landings, in common corridors and in common basements unless the building is sprinklered. Larger residential buildings are covered by the code's full requirements, including approved fire alarm systems where the code requires them. In one- to three-family homes you must keep the alarms working and fix an inoperable alarm within seven days after the tenant or an enforcement official notifies you by certified mail. If you don't, the tenant may have it fixed and deduct the reasonable cost from rent, up to $50 ($20 in a three-family building covered by the new-building rules), and you can still be fined. When you sell, the buyer must get a fire department certificate showing the alarms were inspected within 120 days before the sale; such certificates are valid for at least 120 days. Through the landlord-tenant act, you must comply with these codes as they affect health and safety, and tenants must meet any code duties placed on occupants. Ask your local fire marshal for the exact placement, power and testing rules for your building; the library does not restate the national standards.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute authorizes or caps a set fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, so the library does not offer one. The only tampering crime found covers public fire alarm apparatus, not alarms inside a home. A lease may forbid tampering and make the tenant responsible for the actual cost of repairing or replacing an alarm the tenant damaged or removed, and a tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises. Keep the remedy to actual cost: a fixed penalty beyond your real loss risks being unenforceable, and any fee beyond rent must be listed in the rent section of the lease (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). Your own duty to keep alarms code-compliant doesn't shift to the tenant.

title: Substitute Housing
bodyText: Rhode Island does not make you house a tenant elsewhere during ordinary repairs, after a fire, or during lead hazard work. Three rules still cost you money. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service the lease or the law makes yours, the tenant may, after notice, move to reasonable substitute housing for the period of your noncompliance, owes no rent for that period, and may recover its actual and reasonable cost up to one rental period's rent, plus attorney's fees (not if the tenant's household or guests caused the problem). If fire or casualty substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may vacate and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or stay in the usable part and pay reduced rent; you return the deposit and prepaid rent if the lease ends. And during lead hazard reduction you must make all reasonable efforts to keep occupants out, are not responsible for providing alternative housing, but must reduce the rent pro rata if occupants have to leave for three days or more.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: You must keep in good and safe working order every electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facility and appliance you supply or are required by law to supply. Appliances you don't supply, such as a tenant's own washer, are the tenant's responsibility. Rhode Island has no rule presuming that an appliance left in the unit is yours, so say clearly in the lease which appliances you supply and which you don't; an appliance you list as included is one you must maintain. The housing code requires every unit to have a working stove and refrigerator, among other basic kitchen and bathroom facilities, but a stove and refrigerator need not be installed while the unit is vacant if the incoming tenant is expected to provide them, as long as you provide the space and connections for them. A lease cannot excuse you from code-required facilities or let you collect rent free of your repair duties.

title: Heat Requirements
bodyText: Between October 1 and May 1 you must supply reasonable heat as the state housing code requires, or as a stricter local code requires. The code requires heating facilities, properly installed and kept in safe working condition, able to heat every habitable room, bathroom and toilet room to at least 68°F, measured 18 inches above the floor, under average winter conditions. Unvented flame space heaters are banned, except listed unvented portable oil (such as kerosene) heaters that meet the statute's labeling and safety standards; approved portable electric heaters are acceptable. The heat-supply duty does not apply where the building is not legally required to be equipped for heat, or where the unit's heat comes from equipment in the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct public utility connection. Even then you must keep heating equipment you supply in good and safe working order, and no agreement can make the tenant responsible for bringing heat up to code. Say in the lease who pays for heating fuel. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, the tenant may, after notice, buy reasonable heat and deduct the cost from rent, recover the drop in rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent meanwhile (recovering its cost up to one period's rent), plus attorney's fees, unless the tenant's household or guests caused the problem. Willfully cutting off heat lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Your Repair and Habitability Duties
bodyText:
Rhode Island puts the repair and habitability duties on you for every residential tenancy, with no single-family exception.

You must:
- comply with the building and housing codes affecting health and safety
- make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the unit fit and habitable
- keep common areas clean and safe
- keep in good and safe working order the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances (including elevators) that you supply or must supply
- provide trash receptacles as the housing code requires and arrange for removal
- supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times (the code's heated water is at least 120°F) and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1.

Where the code demands more than these general duties, the code controls.

You may not let a vacant unit unless it is clean, sanitary, fit for occupancy and code-compliant.

No lease, assignment, deed or mortgage can let anyone collect rent free of these duties, and a lease term waiving them is unenforceable (knowingly using one exposes you to up to three months' rent plus fees).

The only way to have a tenant do specified repairs is a good-faith written agreement signed by both of you (in the lease or an addendum) for adequate consideration, which can't cover work needed for code compliance or reduce what you owe other tenants. Tenants who aren't at fault have repair, rent and termination remedies if you fall short.

title: Rent Suspended Under a Code Repair Order
bodyText: If a city or town code officer designates your unit unfit for human habitation under the state housing code and orders it repaired, the tenant's duty to pay you rent is suspended, whatever the lease says, and the rent is paid instead into the city or town's housing revolving fund, which pays for code repairs. Where a city or town has adopted a minimum housing ordinance under the separate minimum housing standards chapter, the same happens when its code officer orders repairs because the dwelling is a serious hazard or imminent peril to the occupants: rent goes into an escrow account the officer sets up, is used to pay for the repairs, and any balance is paid to you when the work is done. While the tenant pays into that escrow you cannot sue for rent or for possession; if the tenant stops paying into it, you may sue, subject to the tenant's defenses. Separately, you may not evict without just cause while you have been served with a code notice of violation or while code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending. No lease term can change these rules. Ask the local code office which procedure and account your city or town uses.

title: Unfit or Placarded Units
bodyText: If a code officer finds your unit damaged, dilapidated, unsanitary, unsafe or vermin-infested, lacking light, ventilation or required heat and sanitary facilities, or in an unsafe location, and that the condition endangers the occupants or the public, the officer must designate it unfit for human habitation, placard it and, if occupied, order it vacated within no more than 30 days. Nobody may live there again until the officer approves in writing and removes the placard, and no one may deface or remove the placard. The officer may not vacate the building until the occupants have been offered decent, safe and sanitary housing; if the city or town relocates them, the cost is a debt you owe. If you are cited for minimum housing violations and the tenant has to move because the local code agency declares the property unfit, you owe the tenant's reasonable moving expenses unless it is determined you did not cause the violations. If you created an apartment by alterations you knew or should have known broke zoning or housing laws, you pay tenants' moving costs to a place in the same city or town. Once you have been served with a notice of violation or order, you may not lease the unit until you comply, unless you first give the new tenant a true copy and notify the code officer in writing. Rent is suspended while an unfit unit is under a repair order, and you may not evict without just cause during the code process. You may contest a designation before the code officer and the housing board of review.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Don't Repair
bodyText: If you breach the lease, or breach your maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, a Rhode Island tenant has several remedies. Termination: the tenant may give written notice naming the breach and a termination date at least 30 days after you receive it; the lease ends then unless you fix the breach within 20 days. If substantially the same breach recurs within six months, the tenant may end the lease on 14 days' written notice. You return the deposit and prepaid rent. Damages: the tenant may sue for actual damages and an injunction for any breach of the lease or your maintenance duties, plus attorney's fees if your breach was willful. Repair and deduct: for code, habitability, facility, trash or water and heat failures costing less than $500 in total per year to fix, the tenant may have the work done skillfully and to code and deduct the reasonable cost from rent after telling you in writing they intend to do so, if you don't fix it within 20 days or show ongoing good-faith efforts (in an emergency, if you can't be reached or don't act promptly), and must give you an itemized statement. Essential services: separate remedies apply when heat, water, hot water, electricity or gas fail. The tenant can also counterclaim in a rent or eviction case, and rent is suspended if a code officer orders an unfit unit repaired. If the unit is not compliant with the lead hazard law (for example, it has no valid certificate of conformance) or a licensed inspector finds lead hazards, the tenant may petition the district court to pay rent into the court's registry, whatever the lease says, until you comply (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-128.1-14(a), (c)), and you may not evict, end the tenancy, raise the rent or reduce services because the tenant in good faith seeks that remedy (§ 42-128.1-14(e)). The termination, repair-and-deduct and essential-services remedies don't apply to a condition the tenant, their family or their guests caused deliberately or negligently.

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: Rhode Island has no notice or other procedure that lets a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' repair remedies. The tenant's rights to end the lease, recover damages, repair and deduct, use the essential-services remedies and counterclaim in a rent or eviction case, and the rent suspension under a code repair order, apply however many units you own, and a lease cannot waive them. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's exclusions turn on the kind of occupancy, not portfolio size: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; a buyer occupying under a contract of sale; members in a fraternal or social organization's building; taxable transient hotel or motel stays; employees housed on condition of working on premises of more than 11 units; cooperative proprietary lessees; commercial lettings; and transitional housing. Even those arrangements come under the Act if the parties expressly agree. Do not add a small-landlord exemption notice to a Rhode Island lease.

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease cannot remove or water down your habitability duties. A term in which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, or excuses or limits your liability under the law, is unenforceable, and knowingly using a lease with such a term lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' rent and attorney's fees. No lease, assignment, deed or mortgage may let anyone collect rent free of the repair duties. What you can do is have the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only by a good-faith agreement in a writing you both sign, supported by adequate consideration (something of value for the tenant, such as reduced rent), that does not cover work needed to meet the building and housing codes and does not reduce what you owe other tenants. The duty itself stays yours: if the tenant doesn't do the agreed work and the unit falls below code, you are still answerable. The housing code itself lets a written owner-occupant agreement assign who puts up screens and storm doors and windows. A settlement in which a tenant gives up a claim can be refused enforcement if a court finds it unconscionable.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Rhode Island statutes create no presumption that you breached your habitability duties because of a code violation or a missing facility, and none presuming that you had notice or took too long to repair. A tenant who claims a breach must prove it, and the tenant-fault exceptions still apply. The one landlord-tenant presumption in the Act concerns retaliation: if a tenant complained to a code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, or complained to you about your repair duties, within six months before you raised rent, cut services or sued or threatened to sue for possession, the court presumes you retaliated unless evidence supports the opposite finding (not if the complaint came after notice of the increase or cut). Retaliation for joining a tenants' union or using other lawful remedies is also prohibited, but without the presumption. Keep records of repair requests and responses, since they decide both kinds of dispute.

title: No Required Fitness Statement
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require your lease to state that you will deliver the unit fit for habitation. The duty exists anyway: at the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the lease and with your repair and code duties, and throughout the tenancy you must keep the unit fit and habitable and up to the building and housing codes. You also may not let a vacant unit unless it is clean, sanitary, fit for human occupancy and code-compliant. A lease sentence promising a habitable unit is harmless, but a sentence saying the tenant accepts the unit as is, or that you make no promise about its condition, cannot excuse these duties and is unenforceable to that extent. The lease does have to carry other required disclosures, such as fees, included utilities, any renters-insurance requirement and your insurance declaration page.

title: Quiet Possession
bodyText: Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act contains no general covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession for tenants; its only 'peaceful enjoyment' language is the tenant's duty not to disturb the neighbors. The protections such a covenant gives come from specific sections instead. At the start of the term you must deliver possession in line with the lease and your repair duties. You may not take back possession yourself, by lockout, removal, or willfully interrupting heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, except after abandonment or surrender or as the Act allows. If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant or willfully cut such a service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. You may enter only on at least two days' notice and at reasonable times (except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable) and may not use entry to harass; an unlawful, unreasonable or harassing entry lets the tenant get an injunction or end the lease, with damages, costs and attorney's fees.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute aimed specifically at renting the same unit or room to two tenants. The failure-to-deliver-possession rules cover it. If you don't deliver possession at the start of the term, the tenant owes no rent until you do and may either end the lease on at least five days' written notice (you then return all prepaid rent and the deposit) or demand performance and sue you for possession. You may sue anyone wrongfully in possession. If a failure to deliver possession is willful and not in good faith, the person harmed may recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, so knowingly signing two leases for the same unit is costly.

title: How Tenants Must Give Repair Notice
bodyText: How a tenant tells you about a repair problem decides which remedies the tenant can use. To end the lease for your breach, the tenant must give you written notice naming the breach. To repair and deduct, the tenant must tell you they intend to fix the condition at your expense, and the 20-day period runs from written notice (in an emergency, the tenant may act if you can't be reached or don't act promptly). For heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant need only give you reasonable notice specifying the breach; the Act does not require it in writing. A repair complaint made to you in any form is protected against retaliation. Under the Act you have notice of a fact you actually know, were notified of, or have reason to know from the circumstances, and a notice reaches you when it comes to your attention or is handed to you or sent first-class mail to the address you hold out for notices. Your lease may ask tenants to report ordinary repairs in writing or through a portal, but that term cannot take away a remedy the Act grants on oral or reasonable notice, or excuse a condition you already know about, because lease terms waiving tenant remedies are unenforceable.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute that lets you name, in the lease, who must do repairs a tenant makes at your expense. The tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy (for problems costing under $500 a year to fix, after notice and 20 days) requires only that the work be done in a skilled manner and in compliance with state and local codes, and the tenant may deduct only the actual and reasonable cost or fair value. A lease clause forcing the tenant to use your contractor for that remedy would narrow a right the Act gives, so it risks being an unenforceable waiver, and knowingly using a prohibited term can cost up to three months' rent plus attorney's fees. You may list preferred vendors and an emergency repair number and ask the tenant to call them first, as long as the lease does not make that a condition of the remedy. When you do work after a tenant's own breach, it too must be done in a skilled manner.

title: No Repair-Cost Termination
bodyText: Rhode Island gives you no right to end a lease because a repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and a lease cannot create one by cutting back the tenant's rights. Your repair duties run for the whole tenancy; to end a periodic tenancy you give the ordinary termination notice, and a fixed-term lease runs to its end. After a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the statute gives the choice to the tenant: vacate and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stay in the usable part at reduced rent. If the lease ends you return the deposit and prepaid rent, and you may sue a tenant who caused the fire negligently or deliberately. The Act gives you no matching right to terminate after a casualty, so any landlord option to do so must come from the lease and must leave the tenant's own choices intact. Cost-against-value tests appear only in code enforcement: a code officer may make repairs at your expense when they cost no more than half the structure's fair market value, and may order an unfit, placarded and vacated building demolished if it does not warrant repair.

title: Promised Repairs
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule that your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit must be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. Promises you make still bind you. The rental agreement includes all agreements, written or oral, so an agreed repair or improvement is part of the lease; you must deliver possession in compliance with it, and if you don't keep the promise the tenant may recover damages and an injunction (with attorney's fees if your breach is willful), and may give you written notice ending the lease on a date at least 30 days after you receive it unless you fix the breach within 20 days. The tenant must allow reasonable access for agreed repairs. Put every promised repair or improvement in the lease or a signed addendum with a target date, so both sides know what was agreed and an entire-agreement clause doesn't leave a dispute about oral promises.

title: No Balcony Inspection Law
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to inspect balconies, decks, porches or other elevated exterior structures on a schedule, or to report on them. Your general duties still cover them: you must comply with the building and housing codes, keep the premises fit and habitable and keep common areas clean and safe, and the housing code requires floors, walls and other parts of the building to be kept in sound condition and good repair, exterior wood to be protected from decay, accessory structures to be structurally sound and in good repair, and all ways and means of egress to meet fire protection laws. Local building officials may run periodic inspections of existing buildings, and minimum housing ordinances may set standards for the condition and repair of stairs and porches, so check your city or town's code. A failing balcony or railing is the kind of condition that can lead to code orders, an unfit designation and tenant remedies, so inspect wooden balconies and railings yourself, especially in multi-unit buildings.

title: No Emergency Number Requirement
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule requiring a dedicated emergency repair phone number or on-call contact. What the law does require is that, at or before the start of the tenancy, you give the tenant in writing the name, address and number of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent authorized to accept service of process and notices, and keep that information current; a manager who fails to disclose becomes your agent for notices and for performing your duties under the lease and the Act. Give a number that works around the clock anyway: in an emergency a tenant may make limited repairs at your expense if you cannot be reached, and may use the essential-services remedies after giving you notice.

title: Tenant Choice of Cable and Internet Provider
bodyText: A tenant in a multiple dwelling may choose their own cable television, telephone, telecommunications or information service provider, free of restraints or conditions you impose. A provider may install facilities to serve a tenant's unit at no cost to you, must indemnify you for installation damage, may not interfere with the building's safety, functioning, appearance or use or with your reasonable rules (including reasonable access rules for soliciting), must review its plans with you first (you may waive that in writing), must honor reasonable installation requests, and maintains its own equipment. The provider has your consent once it delivers a copy of the statute and a signed statement agreeing to be bound. You may charge only a nominal $1 for permitting installation unless you notify the provider by certified mail within 20 days of learning of the planned installation, then state your claim in writing within 30 days and, if it is refused, sue in superior court within six months; you must show a specific alternative use of the space or a loss of rental or resale value. It is an unfair trade practice to charge tenants different rent or other charges based on their choice of service, or to take payment for installation outside this process. You and a provider may not agree to interfere with tenants' use of a master or individual antenna. Mobile home parks have a parallel rule.

title: No Utility Allowance Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on utility allowances, caps on the utilities you pay, or how you may pass utility costs through to tenants in ordinary residential rentals (Rhode Island's General Laws, the 2025-2026 public laws and the loaded regulations were searched; municipal ordinances and case law were not). Mobile home parks that resell electricity, gas or water may not charge residents more than the utility's rate, plus a return on metering costs. A lease may set the split, but two disclosure rules apply: the lease must say which utility costs are included in rent and which are the tenant's, and any fee beyond rent, such as an overage charge above a utility allowance, must be listed in the same section as the rent with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); an undisclosed fee can be recovered by the tenant. Separately, apartment buildings with more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977 may not use an electric master meter: each unit must have its own electric meter (publicly financed elderly or disabled housing may elect a single meter). Whatever you bill, you may not cut off a utility to collect it.

title: No Required Security Devices
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring particular security devices in rental units, such as deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or keyless locks, and no duty to rekey between tenants. Your general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes, keep the premises fit and habitable and keep common areas safe, and local codes may require more. From July 1, 2026 there is one lock rule you must follow. If all tenants in possession ask, or a court order is furnished, because a tenant or adult household member reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking at the premises, you must within two business days make a good-faith effort to change the unit's locks (and give the requester a key) or allow the tenant to change them. You may ask in good faith for written verification and charge no more than the reasonable price customarily charged for changing such locks in that community. If you don't act in time, the tenant may change the locks with locks of similar or better quality and must try to give you a key within two business days. Blocking a lawful change or failing to try to provide a key can cost two months' rent plus costs and attorney's fees, unless a court finds you acted in good faith. Rekeying at turnover is good practice, not a legal requirement.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You may not refuse reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give an occupant with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, such as a reserved accessible parking space, a change in rent-payment method or an exception to a no-pets rule for an assistance animal. You also may not refuse to let a person with a disability make, at their own expense, reasonable modifications to the premises that may be necessary for full enjoyment of them. For a rental, where it is reasonable you may condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. If needed to make sure restoration money will be there at the end of the tenancy, you may negotiate payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account, not exceeding the restoration cost; the interest belongs to the tenant. That restoration deposit does not count toward the one-month deposit cap, but the deposit return rules (itemized refund within 20 days, double damages for wrongful withholding) apply to it. Rhode Island does not require the lease itself to state your restoration right; put any restoration agreement in a separate signed writing. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property, and a disability does not shield a tenant from eviction for disturbing neighbors.

title: Receivership for Abandoned Buildings
bodyText: Rhode Island's receivership law targets abandoned buildings that have become public nuisances. A court infers abandonment from serious code violations posing a health or safety hazard together with facts such as vacancy, unmaintained grounds, an unsound interior, unrepaired vandalism and whether the owner has been collecting rents. If such a building is dangerous or violates the building codes or minimum housing standards, the city or town, a neighboring landowner within 200 feet, or a qualifying housing nonprofit may ask the court for an injunction ordering repairs. If the owner, given a reasonable chance, does not begin correcting a public nuisance, the court first offers the work to mortgagees and lienholders and may then appoint a receiver, a court-certified lawyer, who can take possession, manage the property, collect rents, lease units, evict tenants, make repairs and borrow against the property with a first-priority lien. Separately, after a second Department of Health notice of violation for unmet lead hazard reduction in a rental occupied by a pregnant woman or a child under six, the unit may be treated as abandoned and a public nuisance, and the department, the attorney general, a nonprofit or the city or town may ask for a receiver. Amendments effective June 18, 2026 narrowed the law: a property isn't abandoned just because it is vacant if it is maintained and the owner responds to health or safety issues, or if it is part of a documented, publicly financed redevelopment plan or under a valid purchase and sale agreement; an owner whose property is on the town's abandoned-properties list may cure the listed conditions within a reasonable time before abandonment can be alleged in court; a public nuisance must be documented, for example by code violation notices the owner didn't address in the time given, a condemnation or police reports; and the nonprofit must be one whose primary purpose is producing, preserving or repairing housing. A landlord who keeps an occupied building maintained and answers code notices is outside this law; ignoring repeated code orders is what brings it on.

title: Code Inspections of Rental Units
bodyText: City and town housing code officers may inspect rental units under an adopted inspection plan (including systematic inspection of designated neighborhoods), in response to a complaint, or when they have valid reason to believe the code is being violated. They may enter between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., or at another time by appointment. For a plan inspection, the owner or occupant in charge must give entry and free access once the officer shows proper identification, a copy of the relevant inspection plan and a schedule of the areas and facilities to be inspected; if entry is refused, the officer may get a court order on a showing of probable cause, and disobeying it is contempt. Information unrelated to the code that the officer learns is confidential. When an officer is repairing at your expense after a second violation notice, refusing or obstructing entry carries a $25 civil penalty each time. A lease cannot itself authorize an inspector to enter: your own right of entry is limited to the reasons the Act lists, with at least two days' notice except in emergencies, so arrange inspections with the tenant or through the officer's own powers. The statewide rental registry does not involve inspections. Some cities have their own rental licensing or inspection ordinances.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: If you maintain a swimming, wading or therapeutic pool for your tenants, it is a regulated pool unless it is an individual's own household pool used without charge and not in connection with a business run for profit. You need a Department of Health license before operating it (seasonal, June 1 to September 30, or year-round, expiring December 31); the department inspects before licensing and at least once a year, and its rules govern design, equipment, condition, maintenance and water testing. No lifeguard is required unless a swim club or a group of unsupervised children who may have access uses the pool. When no lifeguard is on duty you must limit access to guests and members by an attendant or a mechanical system, have a person trained in first aid in close proximity, post the required signs (NO LIFEGUARD ON DUTY — SWIM AT YOUR OWN RISK in red letters at least 4 inches high; no one under 18 unless accompanied by an adult; adults should not swim alone; pool hours; no glass; no running or rough housing; no diving; no animals or pets), and for an outdoor pool surround the pool area with a fence at least six feet high with a lockable gate or door. Condominium projects of 45 units or fewer need no lifeguard, but minors may use the pool only with a parent or other responsible adult. Whether a private pool at a single-family rental needs a license is not clear from the statute; ask the department.

title: Which Fire Code Applies
bodyText: When Rhode Island law refers to fire safety requirements, it means the Rhode Island Fire Safety Code: the National Fire Protection Association's Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101), with annexes, as amended and added to by rules of the Fire Safety Code Board of Appeal and Review. The code sets minimum fire safety requirements for new and existing buildings, but not for private dwellings occupied by one, two or three families, except that it sets smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm standards for those dwellings, and three-family dwellings must be equipped with both. For existing buildings, the local fire authority applies the parts of the codes written for existing structures, subject to board rules, variances and written modifications. Cities and towns may adopt stricter fire ordinances only with the board's approval, and may not set their own fire alarm requirements. These rules are part of your repair duty: you must comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety, which the Act defines to include any law, ordinance or regulation on a building's construction, maintenance, operation or occupancy, and the housing code requires egress, construction and equipment to meet fire protection laws. The board's rules, which fix the edition of each NFPA code in force, are regulations not reproduced in the General Laws; check them, and your local fire marshal, for a specific building.

title: After a Disaster
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special rules for tenancies after a declared disaster or an evacuation order: a disaster does not by itself end the lease, and no statute sets debris-removal or hazard-cleanup deadlines for landlords. The fire-or-casualty rule covers storm, flood and other disaster damage. If the damage substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may vacate immediately and end the lease by written notice to you within 14 days (the lease ends as of the date they left), or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stay and vacate only the unusable part, paying rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value. Rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty, and if the lease ends you return the deposit and prepaid rent. Your repair and code duties continue for any tenant who stays, including essential services, and if a code officer designates the unit unfit, rent is suspended under a repair order and the unit may be placarded and vacated. A lease cannot take these rights away. The rule for commercial and other estates that lets an occupant quit after destruction or condemnation does not apply to residential tenancies.

title: No Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island has no local health districts with their own rental-unit regulations, and no rule requiring you to give tenants health-department rental rules on request or to post a notice of occupants' rights. Rental health and safety is handled in two other ways. Each city or town's housing code officer enforces the state Housing Maintenance and Occupancy Code (and any local minimum housing ordinance), inspecting on complaint or under an inspection plan; the code's health officer is the state director of health. The state Department of Health runs the lead poisoning prevention rules and the statewide rental registry. You may not retaliate against a tenant who complains to a code enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, and a rent increase, service cut, or eviction filing or threat within six months after such a complaint is presumed retaliatory (unless the complaint came after your notice of the increase or cut). You may still sue for possession if the tenant is in default in rent, if the code violation was caused primarily by lack of reasonable care by the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, or if code compliance or other public action requires work that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit and the municipality has met its relocation requirements. Treat any such complaint as a repair request and respond in writing.

title: Facilities the Housing Code Requires
bodyText: Beyond the general repair duty, Rhode Island's housing code requires specific facilities in every rental, and you must keep in good and safe working order every facility and appliance you supply or must supply. Required items include: a kitchen with a sink with hot and cold running water, food-storage cabinets or shelves, a counter or table, and (unless the incoming tenant is to provide them) a stove and a refrigerator; a toilet and washbasin in a separate room and a bathtub or shower in a room affording privacy; heated water of at least 120°F; at least one window or skylight in every habitable room, sized at 10% of floor area with at least half openable, or approved ventilation; electric service with at least two outlets per habitable room (one per 60 square feet) and a light fixture in each bathroom, kitchen, laundry, furnace room and public hall; lighted public halls and stairways; dual egress for units above the first floor; screens on doors and ventilation windows during insect season, with self-closing outside screen doors; and rodent-proofing. You must provide and hang screens and storm doors and windows where the code requires them, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise in writing (once installed for a season the tenant maintains them), and shades on bedroom and bathroom windows (replacements are the tenant's). In buildings of four or more units you supply trash containers; in one- to three-family buildings the occupant does.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule on prorating rent for a subsidized tenant when part of the unit becomes unusable. The general fire-or-casualty rule applies to every tenancy: if continued occupancy is lawful, the tenant may vacate the unusable part and the tenant's liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the drop in the unit's fair rental value, or the tenant may vacate and end the lease by written notice within 14 days. The statute does not say how a reduction is split between the tenant's share and the subsidy payment. For public, federally subsidized or regulated housing, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies except where federal law preempts the subject or federal rights and duties directly conflict with it, in which case the federal rules control, so follow your housing assistance payments contract and program rules on abatement and inspections. Separately, if you set a minimum-income standard, it must be applied only to the tenant's portion of the rent, counting any rental assistance.

title: Habitability Rules Rhode Island Lacks
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Rhode Island counterpart. (1) No statutory list of imminently dangerous conditions: whether a condition is a serious hazard or imminent peril is decided case by case by local code officers, whose findings can lead to repair orders, an unfit designation, placarding and rent suspension. (2) Air conditioning is not named as an essential service. If you supply air conditioning you must keep it in good and safe working order, and the essential-services remedies cover heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas and other essential service without defining the last term. (3) No presumption that a code violation proves a breach, no required lease statement of fitness, no small-landlord exemption from tenant remedies, no landlord right to terminate instead of making a costly repair, no designated-repairer rule and no rule that repair promises be written. Each of these has its own explanation in the library. Local codes may add requirements.

title: No Rule on Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on splitting a shared utility bill among tenants. No law bans it, sets a formula (square footage, number of occupants or a ratio), makes a lease term charging for a utility that isn't separately metered unenforceable, or prescribes a disclosure form or lease attachment for it. If you split a shared bill, the general lease rules apply: the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which are the tenant's (with no written lease, tell the tenant in writing), and any charge beyond rent must be listed in the same section as the rent with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). A tenant can recover fees you didn't disclose that way. Electricity has one hard limit: an apartment house with more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977 may not use a master meter, and each unit must have its own electric meter (publicly financed housing for elderly or disabled residents may elect a single meter). City, town and district water charges stay your liability, and a lien on the property, whoever uses the water. You may not cut off service to collect a tenant's share.

title: Learning of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Rhode Island has no procedure for a tenant to authorize the utility to warn you before the tenant's own service is shut off, and no statute requiring a utility to copy a landlord on a tenant's shutoff notice. The general rule is that a public utility supplying heat, light, water or power may not shut off service for nonpayment without written notice at least 10 days before the shutoff date, to the user of the service or the building owner as recorded with the utility; when the account is the tenant's, expect the notice to go to the tenant. If you need to know, the lease may require the tenant to keep the services in the tenant's name on and paid, to show proof of payment on request, and to tell you promptly of any shutoff notice. You may also ask the utility whether it will copy you with the tenant's written consent; its own rules decide that. City, town and district water charges remain your liability and a lien on the property even when the tenant holds the account.

title: When the Utility Account Is Yours
bodyText: When a utility account serving your tenants is in your name, the risk of nonpayment is yours. A public utility supplying heat, light, water or power must give written notice at least 10 days before a shutoff for nonpayment, to the user or to the building owner as recorded with the utility. No Rhode Island statute requires it to warn each tenant or let tenants take over your account (at least one water district's own act requires mailed notice to occupants before it shuts off water for charges more than 60 days overdue). If the lease or the law makes a service yours (running water and reasonable hot water at all times; reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for them or the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection) and you willfully or negligently fail to supply it, the tenant may, after giving you reasonable notice, buy the service and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for lost rental value, or move to substitute housing, owe no rent meanwhile and recover its reasonable cost up to the amount of one period's rent, plus reasonable attorney's fees. These remedies do not apply if the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent deliberately or negligently caused the condition. If you willfully let service be cut off, the tenant may also recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Water charges billed to the building are also a lien on your property.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Rhode Island's shutoff rules bind utilities, not landlords, but they protect your tenants and govern your own house accounts. A public utility supplying heat, light, water or power must give written notice at least 10 days before shutting off service for nonpayment. State law fixes the winter moratorium period for residential electric and gas shutoffs at November 1 through May 1 (the Public Utilities Commission may extend it); who it protects is set by commission rules. All year: a utility must follow commission rules before shutting off electric, gas or water service to a household where every adult is 65 or older or anyone is disabled or seriously ill (a doctor's certification of serious illness puts the shutoff date at least three weeks out); a gas or electric company may not shut off a home where a child under two lives if the customer can't pay because of financial hardship and service wasn't shut off for nonpayment before the child's birth; and the main gas and electric companies may not shut off a household eligible for federal heating assistance (LIHEAP) that owes $300 or less and is no more than two months behind; the same subsection separately says service may not be terminated unless two termination notices have been sent. None of this cancels the debt. You may never cause a tenant's service to be cut off.

title: No Cutoff for Untransferred Utilities
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule letting you shut off utilities still in your name because the tenant didn't move the account into their own name. The lease may require the tenant to put named utilities in the tenant's name by a set date and to pay them, and failing to do so is a lease breach you can pursue (after a 20-day notice to cure for a material breach, or by charging the tenant what you paid if the lease says so). But don't let the service lapse: if you willfully interrupt, or cause the interruption of, heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, and you must return the deposit and prepaid rent. Heat from October 1 to May 1, running water and hot water are yours to supply anyway, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for them or the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection. A utility may not refuse a tenant service because a previous occupant left without paying, unless the service would benefit that occupant.

title: Survivor Lock Changes
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, if all tenants in possession ask, or someone gives you a court order, because a tenant or household member (an authorized occupant 18 or older, or an emancipated minor) reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking at the premises, you must, within two business days, make a good faith effort to change the unit's locks or let them change the locks in a workmanlike manner. If you change them, try to get the requester a key within the same two business days. You may ask in good faith for the written verification the survivor early-termination law accepts. If the threat comes from a tenant or household member, you may change the locks and refuse that person a key once the request comes with a valid protective order against them or another court order requiring the change. Your fee is capped at the reasonable price customarily charged locally for that lock change. If you don't act in two business days, the tenant may change the locks with locks of similar or better quality and must try to give you a key within two business days. Blocking the change, or not trying to give a key, costs two months' rent plus costs and attorneys' fees, unless a court finds you acted in good faith. A lease cannot waive these rules.

title: Entering the Unit in Rhode Island
bodyText:
Rhode Island's entry rule is consent-based. A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter, and enter only at reasonable times.

Without consent you may enter only in an emergency, or during a tenant absence of more than seven days if reasonably necessary to protect the property. You have no other right of access except under a court order, to do repair, replacement or cleaning work to fix a tenant's breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, after the tenant fails to fix it within 20 days of your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), or after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit.

Never abuse access or use it to harass. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order compelling access or terminate the rental agreement; if you enter unlawfully, enter in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated harassing demands, the tenant may get an injunction or terminate. Either way the winner may recover actual damages and must be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees. A lease term waiving these rules is unenforceable.

title: No No-Notice Service Entry
bodyText: Rhode Island has no rule letting a lease authorize entry without notice for regularly scheduled services such as pest control, filter changes or smoke alarm checks. Supplying necessary or agreed services is one of the purposes for which a tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry, but the general notice rule still applies: except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times. A lease term waiving that notice is unenforceable. If you run a recurring service, give the tenant a written schedule with the dates at least two days before each visit, and a fresh notice if a date changes; no statute says a schedule printed in the lease is enough on its own. Entry without consent is limited to emergencies and tenant absences of more than seven days where reasonably necessary to protect the property.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute aimed at smart locks, keypads, key fobs or app-based entry in residential rentals, and no rule requiring you to offer a physical key instead. The ordinary rules apply whatever the technology. Unlocking a unit remotely, or letting a vendor in with a code, is an entry: it needs the tenant's consent (which may not be unreasonably withheld for the listed purposes) and at least two days' notice except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, and you may not use access, or entry data, to harass the tenant. If a tenant or adult household member facing an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking asks under the survivor lock-change law, treat resetting codes and deleting the other person's credentials as changing the locks, within the same two business days. Any charge for fobs, cards or code resets is a fee beyond rent that must be listed in the lease's rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format).

title: No Procedure for Belongings Left Behind
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute on storing, selling or disposing of belongings a tenant leaves behind after moving out or abandoning the unit: no notice form, no storage period and no value threshold. The law defines abandonment (the tenant left without notice and does not intend to return, shown by rent unpaid for more than 15 days and removal of substantially all possessions) and lets you retake an abandoned or surrendered unit without going to court, but you have no lien on the tenant's household goods and may not seize them for rent. So belongings left behind stay the tenant's until a court or general property law says otherwise.

Before disposing of anything, send written notice to the tenant's forwarding or last known address describing the items and giving a reasonable date to collect them, and keep records; the library's optional abandoned-property clause sets that procedure in the lease. A lease term excusing you from liability for the property is unenforceable.

After an eviction, property removed under the execution is released to the tenant only after the tenant pays the moving costs and any prepaid storage charges.

title: Abandonment and Re-Renting
bodyText:
A unit is abandoned in Rhode Island when the tenant has left without notice and does not intend to return, shown by rent unpaid for more than 15 days and removal of substantially all possessions. When that happens, send a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the tenant's last known address saying that unless you hear from the tenant within seven days you will re-rent.

If the letter comes back undeliverable or the tenant doesn't contact you within seven days, you must make reasonable efforts to rent the unit at a fair rental. If you re-rent for a term starting before the old lease would have ended, the old tenancy ends when the new one starts. If you don't make reasonable efforts to re-rent, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment, so expect no rent claim after that date.

More broadly, the act puts a duty to mitigate damages on any party claiming them, so a lease term making the tenant owe the rest of the term's rent whether or not you re-rent will not override it. After termination you may claim reasonable use and occupation, actual damages for the breach and reasonable attorney's fees. Unless the unit meets the abandonment test, don't retake it without a court order.

title: Attorney's Fees in Rhode Island
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney's fees in a way inconsistent with the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using it lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Your fee rights come from the act. You may recover reasonable attorney's fees in a nonpayment eviction only if the tenant received a five-day demand notice in the six months before you filed and the nonpayment was willful; for willful lease noncompliance; for a willful, bad-faith holdover; when the tenant's defense or counterclaim is frivolous; and, in an access dispute, as the winning party (the court must award them). The act also lists attorney's fees among your claims after a lease is terminated; for unpaid rent, assume the narrower nonpayment rule controls. Tenants recover fees for wrongful deposit withholding, your willful noncompliance, willful failure to deliver possession, failure to supply essential services, lockouts and service shutoffs, retaliation, access abuse, and blocked survivor lock changes. Outside the act, a court may award fees to the winner of a contract suit only after a default judgment or where the loser raised no justiciable issue. No statute makes a fee clause reciprocal.

title: After a Fire or Casualty
bodyText:
If fire or another casualty damages the unit or premises so that the tenant's enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may either (1) move out immediately and, within 14 days after leaving, notify you in writing of the intent to end the lease, which then ends on the date of vacating, and you must return the security deposit (less lawful deductions) and all prepaid rent; or (2) if continued occupancy is lawful, stop using the part of the unit made unusable and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value. Either way, rent is accounted as of the date of the fire or casualty.

These options apply whatever caused the damage; if the tenant caused it negligently or deliberately, your remedy is a damages lawsuit.

The act gives you no right of your own to end the lease after a casualty and sets no repair deadline or belongings-retrieval rule; a landlord termination option exists only if the lease provides one (the library's optional casualty-termination clause), and the lease cannot cut down the tenant's options. The fire-and-storm surrender statute in the commercial leasing chapter does not apply to residential tenancies under the act. For a tenant who stays, your duty to repair and keep the unit fit and habitable continues.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: If you, as declarant, or anyone in the business of selling real estate for its own account will offer units in a condominium that includes a building now rented to residential tenants, each residential tenant and subtenant in possession must get notice of the conversion, with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before they must move out; a tenant who has lived in the unit 10 years or more or is 62 or older gets one year. Hand-deliver the notice to the unit or mail it prepaid to the unit or another address the tenant gave, and describe the tenants' rights. During the notice period rent may not rise, the tenancy terms may not change, and no one may be made to leave on less notice except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants. Conversion never lets you end a lease early. For 60 days after the notice (180 days for the long-term or 62-plus tenants) you must offer each residential unit to its tenant; if the tenant doesn't buy, you may not offer it to others on better terms for the next 180 days. A tenant current on lease obligations may cancel the lease without penalty. Pay reasonable moving costs within 50 miles for tenants who are disabled or 62 or older. Missing notice is a defense to eviction. No statement about conversion is required in the lease itself. Time-share conversions follow nearly the same rules, except that the notice need not come with a public offering statement and the moving-cost duty covers only tenants 62 or older, not disabled tenants under 62.

title: Notice and Cure Before Eviction
bodyText:
Rhode Island has two notice-and-cure tracks.

Unpaid rent: once any part of the rent is 15 days in arrears, mail the statutory five-day demand; you may file no earlier than the sixth day after mailing. The tenant may cure by paying the full rent owed before you file, and may also cure at the hearing by paying all arrears plus court costs, unless the tenant received an earlier demand notice (before the one for this case) in the six months before you filed.

Other breaches: for a material noncompliance with the lease, or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, deliver a written notice in the statutory form stating the breach, what will remedy it (acts, repairs or payment of damages), and that the lease will end on a date at least 21 days after mailing unless the tenant remedies it within 20 days of mailing. If the tenant remedies it in time, the lease continues; if not, you may file the day after the termination date.

There is no cure and no notice for maintaining a narcotics nuisance, drug manufacture or dealing, or a crime of violence, or for a qualifying seasonal tenant charged with an ordinance violation or breaching occupancy or noise terms.

If substantially the same breach recurs within six months of a good-faith notice, you may end the lease on 20 days' written notice with no chance to cure. Your lease cannot shorten any of this.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Addenda
bodyText:
No Rhode Island statute requires, authorizes or regulates a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, so one is an ordinary lease term (a federally assisted property may have its own program addendum).

The law already supplies the core: a tenant must not maintain a narcotics nuisance, manufacture, sell or deliver controlled substances on or next to the premises, possess schedule I or II drugs there with intent to sell, or commit a crime of violence there, and for those breaches you may file for eviction without a cure notice. The library's optional criminal-activity clause states those duties.

Two limits matter for any addendum: you may not prohibit a tenant's consumption of cannabis by non-smoked or non-vaporized means, or transfer of cannabis without payment, within the legal limits (you may ban smoking and vaping); and you may not treat a tenant as in breach because they or a household member are a victim of domestic abuse.

If you run a recovery residence (sober home), it must be registered with the state behavioral health department and follow the national recovery-residence certification process from January 1, 2027, and zoning must treat a certified recovery residence as a residential use.

title: Protections for Domestic Abuse Victims
bodyText: Rhode Island's fair housing law protects tenants and applicants who are, have been or are threatened with being victims of domestic abuse, and those who have sought or obtained a court restraining order for protection from domestic abuse, and the protection covers household members' status too. You may not ask about that status, refuse to rent because of it, or treat the tenant differently in the terms, conditions or privileges of the tenancy, which includes ending or refusing to renew a tenancy because of it. The law keeps one exception: you may still evict a tenant who fails to conduct themselves, and to make others on the premises with their consent conduct themselves, so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. Since July 1, 2026, you also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended a lease under the survivor early-termination law or asked for a survivor lock change (nor may a housing subsidy provider deny assistance on that basis), and if a survivor ends their lease you may, in good faith, bring an action against a remaining tenant, co-tenant or household member without facing a retaliation claim. No statute creates a separate eviction defense for victims or a special procedure to remove only the abuser, though a court protective order may itself order the abuser to vacate the household unless the abuser holds sole legal interest in it; use the ordinary eviction process against the person in breach.

title: Survivor Early Lease Termination
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, a tenant may end a lease early, with no penalty, early-termination fee or liability for future rent, if the tenant or a household member was a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking within the last 150 days, or if within the last 150 days an event tied to past abuse makes the victim fear for their safety. The tenant must give you written verification (see the qualifying-documents row) and must move out within 30 days of giving notice, or at another time you both agree. A tenant liable for rent under the lease owes it only through the termination date or the move-out date, whichever is later. If full possession is returned without damage, the tenant gets the deposit under the normal deposit rules and any rent prepaid for later periods, with a full and specific written statement within 20 days after the tenancy ends. The statute does not say whether co-tenants who stay remain bound; you may, in good faith, act against a remaining tenant, co-tenant or household member without a retaliation claim. Keep the verification and the household's personal information strictly confidential. Domestic violence here includes, without being limited to, listed crimes between family or household members; abuse is any act or failure to act that presents an imminent risk of serious harm to someone, whoever commits it, and includes listed crimes such as sexual assault, stalking and trafficking, whether or not reported to police. You may not refuse to rent to someone for having used this right, and a lease cannot waive it.

title: Survivor Verification Documents
bodyText: To use Rhode Island's survivor early-termination right (from July 1, 2026), the tenant or the household member who is the victim gives you written verification of one of these: (1) that they have obtained a valid protective order against the perpetrator; (2) that they have started a legal action for a protective order; (3) that they reported the abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking to a law enforcement agency; or (4) a written statement from a law enforcement official, attorney, healthcare provider, social worker, mental health counselor, therapist, domestic violence advocate, sexual assault advocate, child abuse advocate, or other victim's advocate at a nonprofit, college, university or state agency, that the tenant or household member is a victim. Any one is enough; the statute prescribes no form and does not let you demand more. For a survivor lock change you may ask, in good faith, for the same verification; if the threat comes from a tenant or household member and you are to deny that person a key, the request must come with a copy of a valid protective order against them or another court order requiring the lock change. Keep the verification, the fact of victim status and the household's personal details (address, Social Security number, email, phone, birthdate) strictly confidential, disclosing them only with the victim's written consent or as law requires.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute saying what happens to a lease, or to the rent, when the government takes all or part of the property by eminent domain, and none lets the condemnation court cancel a lease. Your lease and court decisions control, so if you want the lease to end, or the rent to drop, on a taking, say so in the lease and say how any award is split. In proceedings by a housing authority, a person with an estate or interest in the property, which can include a tenant, counts as an owner for valuing the taking. Displaced tenants may be entitled to relocation payments from the acquiring agency under the state and municipal relocation laws, which bind the agency, not you. If a taking or other public action requires work that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit, you may bring an eviction action even within the retaliation window, but only once the municipality's relocation requirements have been met.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination
bodyText: Rhode Island gives you no statutory right to end a lease because a sudden environmental or public health event, or a government order, makes occupancy impossible or unlawful, and no statute lets a lease create one with special effect. What the law does provide runs mostly to the tenant: after fire or other casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease or stay in the usable part at reduced rent, and the housing code's rules on condemned or unfit premises and rent suspension apply when a code officer acts. If you want the lease to end when the unit can't lawfully be occupied, say so in the lease, and still recover possession only through the courts or after a surrender; you may never lock out the tenant or cut services to force them out. A lease term cannot reduce the tenant's own casualty rights.

title: No Hardship Stay Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute giving an evicted tenant a hardship stay, such as extra months to move because of age, disability, children, winter or difficulty finding housing, and no criteria for one. After a judgment for possession, no execution may issue for five days, and if no appeal is claimed and the judgment is unpaid it issues on the sixth day after judgment. A court may still stay execution in its discretion (for example while a motion to vacate the judgment is pending, or on motion for cause shown), and an appeal stops execution. But any stay, by court order or by law, must be conditioned on the tenant paying you amounts equal to the rent, when rent would be due; taking those payments does not waive your right to possession or reinstate the tenancy, and missed payments let you ask for the execution. Court-ordered stays depend on the judge and the case.

title: How a Rhode Island Eviction Works
bodyText: You may recover a Rhode Island rental only through a court eviction (or after abandonment or surrender). Start with the right notice: the five-day demand for unpaid rent, the 20-day cure notice for other breaches, or the periodic termination notice; a fixed term that has ended needs none. To file for nonpayment you must show the court that you are registered with the Department of Health rental registry (with a lead certificate of conformance or exemption for a pre-1978 unit). Nonpayment cases get a hearing date on the summons; other cases give the tenant 20 days to answer. In a nonpayment case the tenant may counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court; if discovery delays the hearing, the court may order interim rent. After judgment no execution issues for five days; if there is no appeal and the judgment is unpaid, it issues on the sixth day to a sheriff or certified constable and lasts one year. Either side may appeal to the superior court within five days; from January 1, 2027 that period counts weekends and holidays and the appellant pays a $75 filing fee instead of costs and a $50 attorney's fee. During a stay or appeal the tenant must keep paying amounts equal to the rent, or you may move for the execution. A tenant may later move to seal a resolved case.

title: Sealing Eviction Records
bodyText: Since January 1, 2024, any party to a Rhode Island eviction case for nonpayment, lease noncompliance or holdover may ask the court to seal the case file, by motion filed at least 30 days after the appeal period has run following the end of the case. The court must grant it if the case was dismissed on a motion to dismiss, was resolved by a stipulation whose terms both sides have satisfied, ended with any money judgment against the moving party paid in full, or was dismissed for lack of prosecution after five years, and if the moving party notified every other party of the motion and has made no other sealing request in the previous five years. Each party may ask once every five years. Expect to receive notice of a tenant's motion; you may respond, but the statute leaves the court no discretion once those findings are made. The statute does not say how a sealed record may be used in tenant screening, and no Rhode Island law requires automatic removal of eviction records from public indexes; the Supreme Court's public-access rules do not list eviction cases.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: Rhode Island does not provide for a lease naming someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant, and for nonpayment cases a lease designation would not help. In a nonpayment eviction the statute fixes service: on filing day you mail the summons, complaint and a blank answer to the tenant by first-class mail, and a sheriff or constable serves them by handing them to the tenant, leaving them at the unit with a person of suitable age and discretion living there, or, if no one is found, posting them on the unit door, at least five days before the hearing. In noncompliance and holdover evictions the statutory summons form lets the officer serve an agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service, as the court's service rule also allows, so a tenant's own written appointment could be used there; the rule doesn't say whether a lease clause signed at move-in counts as that appointment. A tenant who is not a Rhode Island resident may designate an in-state agent for service in a writing filed with the secretary of state; if none is designated, service may be made on the secretary of state with a copy mailed by registered or certified mail. The library offers no clause naming an agent.

title: Evictions for Drug or Violent Crime
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no fast-track court procedure for evictions based on drug or violent crime, and no statute lets a tenant organization, prosecutor, neighbor or the Attorney General bring an eviction against your tenant.

What the law does give you is a shortcut at the notice stage: if the tenant maintains a narcotics nuisance, manufactures, sells or delivers controlled substances (or possesses schedule I or II drugs with intent to do so) on the premises or adjacent public property, or commits a crime of violence there, you need not send a noncompliance notice or allow a cure, and may immediately file a complaint for eviction for reason other than nonpayment. The tenant still has the usual 20 days after service to answer, and the case is heard under the court's ordinary rules.

Separately, it is a crime to knowingly let property you own or control be used as a drug nuisance (a place used for the unlawful sale, use or keeping of controlled substances), and the older common-nuisance laws (prostitution, illegal gaming, disorderly houses, unlicensed liquor) make it a crime to let premises for those uses or knowingly permit them, let the Attorney General or a citizen sue to abate them, and say that such use annuls the lease; even then, recover possession through the eviction process, not self-help.

title: When Rhode Island Requires a Reason to Evict
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general just-cause eviction law.
