You may let a fixed-term lease end, or end a periodic tenancy with the statutory notice, without giving a reason, as long as the real reason is not retaliation or discrimination (including against a victim of domestic abuse). Cause is required only in these settings. (1) A foreclosing lender or other foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units may evict a bona fide tenant only for the statute's just causes, unless the owner is exempt (see the foreclosure row). The other grounds are a signed purchase-and-sale agreement with a bona fide third-party buyer whom the owner has told it may have to evict the occupants, and, in FHA-insured housing, HUD's denial of a tenant's request for an occupied conveyance or the tenant's failure to request continued occupancy by the deadline in the owner's notice of pending acquisition. (2) While housing-code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending, or once you have been served with a notice of violation, you may not evict occupants without just cause. (3) During a condominium or time-share conversion, no tenant may be made to leave on less than 120 days' notice (one year for a tenant of 10 years or aged 62 or older) except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants. (4) A mobile or manufactured home park owner may end a lot tenancy only for listed reasons (nonpayment, law or park-rule violations after notice and a chance to comply, damage, repeated disturbance, or condemnation or change of use) and on at least 60 days' written notice (30 days for nonpayment). No statute ties cause to how long a tenant has lived there. Public housing authority and assisted living tenancies have their own rules, not covered here.

title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: If your mortgage is 120 days delinquent, you must tell your tenants that the property may be foreclosed; they must keep paying you rent until a foreclosure happens. Before a foreclosure sale, your lender must mail each bona fide tenant (it may address it to "Occupant") a notice of the sale date, time and place, telling them to keep paying rent and that it is not an eviction notice. After foreclosure of a building with four or fewer units, a foreclosing lender, servicer, institutional mortgagee, Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac (unless exempt as a Rhode Island-headquartered full-service lender or one with fewer than 15 Rhode Island foreclosures the prior year) may evict a bona fide tenant only for just cause: unpaid rent after written notice of the amount and payee, an uncured material breach, nuisance or substantial damage, illegal use, refusing a like renewal or reasonable access, or code-driven board-up, demolition or repair. It may also evict once a bona fide third-party buyer has signed a binding purchase-and-sale agreement and been told it may have to evict the occupants, or, in FHA-insured housing, once HUD denies a tenant's request for an occupied conveyance or the tenant fails to request continued occupancy by the deadline in the notice of pending acquisition. Within 30 days it must post and deliver a notice giving its contacts, where to pay rent and a continued-occupancy form to return within 30 days. A tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant isn't the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, it was at arm's length, and the rent is near market or subsidized. A tenant may knowingly waive these protections for consideration.

title: Lease Guarantors
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute specific to lease guaranties or co-signers. A guarantor's promise to answer for the tenant's debt is enforceable only if it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor or someone the guarantor authorized. No statute limits a guarantor to the original term, or requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, so whether a guarantor stays liable after a renewal, an extension, a switch to month-to-month or a rent increase depends on what the guaranty says and on contract law; say it expressly in the guaranty. If a guarantor gives you money to secure the tenant's obligations, treat it as part of the security deposit, which may not exceed one month's periodic rent however it is labeled. If you require a guarantor because an applicant's income falls below your minimum, the income standard must be based only on the tenant's share of the rent after any rental assistance or subsidy.

title: No Premium Holdover Charge Offered
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute that sets or caps a holdover rate, so a lease could try to set a daily or premium charge for a tenant who stays after the lease ends. The library does not offer one.

The law already gives you a strong remedy: if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may recover, besides possession, not more than three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees; and after the lease ends you may claim a reasonable sum for use and occupation plus actual damages.

A fixed premium rate risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty, and any agreed holdover charge would be a fee beyond rent that the lease must list in the rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format).

If you consent to a tenant staying on without agreeing a new term, the tenancy becomes week-to-week if the tenant pays weekly and otherwise month-to-month; the statute doesn't say whether accepting rent counts as that consent, but payments equal to rent that you accept while execution of an eviction judgment is stayed do not reinstate the tenancy.

Separately, accepting rent with knowledge of a tenant's default waives your right to terminate for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days; if you take money from a tenant who stays after the lease ends, reserve your rights in writing within 10 days. A landlord may add a holdover-rate clause of its own after taking advice.

title: No Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the protections that keep property from being taken to pay a judgment, and none expressly barring such a waiver; the library offers no waiver clause, and you should not add one. When you collect a judgment for rent or damages, the tenant keeps the statutory exemptions, including household furniture, clothing and family stores (with beds and bedding) up to $9,600 in value, and other exempt property and benefits. A homestead estate of up to $500,000 protects a debtor's principal residence, including a home the person possesses by lease (for example a manufactured home on a rented lot), subject to listed exceptions. Separately, the landlord-tenant act gives you no lien on a tenant's household goods and abolishes distraint for rent, so a lease cannot make the tenant's belongings security for the rent, and an unenforceable lease term you knowingly use can cost up to three months' rent plus damages and fees.

title: Seniors Moving to Care or Elderly Housing
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant who is 65 or older, or who will turn 65 during the lease, may end the lease early to move into a residential care and assisted living facility, a nursing facility, or a unit in a private or public housing complex the federal government designates as housing for the elderly. The tenant gives written notice to the person who usually receives the rent, with documentation of admission or pending admission. The termination takes effect no earlier than 45 days after the first rent due date following delivery of the notice, and rent is owed until then. The statute sets no termination fee, and a lease cannot waive this right. Rhode Island gives no comparable right to a younger tenant who must move because of illness, disability or a need for care, and none tied to a co-tenant's death; those tenants are bound by the lease unless another statutory exit applies (for example the survivor early-termination right). A periodic tenant can always end the tenancy with the ordinary statutory notice.

title: No Landlord Lien on Belongings
bodyText: Rhode Island gives a residential landlord no lien on, and no right to seize or hold, a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. Distraint for rent is abolished, and a lien or security interest in the tenant's household goods is unenforceable (the only exceptions are interests perfected before the 1986 act took effect, and the rule that a tenant whose property was moved under a court execution must pay the moving and storage costs before release, which are reimbursed to you). A lease clause making the tenant's belongings security for the rent, or letting you keep them until the tenant pays, is unenforceable, and knowingly using one can cost up to three months' rent plus damages and attorney's fees. Seizing property or locking the tenant out also breaks the self-help ban. Collect unpaid rent through the eviction case or a court judgment, subject to the statutory exemptions from attachment. A self-storage operator's lien does not apply to a dwelling.

title: Your Remedies for Tenant Breach
bodyText: Rhode Island's act sets your money and possession remedies. In a nonpayment eviction you may recover possession and actual damages (unpaid rent), plus a reasonable attorney's fee only if the tenant received a five-day demand in the six months before you filed and the nonpayment was willful. For other lease or statutory breaches you may recover possession, actual damages and an injunction, with attorney's fees if the breach was willful; you need not end the lease to sue for damages or an injunction. After the lease is terminated you have a claim for possession, a reasonable sum for use and occupation after termination, actual damages for the breach and reasonable attorney's fees. Every claim is subject to your duty to mitigate damages. For a willful, bad-faith holdover you may recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater. Accepting rent knowing of a default waives termination for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days, though partial payment never waives the balance. A tenant who counterclaims in a nonpayment case may be ordered to pay rent into court. You have no lien on the tenant's belongings, and recover possession only through the court.

title: Agreed Damages for Breach
bodyText:
Rhode Island's landlord-tenant act and its other statutes do not address a residential lease term fixing in advance what a tenant owes for a breach (liquidated damages), and no regulation permits or bars one.

Your statutory damages are actual damages for the breach, reasonable use and occupation after termination, and, for a willful bad-faith holdover, up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages; every damages claim is subject to your duty to mitigate.

The security deposit is not liquidated damages: at move-out you may keep only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning and trash-disposal costs and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, itemized in writing.

A fixed charge that is out of proportion to likely harm risks being struck as a penalty under general contract law, and any agreed charge is a fee beyond rent that must be listed in the lease's rent section (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format). An agreed fee for the tenant's option to end a fixed term early is treated differently, as the price of that option; see the library's early-termination clause.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Rhode Island does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, and a lease term that gives you one is unenforceable. You may not recover or take possession of the unit by any action of your own, such as changing the locks or willfully interrupting heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, except after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit or as the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act allows. For unpaid rent the act's route is: once rent is 15 days in arrears, mail the five-day demand notice and, if the tenant does not pay, file an eviction for nonpayment no earlier than the sixth day after mailing. A tenant who is locked out may recover possession or end the lease, and recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees; if the lease ends, you must return the security deposit and all prepaid rent. Distraint for rent is abolished, so you may not hold the tenant's belongings for rent either. Deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited adds up to three months' periodic rent and fees.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute or court rule that bars naming a tenant's minor child in an eviction case, or that requires it. Rhode Island's age of majority is 18. The District Court civil rules govern eviction cases, and two of them matter if a minor is a party: a minor without a guardian or other representative may defend only through a guardian ad litem, whom the court must appoint, and no default judgment may be entered against a minor unless a guardian, guardian ad litem or other representative has appeared for the minor (the clerk may not enter a default judgment against a minor at all). In practice, name the adults who signed the lease or hold the tenancy.

title: Five-Day Demand Before a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText:
Before you can evict for unpaid rent, Rhode Island requires a written five-day demand. Once any part of the rent has been due and unpaid for 15 days, mail the tenant a notice substantially in the statutory 'Five-Day Demand Notice for Nonpayment of Rent' form, stating the amount 15 days in arrears, demanding it, and saying that unless the tenant pays within five days of the mailing date the rental agreement will terminate and you will file an eviction.

The form ends with your certificate that you mailed it by first-class mail. If the tenant does not pay, file a 'Complaint for Eviction for Nonpayment of Rent' with the notice attached, no earlier than the sixth day after mailing.

The tenant may cure by paying the full arrears any time before you file; a tenant who has not received an earlier demand notice (before the one for this case) in the six months before you file may also cure at the hearing by paying all arrears plus court costs. You recover attorney's fees only if the tenant received an earlier demand notice in those six months and the nonpayment was willful.

You may not file a nonpayment eviction unless your Department of Health rental registry filing is current, and you must show the court proof when you file. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies, and a lease cannot waive it.

title: Notices to End a Tenancy Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Your lease may not waive or shorten the notices Rhode Island requires before you end a tenancy: the five-day demand for unpaid rent, the 20-day notice to cure a breach (termination no sooner than 21 days after mailing), and the notice ending a periodic tenancy (10 days for week-to-week; 30 days for month-to-month or any period between a month and a year; three months before the end of the occupation year for year-to-year). A lease term giving up rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. Some steps need no notice by statute, so there is nothing to waive: when a fixed term expires you may file for possession the next day; and for drug, drug-dealing or violent-crime breaches, or a qualifying seasonal tenant charged with an ordinance violation or breaching the lease's occupancy or noise terms, you may file without a noncompliance notice. You may agree to give longer notice than the statute requires.

title: Nuisance Laws and Rental Property
bodyText: Rhode Island's nuisance laws reach a landlord whose rental is used for crime. A place used for prostitution or lewdness, illegal gaming or unlicensed liquor sales, or where disorderly persons habitually gather, is a common nuisance. For those places it is a crime to let a building for those purposes, to knowingly permit that use, or to fail, after five days' notice from an officer or magistrate, to take all reasonable measures to remove the tenant as soon as lawfully possible ($100-$1,000 fine or 60 days to a year in prison), and the attorney general or any citizen may sue in superior court to abate the nuisance and enjoin everyone with an interest in the place; the court may close it for a year, and an owner can lift the closure only by paying costs, posting a bond and proving it neither knew nor could reasonably have learned of the nuisance. An old criminal statute says that use annuls the lease and lets the owner re-enter without court process, but the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act bars self-help. Separately, any place used for the unlawful sale, use or keeping of a controlled substance is a drug nuisance, and knowingly permitting one in a place you own or control carries up to 15 years and $20,000. Use the eviction route: drug nuisance, drug dealing and violent crime on the premises let you file without a cure notice.

title: No Owner Move-In Termination Right
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general just-cause eviction law for ordinary tenancies, and no statute giving you a right to end a lease early so you or a relative can move in, or regulating a lease term that reserves one. Without such a term, a fixed-term lease runs to its end date, and you end a periodic tenancy with the statutory notice: 10 days (week-to-week), 30 days (month-to-month or any period between a month and a year) or three months before the end of the occupation year (year-to-year). Rhode Island's just-cause rules are narrow: they cover tenants of a foreclosing lender-owner of a building with four or fewer units (owner move-in is not one of its grounds), and any tenant while housing-code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending or after you are served with a notice of violation; see the for-cause eviction row. This library does not offer a move-in reservation clause; a landlord who wants one should take advice and add it as their own term.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute letting a tenant give a bond to deliver possession at the end of the term, and a lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment against the tenant on a claim arising from the rental agreement. Such a term is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. If a tenant stays after the lease ends, file an eviction for holding over, which you may do from the first day after the term expires; a willful, bad-faith holdover lets you recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees. Money taken to secure the tenant's performance counts toward the one-month security deposit cap, however it is labelled.

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText:
At the start of the term you must deliver possession of the unit as the lease and Rhode Island's maintenance duties require. If you do not, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least five days' written notice (you must then return all prepaid rent and the security deposit) or insist that you perform and sue you for possession. If your failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant may also recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. If a holdover tenant or anyone else is wrongfully in possession, you may sue that person for possession and the same holdover damages.

Rhode Island has no general duty to provide alternate housing, but if you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, a tenant who has given notice may move to reasonable substitute housing, owe no rent for that period, and recover its cost up to one period's rent.

title: Tenant Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: After a Rhode Island eviction judgment, only a sheriff or certified constable acting on an execution removes the tenant and the tenant's belongings. If no appeal is claimed and the judgment is unpaid, the execution issues on the sixth day after judgment and stays in force for one year. The officer may put the belongings out on the street and then have them removed and stored for the owner; whoever stores them has a lien for reasonable storage and moving fees but may not sell them until they have been in storage at least 30 days. If the tenant is present and claims the items when they are put out, the officer does not store them. The tenant must pay the whole moving cost and any prepaid storage charges before the property is released, and that amount is paid to you as reimbursement; the officer's costs, including reasonable moving costs, may also be added to the execution with the court's approval. Otherwise you have no lien on the tenant's household goods. Rhode Island has no statute on animals left at an eviction and none aimed at a tenant who returns after one.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant behind on rent can stop a nonpayment eviction by paying in full at two points. Before you file, the tenant may cure by tendering all the rent owed, and you must take it. After you file, the tenant may cure at the hearing by paying all rent in arrears plus court costs, but only if the tenant had not received an earlier five-day demand notice from you (before the one for this case) in the six months before you filed, so in practice this right comes round no more than once every six months. After judgment there is no statutory right to redeem by paying; a stay of execution, or an appeal, keeps the tenant in place only while the tenant keeps paying amounts equal to the rent as it falls due, and missed payments let you ask the court to issue the execution. Accepting partial rent does not waive the balance, but accepting rent knowing of a default waives your right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a nonpayment eviction, or a suit for rent while the tenant still lives in the unit, a Rhode Island tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, such as damages for your failure to maintain the unit. The tenant does not have to pay rent into court first, but once a counterclaim is filed the court may order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and accruing. The court nets the claims: whoever is owed a net amount is paid first from the money in court, and if no rent remains due, the tenant wins the possession case. If the counterclaim is frivolous or has no basis in fact, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant who has moved out may counterclaim without paying anything into court. Counterclaims are never compulsory in residential landlord-tenant cases. Separately, a tenant of a unit that is not lead-safe compliant (for example, no valid lead certificate of conformance) may petition the district court to pay rent into the court's registry instead of to you, whatever the lease says, until you comply.

title: False Applications: No Special Remedy
bodyText:
Rhode Island gives you no special statutory right to end a lease because the tenant's application was false. This library's application-accuracy clause makes a materially false answer a breach of the lease, so you would use the ordinary noncompliance route: a 20-day notice to remedy, with termination at least 21 days after mailing, then an eviction if the breach is not cured.

The clause does not reach questions you may not ask. Rhode Island bars any written or oral inquiry about an applicant's race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, veteran or servicemember status, country of ancestral origin, disability, age or familial status, or about domestic-abuse victim status or protective orders (you may ask whether the applicant is 18 or older and confirm the source, amount and expected duration of lawful income), and since July 2, 2025 any inquiry about immigration or citizenship status (identity and financial verification remain allowed). Rhode Island has no rule letting an applicant deny a sealed eviction record.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: In Rhode Island you may take back a rental unit only through the court eviction process, or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered it. You may not change the locks, remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings, or willfully interrupt (or cause the interruption of) heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or any other essential service to force the tenant out. A tenant who is unlawfully removed, locked out or deprived of an essential service may recover possession or end the lease, and in either case recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees; if the lease ends you must return the security deposit and all prepaid rent. The state housing code also bars an owner from shutting off a required service or utility to an occupied unit except for a temporary interruption during actual repairs or an approved emergency. A lease cannot waive these rules. One narrow exception from July 1, 2026: on a tenant's lock-change request accompanied by a protective order against another tenant or household member, you may change the locks and refuse that person a key. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Servicemember Lease Termination
bodyText: Rhode Island gives servicemembers a state-law right to end a lease, alongside the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. A lease of a home occupied (or to be occupied) by a servicemember or dependents may be ended early if the tenant enters military service after signing, or signed while in service and then receives orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of 90 days or more. The tenant must give you or your agent written notice and a copy of the orders. For a lease with monthly rent, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following the notice; for any other lease, on the last day of the month after the month of notice. You may not charge an early termination fee. The tenant owes prorated rent up to the termination date and any other obligations due under the lease, including reasonable excess-wear charges; refund rent paid for any later period within 30 days. Termination also ends any obligation of the servicemember's dependents under the lease. Rhode Island National Guard members on state active duty for more than 90 days get the federal Act's protections, including protection from eviction and the right to end a lease. You also may not ask about, or refuse to rent because of, an applicant's servicemember or veteran status.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special eviction defense, continuance or stay for a tenant who fell behind because a Social Security, public assistance, rental voucher or other government benefit payment arrived late. The ordinary nonpayment rules apply. You must mail the five-day demand once rent is 15 days in arrears and wait until the sixth day after mailing to file. The tenant may cure by paying all the arrears before you file, and a tenant who has not received an earlier demand notice (before the one for this case) in the six months before you file may also cure at the hearing by paying all arrears plus court costs. A court may continue the hearing for discovery on good cause and order interim rent, but that is not tied to benefit delays.

title: When a Tenant May End the Lease Early
bodyText:
Rhode Island lets a tenant end a lease early, whatever the lease says, in these cases.
- (1) A tenant who is 65 or older (or turns 65 during the lease) and is entering assisted living, a nursing facility or federally designated elderly housing: written notice with proof of admission, effective no earlier than 45 days after the next rent due date.
- (2) A servicemember entering service or receiving qualifying orders (see the servicemember row).
- (3) From July 1, 2026, a tenant who is, or whose household member is, a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking within the last 150 days, with written verification; the tenant must vacate within 30 days and owes rent only through termination or move-out, with no termination fee.
- (4) Your noncompliance with the lease, or with your maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, if you don't fix it within 20 days of written notice (termination at least 30 days after notice; 14 days for a repeat within six months), unless the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused the condition.
- (5) Your failure to deliver possession (five days' notice).
- (6) Fire or casualty substantially impairing the unit (notice within 14 days of vacating).
- (7) Lockout or willful essential-service shutoff.
- (8) Unlawful or harassing entry.
- (9) Conversion to condominiums (cancellation without penalty if lease obligations are met).

In cases (4)-(7) you must return the security deposit and prepaid rent.

title: When the Lease Term Ends
bodyText:
A Rhode Island lease for a fixed term ends on its last day without any notice from you. If the tenant stays without your consent, you may file an eviction for holding over as early as the next day, and if the holdover is willful and not in good faith you may also recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. You may not remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings yourself.

If you consent to the tenant staying without agreeing a new term, the tenancy becomes week-to-week (if rent is paid weekly) or month-to-month, and it then ends only on written notice: 10 days for week-to-week, 30 days for month-to-month. A periodic tenancy (no fixed term) never simply expires; it ends on the statutory notice.

If you acquired a building of four or fewer units through foreclosure as a foreclosing owner, you may evict tenants only for just cause unless an exemption applies. You have no lien on the tenant's household goods. Rhode Island has no statute on disposing of belongings a tenant leaves behind after moving out, so get advice before discarding anything of value.

title: Tenancies Without a Set Term
bodyText: Rhode Island's residential landlord-tenant law does not recognize a separate "tenancy at will" for homes and apartments. A rental agreement may be written or oral, and if it does not fix a definite term the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays rent weekly and month-to-month in every other case. Either you or the tenant ends it by written notice in the statutory form: at least 10 days before the termination date for week-to-week, at least 30 days for month-to-month. The same applies when a tenant stays on with your consent after a lease expires and no new term is agreed. Rhode Island's older rules letting a landlord end a tenancy at will or by sufferance on a written notice naming the day apply only to commercial property and other estates outside the residential act, such as transient hotel stays, institutional residence and transitional housing, unless the parties agree to be covered by the residential act.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so. Where the tenant, a family member or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent caused a condition, the tenant cannot use it to end the lease for your noncompliance, repair and deduct at your expense, or claim the essential-service remedies, and you may evict despite a recent code complaint if the tenant's lack of reasonable care mainly caused the violation. Your remedies: for damage affecting health and safety that can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, give written notice; if the tenant does not fix it within 20 days (or promptly in an emergency) you may do the work and bill the reasonable cost as rent on the next due date. You may also serve a 20-day noncompliance notice, sue for actual damages (with attorney's fees if the breach is willful), and deduct damage beyond ordinary wear and tear from the security deposit at move-out. One gap: after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may vacate and end the lease even if the tenant caused it; your remedy is a lawsuit for the damage, not a lease term blocking termination.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: If a tenant dies during the lease and no other person who signed it still lives in the unit, Rhode Island lets the deceased's live-in caregiver, or anyone 18 or older living there, continue the lease for a post-death grace period: three months or the rest of the term, whichever is shorter (longer if you agree), starting on the date of death. A resident who stays more than seven days after the death is treated as having chosen to continue. The grace-period tenant pays the agreed rent (prorated for part months), takes on the other lease obligations, may end the grace period at any time, and is not liable for the deceased's past-due rent, which stays with the estate. If you dispute that the person lived there, they must prove it (for example with a voter registration, ID, utility bill or affidavit), and you may rebut. You may deduct damage from the existing deposit but may not demand a new deposit; the balance goes to the grace-period tenant if the grace period lasts more than a month, otherwise to the estate. Several residents who elect are jointly liable. A pending noncompliance eviction may continue as to the grace-period tenant's own breaches of the lease. Rhode Island has no statute ending the lease at death, giving the estate a special right to end it, or setting how to handle a deceased tenant's belongings; get advice before entering or removing property.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: In Rhode Island either you or the tenant may end a periodic tenancy without giving a reason, by written notice delivered at least: 10 days before the termination date for a week-to-week tenancy; 30 days before it for a month-to-month tenancy or any period longer than a month and shorter than a year; and three months before the end of the occupation year for a year-to-year tenancy. Use the statutory 'Notice of Termination of Tenancy' form or language substantially like it. The form tells the tenant to vacate on the first day after the end of the current rental period, says rent must be paid until then, and ends with your certificate of first-class mailing; so pick a date that is the day after a rental period ends and at least the required number of days after delivery. A fixed-term lease needs no termination notice: it ends on its last day. If the lease does not fix a term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly and otherwise month-to-month. Your lease may give longer notice but may not shorten these periods. Separate rules apply to foreclosing owners of buildings with four or fewer units (just cause required), to a tenant's breach (20-day cure notice) and to unpaid rent (five-day demand).

title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: Rhode Island has no special fast-track for removing squatters, and no procedure for police to remove a person on an owner's affidavit. Two routes exist. First, criminal trespass: anyone who, with no legitimate purpose, stays on the premises of a home after being told to leave by the owner, the owner's authorized agent or the person entitled to possession commits willful trespass (up to a $1,000 fine or a year in jail), which the police may enforce. But that law does not apply to tenants or occupants who rightfully entered the premises when their tenancy or occupancy began and stayed after it ended or was said to have ended; against them you may recover possession only through a civil court case. So a tenant's guest who moved in with the tenant's permission, or a former tenant, must be removed through the courts, not the police. Second, the civil route: you may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession and, if the holdover is willful and in bad faith, recover up to three months' periodic rent or three times your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Never change the locks or remove the person or belongings yourself.

title: Agreed Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no special "actual notice" rule and no provision letting you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as text messages, that counts as notice. The act's general rule: a person has notice of a fact if they actually know it, have received a notice of it, or have reason to know it from the circumstances; you give notice by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the tenant in the ordinary course; and the tenant receives it when it comes to their attention or when it is delivered by hand or sent by first-class mail to the address they gave for notices (or, if none, their last known residence). The two days' notice before entry has no prescribed method. Where a statute or statutory form calls for first-class mail (the five-day demand, the 20-day noncompliance notice, the termination notice), use it. E-mail or text works only if both sides have agreed to deal electronically, either may later refuse further electronic dealings, and it cannot replace a mailing method a statute requires unless that statute allows it.

title: No Statutory Addendum Precedence
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute requiring a separate addendum that overrides the lease, and no rule on which lease document wins when they conflict, so the lease's own precedence clause governs. Two limits apply.

First, the lead disclosure acknowledgment must be either a stand-alone document that includes the property address or its own separate page within a written lease, and it is required for every lease of pre-1978 housing covered by the lead rules, including oral leases.

Second, no addendum or precedence clause can take away a tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: a term waiving them is unenforceable, and knowingly using a prohibited term exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. In public or federally subsidized housing, federal rules that directly conflict with the act control.

title: Telling Tenants About a Possible Foreclosure
bodyText: If you fall 120 days behind on a mortgage on the property where the unit is located, Rhode Island requires you to notify your tenant that the property may be subject to foreclosure. Until a foreclosure actually occurs, the tenant must keep paying rent to you under the lease. The statute sets no form or method for this notice; give it in writing and keep a copy. Separately, the lender foreclosing the mortgage must mail each bona fide tenant (not the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, in an arm's-length tenancy at roughly market rent) a notice of the scheduled sale telling them to keep paying rent and that it is not an eviction notice. After a foreclosure, a foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units, unless exempt, must post and mail its contact details and the address for rent within 30 days and may evict only for just cause or after a binding sale contract with a bona fide buyer (see the foreclosure row). Rhode Island has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about a foreclosure, tax proceeding or other claim against the property; if you want that, it must come from the lease.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText:
No Rhode Island statute regulates automatic renewal clauses in residential leases: there is no required notice, type size or reminder before a lease renews itself. Rhode Island's automatic-renewal notice law (45 to 90 days' written notice, or the renewal is voidable by the lessee) applies only to written leases of personal property, such as equipment, with a term of a year or more, not to apartments or houses.

A residential lease may therefore include a renewal or extension term the parties agree to, subject to the general rule that it cannot waive the tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Without a renewal clause, a fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and if the tenant stays with your consent and no new term is agreed, the tenancy becomes week-to-week (weekly rent) or month-to-month, ended on 10 or 30 days' written notice.

Good practice: remind the tenant in writing before a renewal date.

title: Other Rules Rhode Island Does Not Have
bodyText: Three rules some states have do not exist in Rhode Island law. (1) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it; general contract law applies, and if you can't deliver possession to a tenant at the start of the term, rent abates and the tenant may end the lease on five days' notice. (2) No statute makes smoke-alarm compliance inadmissible in an injury case or limits what an insurer may do because of it; the fire and housing codes still require the alarms. (3) No statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false; the lease's application-accuracy section makes a material falsehood a breach handled through the 20-day noncompliance notice, and general fraud and misrepresentation law still applies. By contrast, Rhode Island does have a payment-method rule: you may not charge a convenience fee on a rent payment unless you also accept a form of payment that carries no fee.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: (1) There is no squatter-specific removal procedure. Willful trespass is a crime, but it does not reach tenants or occupants who rightfully entered and stayed after their occupancy ended; you remove them through a civil eviction case. (2) There is no duty to give a receipt for rent paid in cash; give one anyway, as it is your proof of payment too. (3) Unlike many states, Rhode Island does make registration a precondition to one kind of eviction: you may not file a nonpayment-of-rent eviction unless your statewide rental registry filing with the Department of Health is current (with a lead certificate of conformance or proof of exemption for covered pre-1978 units), and you must show the court proof when you file. The rule does not apply to holdover or lease-violation evictions. General business filings can also hold up any eviction. If you rent under a trade name rather than your own full name, you must file a trade name certificate with the secretary of state, and until you do you may not maintain any suit in a Rhode Island court; a limited liability company renting under a name other than its registered name must file a fictitious business name statement before it can sue on leases made in that name (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 6-1-1, 6-1-6 and 7-16-9(b)(5)). And an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business here may not maintain an eviction or any other suit until it has registered with the secretary of state or obtained a certificate of authority (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 7-16-49, 7-16-54 and 7-1.2-1418); whether renting out property is transacting business is a case-law question, so register before you need to file. In each case the lease stays valid and you may still defend a suit. Separately, a state statute requires everyone who owns and leases property in Providence or Warwick to register their name, home address and telephone number with that city's clerk, and cities may have their own ordinances.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Rhode Island has not moved its protective-order laws. Orders still issue under the divorce statute's restraining-order section, the family court's Domestic Abuse Prevention Act (chapter 15-15), the district court's protective-order chapter (chapter 8-8.1) and the criminal no-contact order section (§ 12-29-4), and the new survivor-protection definitions cite them correctly. From July 1, 2026, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act defines "abuse", "domestic violence" and "household member" for the first time and renumbers every other definition in its definitions section; cite those definitions by term, not number, in leases and notices. "Domestic violence" there includes, without being limited to, listed crimes (from simple assault and trespass to stalking, cyberstalking, violating a protective order and abuse) committed by one family or household member against another, whether or not reported to police. The lock-change and early-termination sections refer to a "valid protective order" without citing a chapter, and the fair housing ban on asking about domestic abuse refers to court restraining orders generally, so neither depends on a section number.

title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices
bodyText:
Rhode Island's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you and a tenant sign the lease and keep records electronically, but only if both of you have agreed to do business electronically (agreement can be shown by the circumstances and conduct). An electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, and an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature, so a lease and the required written disclosures may be signed electronically.

A tenant who agreed to one electronic transaction may refuse to do others electronically, and the lease cannot take that right away. An electronic record does not count as a written notice if you send it in a way that stops the tenant from printing or storing it, and then it is not enforceable against the tenant.

Unlike Connecticut and Massachusetts, Rhode Island's Act does not exclude eviction, default or cure notices; but where a statute or statutory form calls for first-class mail (the five-day demand, the noncompliance notice, the termination notice), you must still mail it, because e-mail can replace a required mailing method only if that statute allows it.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute that expressly protects a tenant's right to call the police or emergency services, bars a lease penalty for such calls, or limits nuisance or crime-free programs that count calls for service. Don't penalize those calls anyway. Rhode Island's retaliation law bars raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an eviction because a tenant used any lawful right or remedy, and a complaint in the six months before your action creates a presumption of retaliation. Fair housing law bars refusing to rent to, or setting different terms for, a tenant or applicant because they or a household member are or have been a victim of domestic abuse or have sought a restraining order, and bars asking about it. From July 1, 2026, you also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended an earlier lease as a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or asked for a lock change. This library's Rhode Island clauses contain no call-penalty term; do not add one.

title: Changing the Lease After Signing
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute letting you amend existing leases by written notice to comply with new laws, so a clause requiring signed written amendments gives up no statutory right. New laws that apply to existing tenancies operate on their own terms.

Three narrower changes are possible without a signed amendment.
- (1) Rules: you may adopt a rule about the tenant's use and occupancy, but it is enforceable only if it promotes the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects the property from abusive use or fairly shares services; is reasonably related to that purpose; is clear enough to tell the tenant what to do; applies fairly to all tenants; does not evade your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when the lease was signed or when the rule was adopted. A rule adopted later that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain is not valid without the tenant's written consent.
- (2) Fees: if there is no written lease, give the tenant a written list of fees and disclose any change at least 30 days before it takes effect.
- (3) Rent: give written notice of an increase at least 60 days before it takes effect (120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62), subject to any fixed rent in the lease.

title: Pre-Suit Dispute Clauses
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute authorizing or regulating lease clauses that require you and the tenant to try informal resolution or mediation before going to court, and no statute requiring mediation in landlord-tenant cases. Rhode Island's arbitration act makes a clearly written agreement in a written contract to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable on ordinary contract grounds. But a lease may not make a tenant waive or give up any right or remedy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. So if you use a pre-suit or mediation clause, keep it voluntary in effect: it must not delay or condition the five-day demand, the 20-day cure notice, the termination notices, an eviction, or the tenant's own remedies such as repair and deduct, rent abatement or a retaliation defense. Whether a residential arbitration clause can cover eviction or chapter 34-18 claims is a question for case law; get advice before adding one.

title: You Must Carry Liability Insurance
bodyText:
Rhode Island requires every residential landlord to obtain and keep in force a general liability insurance policy of at least $100,000 covering people injured on the premises because of your negligence. You must give the tenant a copy of the carrier's declaration page showing the policy with the written lease at the beginning of the tenancy, and a new copy each time the policy renews.

The duty is part of your statutory maintenance obligations, so it applies to every tenancy type and building size and cannot be waived in the lease; a lease term limiting your liability or making the tenant indemnify you for it is also unenforceable. If you don't comply, the tenant may recover actual damages and get a court order, with attorney's fees if the failure is willful, and a tenant who complains to you about it is protected from retaliation. The statute names a written lease; for an oral tenancy, hand over the declaration page at move-in anyway. The library's insurance-disclosure clause records delivery of the page.

title: Statewide Rental Registry
bodyText: Every Rhode Island residential landlord must register with the Department of Health: the names of the individual landlords or business entity, an active mailing address, e-mail address and telephone number, any property manager, management company or agent (with the same contact details), and information identifying each dwelling unit. If you lease a unit in a building built before 1978 that is not exempt from the lead hazard mitigation law, you must also file a valid lead certificate of conformance for each unit, or evidence that it is exempt. Register within 30 days after you acquire a rental property or begin leasing to a new tenant, whichever is earlier, and re-register or confirm your information by October 1 every year. Failing to register costs at least $50 a month ($125 a month for missing lead information), with further penalties for repeated failures. Most importantly, you may not file an eviction for nonpayment of rent unless your registration is current when you file, and you must give the court evidence of compliance; holdover and lease-violation evictions are not affected. Short-term rentals of 30 nights or fewer listed on hosting platforms register separately with the Department of Business Regulation.

title: Providence and Warwick Owner Registration
bodyText: If you own and lease property in the city of Providence or the city of Warwick, a state statute requires you, whether you are an individual or an entity, to register your name, home address (including zip code) and telephone number with the city clerk of the city where the property is located. This applies only to property in those two cities; it is in addition to the statewide Department of Health rental registry, which applies everywhere in Rhode Island. The statute does not set a deadline, fee or penalty itself; check with the city clerk, because each city's own ordinance may add requirements. Other cities and towns may have their own registration ordinances, which this library does not track.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, or treating a blank as a breach (a fill-every-term rule exists only for mobile home leases in the town of Exeter). Fill in or strike every blank anyway, because several Rhode Island rules turn on what the written lease says: any fees beyond rent must be disclosed in the same section as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); the lease must say which utilities are included in the rent and which the tenant pays; any renters-insurance requirement must be stated in the lease; and a tenant may recover any fee that was not disclosed as required. A court that finds a rental agreement or any term unconscionable when made may refuse to enforce it, strike the term or limit it. A blank filled in after signing invites a dispute over what was agreed.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: Apart from mobile home leases in the town of Exeter, no Rhode Island statute requires you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease by a deadline, and not giving one is not a statutory defense when you enforce the lease. Give every tenant a fully signed copy at signing anyway: you will need it to prove the terms, and several Rhode Island rules depend on what the written lease says. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson handles the lease for you, the licensee must furnish a copy to everyone who signed it at the time it is signed, or risk license discipline and an administrative penalty of up to $2,000. Mobile home park leases have their own rules: the park must show the prospective resident a copy of the written lease before move-in and may not rent until a written lease is signed, and in the town of Exeter the lease must be executed in duplicate originals with one given to the lessee within 30 days of signing. Rules you adopt bind the tenant only if the tenant has notice of them when the rental agreement is made or when they are adopted, so hand over your written rules with the lease.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term for that term to bind the tenant; the tenant's signature on the lease is enough as far as the statutes go. That does not make every term lawful: the statutory notice to end a periodic tenancy belongs to the tenant as well as to you, so a term requiring the tenant to give more notice than the statute requires risks being an unenforceable waiver. The statutory notice to end a periodic tenancy runs both ways: at least 10 days for a week-to-week tenancy, at least 30 days for a month-to-month tenancy (or any period between a month and a year), and at least three months before the end of the occupation year for a year-to-year tenancy, each in writing in a form substantially like the statutory form. A lease term in which the tenant gives up a right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Having the tenant initial an unusual term is still good evidence the tenant saw it, but it cannot rescue a prohibited term.

title: Lease Length and Signatures
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no maximum length for a residential lease, but how the lease is made can limit it. If you sign and deliver a written lease and the tenant never signs it, the tenant's taking possession and paying rent without reservation makes it binding as if signed; if the tenant signs and delivers it and you never sign, your accepting rent without reservation does the same. A lease given effect this way that provides for a term longer than one year is effective for only one year. A lease of one year or less is valid even if oral, but a lease for a longer term is void against buyers, lenders and others without notice of it unless it is in writing, signed, acknowledged, delivered and recorded in the city or town land records (a memorandum of lease may be recorded instead). If no definite term is fixed, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer paying weekly). Mobile home park leases have a one-year minimum unless the resident asks in writing for a shorter term. Have every tenant and every landlord sign before move-in.

title: Out-of-State Landlords Must Name a Rhode Island Agent
bodyText: If you are not a Rhode Island resident, you must designate, and keep in place for as long as you rent, an agent in Rhode Island who can be served with any legal process, notice or demand, including notices of minimum housing code violations. The agent must be a Rhode Island resident or a corporation authorized to do business here. The designation must be in writing, give the agent's name and address and the street address of each property assigned to the agent, and be filed with both the secretary of state and the clerk of the city or town where the unit is. The fine for not complying is $100 a month, up to $1,200 in a calendar year, or one month's rent for the year if your monthly rent is more than $1,200, payable to the municipality. The minimum housing code separately requires a nonresident owner to keep a registered agent on file with the city or town clerk, with a $100 fine; one filing that meets the landlord-tenant statute covers both. The lease does not have to name the agent, but you must still give every tenant, in writing, the name, address and number of the manager and of an owner or agent for service of notices. Rhode Island does not require tenants to withhold tax from rent paid to you. If you own through an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation, it must also register with the secretary of state, naming a Rhode Island resident or registered agent, before transacting business here, and until it does it may not maintain an eviction or any other suit in a Rhode Island court; an LLC that transacts business here unregistered appoints the secretary of state as its agent for service of process on claims arising from that business (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 7-16-49, 7-16-54 and 7-1.2-1418). Whether renting out property is transacting business is a case-law question, so register before you need to file. And a nonresident with the minimum contacts the Constitution requires can be sued in a Rhode Island court and served inside or outside the state (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-5-33); owning and renting out property here is likely to supply those contacts for claims about it.

title: How to Deliver Rhode Island Notices
bodyText:
Rhode Island sets the delivery method notice by notice, and your lease cannot change a method a statute requires. Mail the five-day demand for unpaid rent and the 20-day noncompliance notice by regular first-class mail: both deadlines run from the date of mailing, and the statutory forms end with your signed certificate that you mailed them first class, postage prepaid.

The termination notice for a periodic tenancy must be delivered at least 10 days, 30 days or three months ahead; its statutory form also ends with a first-class mailing certificate, so mail it and allow time for delivery.

If a tenant abandons the unit, send a certified letter, return receipt requested, to the last known address. Rent increase notices and the written notice that keeps your right to terminate after accepting rent must be in writing, with no set method; use one you can prove. A foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units must post its notice in the building, mail it first class to each unit and slide it under each door.

No statute requires a sheriff or constable to deliver your notices, but once you file an eviction you must mail the summons and complaint to the tenant that day, and a deputy sheriff or constable serves them by hand, with a suitable adult at the unit, or by posting on the door.

title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute governing a move-out notice form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to what the tenant's notice needs: the tenant's written notice ending a periodic tenancy must be delivered at least 10 days ahead (week-to-week), 30 days ahead (month-to-month) or three months before the end of the occupation year (year-to-year), in a form substantially like the statutory termination notice. Any added term in which the tenant gives up a right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (for example, agreeing to a deposit deduction the statute does not allow) is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. A new rule adopted during the tenancy that substantially changes the bargain is valid only if the tenant consents in writing. Put any genuine new agreement, such as an agreed early move-out date, in a separate signed amendment.

title: Where Rhode Island Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Rhode Island rules depend on what the lease says, and a silent lease takes the statutory default. (1) Rent is due without demand at the agreed time and place; if the lease is silent, it is payable at the unit, at the start of each period of a month or less (otherwise monthly in advance), and is apportioned day by day. (2) Without a definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer paying weekly). (3) Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant may use the unit only as a dwelling. (4) Only if the lease requires it must the tenant tell you of an absence longer than ten days, by the first day of the absence. (5) The tenant does repairs or maintenance only under a separate good-faith writing signed by both of you, for adequate consideration, never to cure a housing code violation. (6) A renters-insurance requirement, any fees beyond rent (stated in the rent section unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format) and the utility split must be in the lease, or in writing if there is no written lease; otherwise the tenant can recover undisclosed fees. (7) A seasonal lease within the statutory dates lets you skip the cure notice for occupancy or noise breaches.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Rhode Island has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases, no readability test, and no required statement listing the rights a tenant gives up under the lease. Plain-language rules exist only for other kinds of contracts. What limits a Rhode Island lease instead is the list of prohibited provisions: a lease may not have the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, authorize anyone to confess judgment, agree to pay your attorney's fees except as the Act allows, or excuse or limit your legal liability or make the tenant indemnify you for it. Such a provision is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing one, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Write the lease clearly anyway: required disclosures (fees in the rent section, the utility split, any renters-insurance requirement) must be understandable to do their job.

title: Rules That Depend on Building Size
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant duties do not change with how many units you own, and there is no general small-landlord exemption; a few rules turn on the size of the building instead. If you buy a building of four or fewer units at foreclosure as a foreclosing owner, you may evict only for just cause, unless you are headquartered and fully operating in Rhode Island or conducted fewer than 15 Rhode Island foreclosures in the prior calendar year. Anyone other than a bona fide third-party purchaser who takes a building of four or fewer units from a seller or mortgagor takes it subject to the existing tenants' rights. Fair housing law lets an owner decline to rent to a family with children only in a two-unit building the owner lives in, or a building of four or fewer units the owner lives in where a senior or infirm occupant would suffer demonstrated hardship (or qualifying elderly housing). An owner living in a building of three or fewer units may refuse a tenant based on lawful source of income. A building employee's housing falls outside the Act only if the premises have more than eleven units.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText:
You may require a Rhode Island tenant to carry renter's insurance, but only if the requirement is stated in the lease; if there is no written lease, you must give the tenant the requirement in writing. If you charge any fee connected with insurance (for example, for a program you arrange), disclose it in the rent section of the lease with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it.

No Rhode Island statute regulates which insurer the tenant uses, how soon the tenant must show proof, force-placed coverage, or a notice that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, so those are contract terms.

An insurance requirement cannot shift your own legal duties: a lease term excusing or limiting your liability, or making the tenant indemnify you for it, is unenforceable, and you still must make repairs and keep the premises fit.

Separately, you must carry your own general liability policy of at least $100,000 and give the tenant the declaration page with the lease.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: When you sell a rented Rhode Island property in good faith to a bona fide buyer, you are released from liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act only for events after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, and never for anything before the sale itself. The notice must give the buyer's names, address and telephone number and must certify that you complied with the housing-code rule on transfers: if the building has an outstanding violation notice, you may not sell or lease it until the violation is corrected, or until you give the buyer a copy of every notice and tell the code officer in writing of the intended sale. A manager who leaves is released after written notice to the tenant naming the new manager or the person in Rhode Island responsible for the property. Keep your written owner and manager disclosure current; it binds every successor. A family member or other successor who is not a bona fide third-party buyer of a building of four or fewer units takes it subject to the tenant's existing rights. No sale or mortgage can let anyone collect rent without the repair duties. Tenants may not unreasonably refuse showings to buyers or lenders, on two days' notice at reasonable times. For deposits on a sale, see the deposit-transfer row.

title: What the Rhode Island Act Covers
bodyText: Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies statewide to every rental agreement for a dwelling unit in Rhode Island, wherever the lease was signed; a dwelling unit is any structure or part of one designed or intended as a home, residence or sleeping place. Unless you and the occupant expressly agree to be governed by the Act, it does not cover: residence in an institution incidental to detention, medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; a buyer occupying under a contract of sale; fraternal or social organization housing; transient stays in a hotel, motel or other lodging subject to sales or lodging tax; a paid employee whose housing depends on working on premises of more than eleven units; a cooperative shareholder's proprietary lease; commercial lettings; and transitional housing. Mobile home park lots have their own act, which uses the Act's eviction procedure but limits the grounds and requires at least 60 days' written notice (30 days for nonpayment). Homes on leased land and commercial leases have separate chapters. This library's Rhode Island rows cover Act tenancies only. One state statute (absentee landlord registration) applies only in Providence and Warwick, and city ordinances are not covered.

title: Severability Cannot Cure Banned Terms
bodyText: Rhode Island strikes bad lease terms one at a time, so a severability clause works as intended: a provision the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act prohibits is unenforceable, and a court that finds a term unconscionable when made may enforce the rest of the lease without it or limit the term. But a severability clause is no safety net. If a court finds the agreement unconscionable as a whole, it may refuse to enforce any of it. And if you deliberately use a lease containing terms you know are prohibited (a waiver of the tenant's rights under the Act, a confession of judgment, attorney's fees the Act does not allow, or an exculpation or indemnity for your own liability), the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees, whatever the severability clause says.

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Rhode Island a lease for longer than one year cannot be enforced against a party unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by that party or someone lawfully authorized by them. A lease of one year or less is valid even if oral, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act protects oral tenants too. A lease for more than one year is also a conveyance: between you and the tenant it binds once signed and delivered, but to bind a buyer or lender without notice of it, it must be acknowledged and recorded in the city or town land records (a memorandum naming the parties, the property and the duration, including renewal and purchase options, may be recorded instead). If you promise a lease longer than a year to get someone to move in and then refuse to give it, you may have to repay the cost of improvements they made with your approval, unless rent was reserved for a definite letting or they occupy under a signed writing. Sign every lease, and record any lease longer than a year.

title: Forms Rhode Island Law Supplies
bodyText: Rhode Island prescribes no form for a residential lease, but its landlord-tenant act supplies the forms for the three notices that matter most, and the statute requires your notice to be in a form substantially similar to them: the Five-Day Demand Notice for Nonpayment of Rent, the Notice of Noncompliance (20 days to remedy a breach) and the Notice of Termination of Tenancy. Each form has a date of mailing and ends with your signed certificate that you mailed a copy by regular first-class mail, postage prepaid. The same section supplies the Complaint for Eviction for Nonpayment of Rent (with the five-day notice attached), the Complaint for Eviction for Reason Other Than Nonpayment of Rent (with the noncompliance or termination notice attached), a landlord-tenant complaint for other claims, the court summonses and the tenant's blank answer form, which lists defenses such as no required notice and retaliation. Copy the statutory wording rather than drafting your own. Mobile home park leases must print the park-tenancy notice word for word. The Executive Office of Housing publishes a landlord-tenant guide in English and Spanish; you are not required to give it to tenants. The lead disclosure documents have their own required content (see the lead rows).

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on tenant portals as such, but two rules limit how you use one. First, you may not charge a convenience fee on a tenant's rent payment (such as a portal or card-processing fee) unless you also accept a way of paying rent that carries no convenience fee; offer at least one free method. Second, Rhode Island's electronic-transactions law applies only when both you and the tenant have agreed to deal electronically, nothing in it requires anyone to use electronic records or signatures, and a tenant who agreed to one electronic transaction may refuse to conduct others electronically; that right cannot be waived in the lease. So you may offer a portal for payments, maintenance requests and signatures, but a lease term making the portal the only way to sign or receive documents will not bind a tenant who later declines. Notices the statutes require by first-class or certified mail still go by mail.

title: Tenant Ledgers and Personal Information
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to give a tenant a rent ledger or payment history, though keeping one is the best proof in a nonpayment case. If you collect or keep an applicant's or tenant's name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, a bank or card number with its access code, medical or health insurance information, or an e-mail address with its password, Rhode Island's Identity Theft Protection Act applies to you, whatever your size. You must keep a risk-based information security program with reasonable safeguards for the size of your business and the information; keep the data no longer than reasonably needed or than your written retention policy or the law requires; destroy it securely (shredding, erasure and the like); and require by written contract that any outside company you share it with protects it. If a breach poses a significant risk of identity theft, notify each affected Rhode Island resident within 45 days after confirming it, and notify the attorney general and the credit reporting agencies if more than 500 residents are affected. Penalties run up to $100 per record for reckless violations and $200 per record for knowing ones.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 9, 2026, none of Rhode Island's landlord-tenant statutes, including the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's deposit, notice, eviction, retaliation and fee rules, the fair housing act and the foreclosure just-cause law, carries a repeal or expiration date. The dated changes run the other way: the domestic-violence survivor protections (early lease termination, no refusal to rent for having used it, lock changes on request within two business days) took effect July 1, 2026, and the written shoreline-access disclosure for shoreline property takes effect January 1, 2027. Plan for the current rules to stay in force until the General Assembly changes them, and watch each year's new public laws, since Rhode Island amends this area most sessions.

title: No Translation Duty
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to translate a lease or any landlord notice into the tenant's language, even if you advertised or negotiated in another language, and it sets no minimum type size for residential lease text. Once you file an eviction, the District Court rules require the court's Language Assistance Notice, which tells the tenant of the right to a free interpreter, to be served with the summons and complaint. The state's Executive Office of Housing must publish its landlord-tenant guide in both English and Spanish on its website, which you can point tenants to. If you negotiate in a language other than English, giving the tenant a translation (and keeping the English lease as the controlling text) reduces later disputes about what was agreed.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Many Rhode Island landlord notices must be written, and a lease cannot downgrade them to verbal notice, because a lease term waiving a tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable.

In writing:
- the names, addresses and numbers of the manager and of an owner or agent for notices, at or before move-in
- where there is no written lease, the list of fees, any fee change (30 days ahead), the utility split and any renters-insurance requirement
- a rent increase (60 days ahead, or 120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62)
- the itemized deposit deductions with the refund, within 20 days
- notice that you have sold the property or that a manager has left
- the five-day demand for unpaid rent, the 20-day noncompliance notice, the repeat-breach notice and the notice ending a periodic tenancy
- the certified letter after abandonment
- if you accept rent knowing of a default, the notice within 10 days that keeps your right to terminate.

The two days' notice before entering is not required to be written, but a written or texted notice is the easiest to prove.

title: Assistance Animals in Rhode Island
bodyText:
Rhode Island's fair housing law requires you to make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services when needed to give a tenant or occupant with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home; waiving a no-pet rule or pet fees for an assistance animal is the usual example.

Two Rhode Island statutes go further for a guide dog or other personal assistive animal (one specifically trained by a certified animal training program to help a person with a disability with independent living tasks): the person is entitled to full and equal access to housing and may not be charged extra for the animal, but is liable for any damage it does.

Rhode Island statutes do not mention emotional support animals or say what documentation you may request; untrained support animals are handled as reasonable-accommodation requests, and federal fair housing guidance governs documentation. You need not accommodate a tenancy that would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. Violations are unlawful housing practices enforced by the Commission for Human Rights.

title: Penalties for Refusing an Assistance Animal
bodyText:
Refusing to rent to, or to accommodate, a tenant with a disability who needs a guide dog, a trained assistive animal or another assistance animal is an unlawful housing practice under Rhode Island's fair housing law, and so is charging extra for a guide dog or trained assistive animal. A tenant may file a charge with the Commission for Human Rights within one year.
