If the Commission finds a violation, it may order you to stop, take corrective action, pay the tenant's damages and reasonable attorney's fees, and pay a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for a first violation, up to $25,000 if you were found to have committed another discriminatory housing practice in the prior five years, and up to $50,000 for two or more in the prior seven years; the case can also move to superior court with a jury, where punitive damages are also possible.

Rhode Island's separate service-animal law makes denying access a misdemeanor (up to six months in jail or a fine of at least $100, plus actual and punitive damages), but it covers streets, public buildings, transportation, schools, hotels, restaurants and other places open to the public, not ordinary rental homes. Treat common areas open to the public with care.

title: Misrepresentation Penalty Does Not Reach Housing
bodyText: Rhode Island's service-animal misrepresentation law does not reach rental housing. It makes it a civil violation, punishable by up to 30 hours of community service for an organization serving people with disabilities, for someone to claim a pet is a service animal to get into or stay in a public area where pets are not allowed, when they knew or should have known it was not one. A public area is the part of a public place listed in the service-animal chapter (streets, public buildings, transportation, schools, hotels, restaurants and similar places) that is open to the general public, and a service animal there means a specially trained dog. No Rhode Island statute penalizes a tenant who misrepresents an emotional support or other assistance animal to a landlord. If you doubt a request, handle it through the reasonable-accommodation process rather than accusing the tenant of fraud; a lease term making a false accommodation request a default is your own contract term, not a statutory penalty.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Rhode Island has no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that you must give a tenant who has a dog or cat, and its eviction statutes have no special rule for animals left in a unit. If a tenant is evicted or leaves a pet behind, the general animal-care and animal-control laws apply; contact the local animal control officer rather than disposing of the animal yourself. The only state handout you must give with a lease is the lead-poisoning pamphlet with its Rhode Island insert for housing covered by the lead rules (see the lead disclosure rows).

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees
bodyText:
In Rhode Island a refundable pet deposit is a security deposit, whatever you call it, so it counts toward the one-month limit on all deposits: the pet deposit plus the general deposit together may not exceed one month's periodic rent (a separate furniture deposit is allowed only for furniture worth $5,000 or more). At move-out you may deduct pet damage only as physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, itemized in writing with the refund within 20 days.

Monthly pet rent or a nonrefundable pet fee is not prohibited, but every fee beyond rent must be stated in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); if it is not, the tenant can recover what was paid.

You may not charge anything extra for a guide dog or trained assistive animal, and assistance animals approved as a reasonable accommodation should not carry pet fees. Mobile home parks may charge a pet fee only for special pet facilities or services they actually provide, reasonably related to the cost.

title: Pet Rules in Rhode Island
bodyText:
Rhode Island does not require you to allow pets in an ordinary rental, and no statute gives older tenants or public housing residents a right to keep one, so your lease may ban pets or limit their number, kind and size, apart from assistance animals.

A pet rule adopted after the lease is signed binds the tenant only if it meets the statute's tests for rules and the tenant had notice of it; a new rule that substantially changes the tenant's bargain, such as banning a pet you already allowed, needs the tenant's written consent.

To deal with a pet problem, enter only for the purposes the statute allows (inspection, repairs, services, showings) with two days' notice at reasonable times, or without consent in an emergency or during an absence of more than seven days if reasonably necessary to protect the property; otherwise you may enter only by court order, after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit, or, where pet damage or mess breaches the tenant's statutory duties in a way that affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, to do the work yourself after the tenant fails to fix it within 20 days of your written notice, billing the reasonable cost as rent.

You may not seize or hold a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, or lock a tenant out, so enforce pet violations through the 20-day noncompliance notice. A clause making the tenant answer for damage and injuries the tenant's pet causes is fine, but not one that excuses or limits any liability the law places on you, or makes the tenant indemnify you for it.

Mobile home parks cannot apply a new no-pet rule to a pet already there that met the old rules, and the resident may replace that pet if it dies.

title: No Tenant EV-Charging Right
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no statutory right to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental, and sets no rules for how you approve, price or remove one, so charging is a matter for your lease and your own consent. Two state rules touch parking: if you build a new parking lot, or expand one by 50 percent or more, for a privately owned housing development of more than 20 units that received public funding for a project awarded after January 1, 2024, you must designate EV-ready or EV-capable spaces (none for fewer than 10 spaces, one for 10-25, rising to six percent of all spaces, rounded up, for lots of 201 or more); and anyone who parks a vehicle not connected to the charger in a signed charging space commits a parking violation.

title: No Charger Removal Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on who owns, or who must remove, electric vehicle charging equipment a tenant installed when the tenancy ends. If you allow a tenant to install a charger, say in a written agreement who owns it, whether the tenant must remove it and restore the space at move-out, and who pays; any restoration cost you deduct from the deposit must be physical damage, beyond ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's statutory duties, itemized in a written notice sent with the refund within 20 days after the later of the end of the tenancy, the return of possession or the tenant's forwarding address; recover any other agreed restoration cost as a separate claim.

title: No EV Charger Installation Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no landlord-tenant rules for a tenant-installed electric vehicle charging system, such as registration with the landlord, insurance, a licensed electrician or separate metering. Because the tenant has no statutory charging right, any conditions you attach are your own lease or side-agreement terms; electrical work remains subject to the state building and electrical codes and permits.

title: No Shared Charging Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on tenant electric vehicle charging in shared parking at a rental property, on charging a tenant for installing in a common area, or on sharing a charger among tenants. Those are matters for your lease and rules. If you have signed charging spaces, a vehicle parked there without being connected to the charger can be ticketed under state law, and a new lot, or one expanded by 50 percent or more, of 10 or more spaces at a private housing development of more than 20 units, in a project awarded after January 1, 2024 that receives public funding, must include EV-ready or EV-capable spaces.

title: Towing From Your Rental Property
bodyText:
As the owner or person in control of a Rhode Island property, you may have a vehicle that is parked there without your consent towed without going to court, but only by hiring, in writing, a tow company holding a state certificate (a certificated tower). The tower must keep your written direction, take the vehicle to its own impound lot within 10 miles, and keep the lot open to release vehicles during the same hours it receives them.

The vehicle's owner pays the towing and storage charges in the tower's published tariff; but if the owner later proves in court that the vehicle was not trespassing, you must pay those charges. A vehicle left on your property without consent for more than three days counts as abandoned, and you may also order an abandoned or unattended vehicle removed. State law sets no sign-posting requirement, though a city ordinance may.

Because the statute covers vehicles present without consent, be cautious about towing a tenant's own car for breaking a parking rule: enforce parking rules through the lease (a noncompliance notice) unless the lease clearly withdraws consent to park in that place.

title: No Residential Parking Statute
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute regulating parking terms in residential leases: you may include or exclude parking, assign spaces and set parking rules by lease.

Two general rules apply. If you charge for parking separately from rent, it is a fee beyond rent that must be stated in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant can recover it. Parking rules adopted after signing must meet the statute's tests for rules, and one that substantially changes the tenant's bargain needs the tenant's written consent. Mobile home parks must provide space to park one car for each lot. Towing has its own rules (see the towing row).

title: Giving Notice of Parking Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to hand over parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, use a particular heading, or limit what vehicle information you collect. Parking rules are treated like your other building rules: one is enforceable against a tenant only if it serves the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects the property or fairly shares facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; is clear enough to tell the tenant what to do; applies fairly to all tenants; does not evade your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when you adopted it. A parking rule adopted later that substantially changes the tenant's bargain, such as taking away a space the tenant was promised, is valid only with the tenant's written consent. Give tenants the parking rules in writing at signing and whenever they change.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to offer parking separately from rent, and it does not regulate how you price a separate parking space. If you charge for parking apart from rent, the charge is a fee beyond rent: list it in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or the tenant may recover what was paid. If there is no written lease, give the tenant a written list of fees, and give written notice at least 30 days before changing one.

title: Cannabis in Rhode Island Rentals
bodyText: Rhode Island's adult-use cannabis law limits what your lease can ban. You may not prohibit a tenant from consuming cannabis by means other than smoking or vaping (for example edibles), or from giving cannabis to another adult without payment, as long as the tenant stays within the legal possession and transfer limits. You may prohibit smoking and vaping cannabis in the unit and on the property; the smoking-policy clause covers this. Adults 21 and over may legally grow, for personal use within a residence, up to three mature and three immature plants per dwelling unit, however many people live there, if they meet the Cannabis Control Commission's security requirements; the statute does not say whether a lease may ban home growing, so take advice before relying on a cultivation ban against an adult-use tenant. Under the medical marijuana law you may not refuse to rent to, or penalize, someone solely because they hold a medical marijuana card, but you may decline to lease, or to continue leasing, to a cardholder who grows, manufactures, processes, smokes or vaporizes medical marijuana in the unit.

title: Religious Items on the Entry Door
bodyText: Rhode Island bars a landlord from prohibiting a tenant from displaying or affixing religious items on the entry to the tenant's unit when the display is motivated by the tenant's sincere religious belief (a mezuzah is a common example). You may still limit an item that threatens public health or safety, violates fair housing or other law, sits anywhere other than the entry door or door frame or extends past the frame's outer edge, or that, with the other religious items on the door or frame, totals more than 25 square inches. The rule does not let the tenant repaint or alter the door or frame against your rules. The protection covers religious items only; Rhode Island has no statute protecting purely cultural displays. Apart from this, Rhode Island has no statute on tenant displays, signs, waterbeds or fastening items in a rental, so the lease's common-area and use rules are contract terms, subject to the statute's tests for rules.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a fire, storm or other disaster in spite of the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting what you may charge or require when they stay. Your lease's guest terms apply, subject to the housing code's occupancy limits; if a tenant asks to house displaced family or friends, a written temporary consent with an end date avoids later disputes. The state's disaster laws give the governor and cities and towns powers to arrange temporary housing for disaster victims and provide relocation payments when government action displaces people, but they do not change private leases.

title: Guests in Rhode Island Rentals
bodyText:
No Rhode Island statute limits how long a tenant's guests may stay or gives guests any right to stay, so a lease guest limit is a contract term you enforce like any other (the 20-day noncompliance notice, not a lockout). The tenant must require anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent to behave so as not to disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment, and answers for a guest who damages the premises with the tenant's knowledge.

The state minimum housing code limits a unit to one family plus two unrelated occupants, or one household of unrelated people, unless a rooming-house permit has been granted; guests and domestic employees are not counted, but a 'guest' who has in fact moved in may be. Apply guest limits the same way to every household: limits that fall harder on families with children or on a domestic-abuse survivor's household can raise fair housing problems. Mobile home parks must make reasonable rules for guest parking.

title: No Firearms Lease Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on firearms in residential leases. No state law stops you from restricting a tenant's lawful possession of firearms in the unit or common areas, and none requires you to allow them, so any firearms term is a contract term. Before adding one, consider that Rhode Island's criminal firearms laws, not your lease, govern who may possess and carry, that a restriction must be clear and applied evenly to be enforced, and that public housing and federally assisted housing raise separate federal questions not reviewed here. A tenant's crime of violence on the premises or on adjacent public property, including assault with a dangerous weapon, already breaches the tenant's statutory duties, and you may file for eviction for it without first sending a noncompliance notice.

title: No Guest or Visitor Rights Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute guaranteeing tenants the right to have guests, visitors, caregivers, tradespeople or delivery people, and no statute bars a guest fee, so lease terms on guests and visitors are contract terms. A guest fee is a fee beyond rent: list it in the same section of the lease as the rent, with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), or, with no written lease, in a written fee list, or the tenant may recover it. Two state rules still shape them. The state minimum housing code treats a person who shares a unit in a nonpermanent status for not more than 30 days as a guest, and guests are not counted as occupants for the code's occupancy limits; someone who stays longer may be counted. And a guest rule must be applied the same way to every household, because fair housing law protects familial status, disability and domestic-abuse victim status, among others.

title: Routine Inspections in Rhode Island
bodyText:
Inspecting the premises is one of the purposes for which a Rhode Island tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry. Give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, and enter only at reasonable times.

No statute sets how often you may inspect, but you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant: if you enter unlawfully, enter in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that unreasonably harass the tenant, the tenant may get a court order or terminate the lease. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order compelling it or terminate the lease. Either way the winner recovers actual damages and must be awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Apart from emergencies, absences over seven days (to protect the property), a court order, a repair after an ignored 20-day notice, or an abandoned or surrendered unit, you have no other right of entry.

title: Keys and Lock Changes in Rhode Island
bodyText:
Rhode Island has no statute on how many keys you issue, key receipts, lost-key charges or rekeying between tenants, so those are lease terms.

Two money rules apply. A refundable key deposit is part of the security deposit, which may not exceed one month's periodic rent in total, whatever you call it. And a lost-key or rekey charge is a fee beyond rent, so it must be listed in the lease's rent section with a statement that additional fees may apply (or, with no written lease, in a written fee list), unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format.

In a rooming house, each rooming unit door must have an operating lock.

Since July 1, 2026, if all tenants in possession ask (or a court order is furnished) because a tenant or adult household member reasonably believes they face an imminent threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must, within two business days, make a good faith effort to change the unit's locks (and get them a key) or let them change the locks; you may charge no more than the customary local price. Blocking the change or failing to try to give them a key costs two months' rent plus fees unless you acted in good faith. A lease cannot waive these rules.

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building to reach tenants' doors, and no duty to set aside an area for campaign or voter literature. Whether outsiders may canvass in locked hallways and other common areas is up to your building rules, which must be reasonable and applied evenly. Your tenants themselves may invite whomever they like to their own unit, subject to the lease's guest and conduct terms. Two related protections apply: you may not retaliate against tenants for organizing or joining a tenants' union, and in a mobile home park, park rules may not stop residents from meeting in the common areas or stop a home owner from canvassing other owners about association matters, at reasonable times and in a reasonable manner.

title: Flags and Political Signs
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute gives a tenant a right to display the U.S. flag, another flag, a banner or a political sign against your lease rules, and none limits a condominium or homeowners' association's display rules for occupants, so the lease's sign and display terms govern. Write them as neutral rules on size, placement, attachment and damage, and apply them evenly: a rule aimed at one tenant's message or at a protected group's displays can raise fair housing or retaliation problems. The one display right Rhode Island does protect is for religious items on the unit's entry door or door frame (see the religious display row).

title: No Window Unit Right
bodyText: Rhode Island gives tenants no statutory right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and the lease need not say anything about it. Your lease may allow, limit or ban tenant-owned units, for example by requiring your approval, proper brackets and no blocking of a window needed as a fire exit. A rule adopted after the lease starts must meet the statute's tests for rules. No state law requires you to provide cooling. If you do supply air conditioning, you must keep it in good and safe working order, and the tenant must use it in a reasonable manner and must not damage the premises, which includes damage from installing a window unit.

title: No Plug-In Solar Right
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute giving tenants a right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, and no law that voids lease or covenant restrictions on solar equipment. Treat a tenant's request under the lease's alterations and appliance terms: you may allow it, set conditions (safe mounting, no damage, approved equipment, removal at move-out) or refuse. The tenant must not damage the premises in installing or removing it. Rhode Island's solar easement law only lets property owners grant recorded easements protecting a solar system's sun exposure, and its solar consumer-protection law covers companies selling or leasing solar systems to homeowners; neither gives tenants rights against you.

title: Recycling
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to tell tenants where and how to recycle, or to provide a recycling service, so the lease need not say anything about it. In a building of four or more units you must supply containers for the sanitary storage and disposal of rubbish and garbage; in a one-, two- or three-family house the state housing code makes the occupant furnish them, unless a stricter local code says otherwise, and in either case you must arrange for waste removal. The tenant must dispose of all waste from the unit in a clean and safe manner. Rhode Island's cities and towns run their own curbside and recycling programs and may require residents or building owners to separate recyclables; check the local ordinance and, if it applies, describe the recycling setup in your rules.

title: Smoke From Other Units
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on smoke drifting between units and no statute letting a tenant waive smoke-drift claims. Don't use a lease term that makes the tenant give up or limit claims against you over drifting smoke: a rental agreement may not have the tenant agree to excuse or limit any liability the law places on you, or to indemnify you for it. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease with prohibited terms the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. A plain statement that smoking is allowed in other units, with no release, is not prohibited by statute. State law already bans smoking, including e-cigarettes, in lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings and other residential buildings with more than four units; units themselves are exempt as private residences. In smaller buildings, the separate workplace smoking ban may reach enclosed hallways and stairs your employees work in.

title: Snow and Ice
bodyText:
No Rhode Island statute says who clears snow and ice at a rental. You must keep all common areas clean and safe, including shared walks, steps, driveways and parking areas, and you cannot shift that duty for shared areas to one tenant in a way that reduces what you owe the other tenants.

You may have a tenant clear snow and ice from areas only that tenant uses, such as the walk and driveway of a single-family home, but only under a writing signed by both of you, made in good faith and supported by adequate consideration; the task can't be something needed to bring the property up to code. Put the duty in the signed lease, list the areas, and state the consideration (for example, that the rent reflects the tenant's snow work).

Cities and towns may set their own sidewalk snow-clearing rules by ordinance, and an ordinance may make the property owner responsible whatever the lease says.

title: Tenant Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or video doorbell, so the lease controls: its alterations terms for anything drilled or wired in, and your building rules, which must be reasonable, clear and applied fairly to all tenants. The tenant must not damage the premises in installing or removing a device. Consider allowing devices that mount without damage and aim only at the tenant's own door or unit. Audio is a separate question: Rhode Island makes it a crime to willfully intercept a wire, electronic or oral communication, but a private person who is a party to the conversation, or has one party's prior consent, may record it unless the purpose is criminal, tortious or otherwise injurious, so a doorbell that records strangers' conversations in a hallway can raise legal problems. Never place or allow a camera that views inside a tenant's home or private areas: apart from privacy claims, using an imaging device to view intimate areas or the inside of an occupied dwelling for a sexual purpose is the crime of video voyeurism (up to three years and/or $5,000).

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in rentals. Nothing gives a tenant a right to one, and nothing limits a lease term that bans them, requires your written consent, or conditions them on proof of insurance and a safe installation. A rule on water-filled furniture adopted after the lease is signed must meet the statute's tests for rules and, if it substantially changes the tenant's bargain, needs the tenant's written consent. Whatever the lease says, the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and remains liable for water damage the tenant causes.

title: Renting a Condominium Unit
bodyText:
If you rent out a Rhode Island condominium unit, the association enforces the condominium's declaration, bylaws and rules against you. In a condominium under the older Condominium Ownership Act (one created before July 1, 1982 that has not accepted the 1982 Condominium Law), the statute itself makes tenants subject to the declaration and bylaws; under the 1982 Condominium Law no statute binds the tenant directly, so the tenant's duty to follow them rests on your lease.

After notice and a chance for a hearing the association may fine the unit owner, up to $100 a day for continuing violations or $500 per other fine in a residential condominium, and the fines, the hearing costs and any reasonable attorney's fees awarded (when the prevailing side has a Rhode Island lawyer) become a lien on your unit. The lease's association-compliance clause lets you pass those consequences to the tenant.

If your common-expense assessments go unpaid for 60 days while a tenant lives in the unit, the association may demand that the tenant pay the overdue amount and later monthly assessments directly to it; whatever the tenant pays the association counts as rent paid to you, so a demand can cut off your rent until the arrears are cleared. This direct-demand rule applies to condominiums under the 1982 Condominium Law (created after July 1, 1982, or that opted in).

No state statute addresses association rules on satellite dishes or antennas. As landlord, though, you may not agree to or do anything that would interfere with a tenant's use of a master or individual antenna system in a building served by cable television (see the telecommunications-access row).

title: Association Rules on Renting
bodyText: Rhode Island's condominium laws do not cap fees an association charges to approve a lease, regulate deposits an association collects from tenants, limit what tenant information it may ask for, or say whether a new rental restriction binds owners who bought before it was adopted. Those questions are answered by the condominium's declaration, bylaws and rules, so read them before you sign a lease and build any approval step into your timeline. In a condominium under the 1982 Condominium Law (created after July 1, 1982, or one that accepted that law), two statutory rules matter: if your assessments are 60 days overdue, the association may collect them directly from your tenant, and the tenant's payments count against rent owed to you; and if the declaration gives lessees the vote on specified matters, your tenant votes on them instead of you and gets meeting notices and records access for them. Rhode Island has no general homeowners' association statute for planned communities, so their covenants govern.

title: No Association Document Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require a lease for a condominium or other association unit to describe the association's obligations, and no statute requires you to hand the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules. Give them anyway. Your tenant will be expected to follow them, the association can fine you for the tenant's violations, and your lease can pass those fines on only if the tenant knew the rules: a rule you rely on binds a tenant only if the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when it was adopted. Attach the association's current rules to the lease, or list where the tenant can read them, and send changes when the association adopts them.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose a unit's bed bug or pest history or setting a treatment timeline. Three general rules still apply. You may not rent out a vacant unit unless it and the premises are clean, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, so treat a known infestation before a new tenant moves in. Before signing any lease you must tell the prospective tenant about any outstanding minimum housing code violations on the building, which includes an infestation an inspector has cited, and within 30 days of a citation you must give every affected tenant a copy unless you have corrected it. And the housing code decides who pays for extermination (see the pest treatment row). Disclosing a recent, treated infestation voluntarily is lawful and reduces later disputes.

title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, or to give the tenant a copy. But a newly built building may not be used or occupied until the local building official issues a certificate of use and occupancy, which is issued only after the work meets the building and fire codes and, for a property on a private well, after you document the required drinking water testing. Don't lease a unit that needs a certificate and lacks one. If an inspector has cited the building for an outstanding minimum housing code violation, you must tell a prospective tenant before signing. Your city or town may require more, such as a rental permit or inspection.

title: No Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose defective, corrosive or sulfur-emitting drywall, or a crumbling foundation, to a tenant. If such a condition affects health or safety, it falls under your general duties to comply with building and housing codes and to make all repairs needed to keep the premises fit and habitable, and if an inspector has cited it as an outstanding minimum housing code violation you must tell a prospective tenant before signing the lease.

title: Submetered Electricity
bodyText: Rhode Island has no lease disclosure rule specific to submetered electricity. The general rule covers it: the lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which are the tenant's, so if you bill the tenant for electricity measured by your own meter, say so in the lease, or the tenant may recover undisclosed fees. In an apartment house of more than ten units whose construction began after July 1, 1977, you may not use a master meter for electricity: each unit must have its own meter (publicly financed housing for elderly or disabled residents may elect a single meter). Anyone who charges for electricity furnished to a building must show on each bill the kilowatt hours used and the separate charges (base rate, adjustments, conservation costs, credits, taxes and any other fees), so use that format if you bill tenants for electricity.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to tell a tenant whether the property is in a flood zone, has flooded before, or carries flood insurance. The state's property-condition disclosure, which asks about flood plains and flood insurance, applies when real estate is sold, not when it is rented. Consider telling tenants anyway if a unit, especially a basement unit, has a known flooding history, and remind them that renters insurance often excludes flood. If a flooding problem has been cited as an outstanding housing code violation, you must tell a prospective tenant before signing. From January 1, 2027, rentals of shoreline property also need a written shoreline access disclosure, a separate rule covered in its own row.

title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general good-cause eviction law and no notice you must give tenants about one. You may end a periodic tenancy with the statutory notice, or decline to renew a fixed term, without stating a reason, as long as the reason is not retaliatory or discriminatory. Just cause is required only in narrow cases. A foreclosing lender or other foreclosing owner of a building with four or fewer units (unless exempt as a Rhode Island-based full-service lender or one with fewer than 15 Rhode Island foreclosures the prior year) may evict a bona fide tenant only for just cause (or after a disclosed binding sale contract with a bona fide buyer, and in some FHA-insured cases; a tenant may knowingly waive the protection for consideration), and within 30 days after the foreclosure must post and mail a notice giving its contact details, the address for rent and a continued-occupancy form. And no owner may evict occupants without just cause while housing-code conferences, hearings or appeals are pending or after being served with a notice of violation (see the code-order row). A mobile home park may end a lot tenancy only for the reasons in the mobile home statute, and public housing authorities must have just-cause rules.

title: No Contamination Disclosure Statute
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to tell a residential tenant that the property is or was contaminated with hazardous materials, is on a federal Superfund list, or is subject to a recorded environmental land usage restriction. If your property has a recorded environmental land usage restriction from a state-supervised cleanup, read it before leasing. Under the Department of Environmental Management's remediation rules, every such restriction runs with the land, describes the allowed uses, bars activities that could interfere with the cleanup or expose people to the remaining contamination, and lets the department enter to check compliance. It also requires you to notify the department before conveying any interest in the property and not to complete the conveyance without full disclosure of the cleanup plans and procedures. Whether a lease counts as conveying an interest for this purpose isn't settled by the rules, and court decisions weren't searched, so the cautious course is to notify the department and give the tenant the restriction's terms before signing. Owners of homes where arsenic-contaminated soil was capped must also keep the caps and other controls in place. Separate rules cover lead, radon and private wells; see those rows.

title: Disclosing Housing Code Violations
bodyText:
Before you sign any lease, tell the prospective tenant about every outstanding minimum housing code violation on the building. If an enforcing officer has served you with a notice of violation or order that you have not yet complied with, the housing code adds two steps before you lease: give the new tenant a true copy of each notice or order, and at the same time notify the enforcing officer in writing that you intend to lease, with the tenant's name and address, either by hand delivery for a receipt or by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested. Leasing without these steps is unlawful under the housing code.

During the tenancy, if you are cited, deliver a copy of the violation notice to each tenant of the affected building within 30 days unless you correct every violation to the agency's satisfaction within that time. Keep proof of each disclosure. If a unit has been designated unfit, see the condemned-premises row.

title: Rhode Island Lead Disclosure
bodyText:
For housing built before 1978, Rhode Island adds to the federal lead disclosure. Before the tenant is bound by any lease, including an oral one:
- give the EPA pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home with the insert What You Should Know about the Rhode Island Lead Law
- include a lead warning statement and a signed disclosure acknowledgment
- disclose, for the address and unit, everything you know about lead-based paint or lead hazards, a copy of each current lead certificate for the unit and common areas, a dated list of all lead inspection reports and certificates, how to get copies (you must deliver them free within 7 days of a request), basic information about the state lead rules and how they apply, and the name and contact details of the owner, registered agent or person responsible for maintaining the property.

The acknowledgment must be a stand-alone document with the property address, or its own separate page of a written lease. Keep the signed copy for 3 years or the whole tenancy, whichever is longer.

Exempt: housing built after January 1, 1978; units with a lead-free or full lead-safe certificate given to the tenant; renewals where you fully complied before and kept proof; zero-bedroom units and elderly or disability housing where no child lives; and leases of 100 days or less that cannot be renewed.

Tell occupants of any inspection results within 7 days. The Department of Health may fine up to $5,000 per violation per day.

title: Lead Certificates for Pre-1978 Rentals
bodyText:
If your rental unit was built before 1978, Rhode Island requires a valid lead certificate for every non-exempt unit, obtained by hiring a licensed lead inspector, and you must keep the property lead-safe. Give the tenant a copy of each current lead certificate for the unit and common areas as part of the pre-lease lead disclosure.

Until a pre-1978 rental dwelling has been made lead safe or lead hazard abated, you (or someone you designate) must take a lead hazard awareness seminar, have the unit and premises evaluated, correct lead hazards and keep them corrected, and give tenants basic information about lead hazard control, a copy of the independent clearance inspection and instructions for reporting deteriorating conditions.

These mitigation duties apply from the first change of ownership or tenancy after November 1, 2005, and do not let you make a tenant who has stayed continuously since January 1, 2004 move out, even temporarily, unless a child under six or pregnant occupant asks and agrees.

If a tenant in a unit where a child under six or a pregnant woman has lived for at least 30 days reports a hazard, correct it within 30 days. A new owner of a unit with such an occupant, where the previous owner had not met the requirements, gets up to 60 days, if it is visually inspected within 30 business days of the purchase.

Lead-safe or lead-free units, temporary housing, elderly housing and condominium association common areas are outside these duties. Such a household may sue to compel compliance, and whoever prevails recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees; a court may also award double or treble damages. The registry row explains the rental registry's lead certificate information and its effect on eviction filings.

title: Rhode Island Lead Notices to Tenants
bodyText:
Rhode Island's lead notices go beyond the federal disclosure and continue during the tenancy. At signing, for pre-1978 housing: the EPA pamphlet with the state insert, basic information about the state lead rules, and the certificates and report list described in the lead disclosure row; and, until the unit has been made lead safe, basic information about lead hazard control, a copy of the independent clearance inspection, and instructions for reporting deteriorating paint.

After a comprehensive environmental lead inspection, tell current occupants the results within five business days after you receive them, and tell every prospective occupant before a lease is signed (or before move-in without a lease) while a significant lead hazard remains; this duty ends once the unit reaches at least lead-safe level. Missing these notices costs $100 to $500 per violation.

For other lead inspections, notify occupants within 7 days and give a full report copy on request.

If your water supplier finds a lead service line, you must inform your tenants; and if you refuse or ignore a tenant's second request to replace a lead service line for 60 days, the tenant may end the lease and you may not withhold the deposit for that.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no meter conservation charge, on-bill energy-efficiency loan or similar meter-tied charge that you must disclose to a new tenant or deduct from rent. Electric bills show a conservation-cost line, but that is part of every customer's utility bill, not a charge you need to disclose. If the tenant pays utilities, the lease must still say which utility costs are included in rent and which are the tenant's.

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose that a rental was used to make methamphetamine or other drugs, to report a suspected drug lab, or to decontaminate before re-renting, and no law bars occupying such a property. Your general duties still apply: the unit must be fit and habitable and code-compliant when rented, and a contamination hazard that a code officer cites must be disclosed to a prospective tenant before signing. A tenant must not use the premises to maintain a narcotics nuisance or to manufacture, sell or deliver controlled substances, and for those breaches you may file for eviction without giving a chance to cure.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that the property is near a military installation or airfield, or in an aircraft noise or accident potential zone, and no law giving a tenant a right to end the lease for a missing disclosure. If a rental is close to an active airfield consider telling prospective tenants about aircraft noise anyway.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance site nearby, a demolition permit you have applied for, or a gas or electric meter that also serves other units or common areas. Two general rules still matter. If the tenant pays a utility, the lease must say which utility costs are included in rent and which are the tenant's, so a tenant-paid meter that also carries hallway lights or another unit's usage should be disclosed and the arrangement stated, or the tenant may recover the undisclosed charges. And if you plan to demolish, remember that a fixed-term lease runs to its end and a periodic tenancy needs the statutory notice to end it.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring you to disclose mold to a tenant or setting mold-specific duties. Mold falls under your general obligations: comply with the building and housing codes affecting health and safety, make all repairs needed to keep the premises fit and habitable, and, before signing any lease, tell the prospective tenant about any outstanding minimum housing code violations on the building, which would include a cited moisture or mold condition. The tenant must keep the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits and use facilities such as ventilation reasonably. Fixing leaks promptly and documenting the unit's condition at move-in is the practical protection.

title: Owner and Manager Disclosure
bodyText:
At or before the start of every tenancy, give the tenant in writing the name, address and number of (1) the person authorized to manage the premises and (2) an owner, or a person authorized to act for the owner, for service of legal papers and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. Keep the information current, for example after a sale or a change of manager; the duty binds every successor landlord, owner or manager.

Whoever fails to make the disclosure becomes the landlord's agent for service of process and notices, and for performing the landlord's obligations under the law and the lease and applying the rent collected to them; a manager who doesn't disclose is treated as the landlord.

The lease is a convenient place for the disclosure. Failing to disclose does not by itself block an eviction, but separate rules do: a landlord not in compliance with the state rental registry may not file a nonpayment eviction (see the registry row), and nonresident landlords must keep an in-state agent (see that row).

title: Private Well Test Results
bodyText: If the rental is served by a private well, give the tenant the results of any previous well water testing before the lease is signed. Rhode Island's law directs the Department of Health to make its rules require property owners to disclose those results before a sale or lease of the property. The department's current private well rule spells out only the sale side (an owner must make the last ten years of well test reports available to a buyer), so no rule sets a form or deadline for leases. Treat the statute's direction as a pre-lease disclosure anyway and keep proof you made it. State law does not require you to test the well before leasing. Testing is required before a sale or transfer, before a certificate of occupancy is issued for a building the well serves (new or previously occupied), and when a new well is put in to serve an existing building. A well you supply is part of the plumbing and water supply you must keep in working order and safe, and the department's rule treats elevated results as calling for bottled or other safe drinking water until the problem is fixed.

title: No Pest Control Notice Rule
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to tell tenants about a pest control contract or to give advance notice before pesticides are applied in a rental building, and the lease need not say anything about it. If treatment requires entering a unit, the ordinary access rules apply: at least two days' notice, entry only at reasonable times, except in an emergency. One special case: if a tenant runs a family day care home or other child care program in the unit, only a certified or licensed commercial applicator may apply pesticides there during regular business hours, enrolled children may not enter a treated area until the label says it is safe, and the parents of enrolled children must get notice at least 24 hours before any application (gels, baits in tamper-resistant containers, disinfectants and similar products are excluded); coordinate with the provider before any treatment. Telling all tenants in advance about building-wide treatments is good practice.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warnings do not apply in Rhode Island, and Rhode Island has no similar law requiring landlords to warn tenants about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm on rental property. Rhode Island's chemical right-to-know rules protect employees in workplaces, so they matter only for your own staff, not your tenants. Lead, radon and private well rules are separate; see those rows.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether annually or when rent changes. A tenant who is 65 or older or disabled, and was domiciled in Rhode Island for the whole year, may claim the state property tax relief credit if their household income qualifies; the statute counts 20% of the gross rent they paid for the year as the property tax they bore (none if the unit is legally exempt from property tax), so no landlord figure is needed. The tenant must give the Division of Taxation reasonable proof of rent paid and your name and address (or your managing agent's). You are not required by statute to sign a rent certificate or issue receipts, but providing a year-end rent statement on request helps older and disabled tenants claim the credit and costs you little.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to test a rental for radon or to disclose radon results to tenants, and the rule does not vary by floor level. Mandatory radon testing and mitigation apply to public buildings (buildings a state or town agency owns, manages, leases, furnishes or occupies, and public schools) and 'high priority' buildings: schools and licensed child care facilities caring for five or more unrelated children. If such a child care facility operates in your building, ask the Department of Health whether the testing duty reaches you as owner. Sales are different: for purchase and sale agreements signed on or after June 1, 2027, selling a residential property, including a multi-family home or apartment complex, will require a radon test within a year before closing, with results shared with the buyer and lender and mitigation of levels above 4.0 pCi/L, unless an exemption applies. If you know of high radon results in a rental, telling tenants is good practice.

title: Rhode Island Required Disclosures
bodyText: Rhode Island's required disclosures, by timing. At or before the tenancy starts, in writing: the name, address and number of the manager and of the owner or owner's agent for legal papers and notices. In the lease: any fees beyond rent, listed in the rent section with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format); which utilities rent includes and which the tenant pays; and any renters-insurance requirement (without a written lease, give these in writing). With the written lease: a copy of your liability insurance declaration page, and a new copy at each renewal. Before signing: any outstanding minimum housing code violations, plus a true copy of any unresolved violation notice or order with written notice to the enforcing officer; for pre-1978 housing, the state lead disclosure on its own page; for a private well, prior test results (the statute directs the health department to require this before a lease, and its rule so far covers only sales, so give them anyway). From January 1, 2027, for shoreline property: the written shoreline access disclosure. During the tenancy: 60 days' written notice of a rent increase (120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62; neither applies in independent living, assisted living or congregate care facilities); 30 days' written notice before a required fee changes; copies of new code violation notices within 30 days; lead inspection results; and notice once you are 120 days behind on the mortgage. Undisclosed fees can be recovered. No state form must open the lease, and no just-cause coverage notice is required.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no state rule requiring you to give tenants a copy of, or attach to the lease, a variance or extension granted from the housing code. Local housing boards of review can modify an enforcing officer's order, extend the time to comply or grant a variance, and none of those decisions carries a statutory tenant-notice duty. But a violation that a variance or extension leaves uncorrected is still an outstanding violation: tell a prospective tenant about it before signing, and give current tenants a copy of a new violation notice within 30 days unless you correct it. Sharing the board's decision with affected tenants is good practice.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require a lease notice about the sex offender registry, does not require you to tell tenants that a registered offender lives in or near the building, and has no statute barring landlords from considering registry information. The state's public registry website warns that its information must not be used to unlawfully injure or harass anyone named in it, so never share or act on it in a way that does. Residency limits apply to the registrant, not to you: a registered offender may not knowingly live within 300 feet of a school, or within 1,000 feet for a level-three offender. If you screen applicants for criminal history, apply one written policy to everyone.

title: Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: Rhode Island limits where registered sex offenders may live, but the duty is the offender's, not yours. A person required to register who knowingly lives within 300 feet of a school commits a felony; for a level-three offender the distance is 1,000 feet. A school here means the buildings and land of a public or private kindergarten, elementary, middle or secondary school, and the distance runs from the nearest boundary line of the residence's property to the nearest boundary line of the school's property. No Rhode Island statute requires you to check the registry, bars you from renting to a registrant, makes it a crime to lease to two registrants who live together, or requires you to disclose nearby registrants. If you screen applicants for registration status, apply the same written standard to everyone.

title: Lease Layout Rules
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no font size, type size or first-page placement for a residential lease or any lease disclosure, and has no single-family residence occupancy notice. Two placement rules do apply. If any fee beyond rent applies to the unit, the lease must list it in the same section as the rent and say that additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy program requires a different lease format); a tenant may recover any fee that was not disclosed this way. And for target housing (generally pre-1978), the lead disclosure acknowledgment must be a stand-alone document that includes the property address, or its own separate page if it is part of a written lease. Otherwise you choose the layout; a readable type size and clear headings still help show the tenant saw each required term.

title: Source of Income and Housing Vouchers
bodyText: Rhode Island fair housing law protects a renter's lawful source of income: child support, alimony, Social Security, SSI, any other public assistance (including medical or veterans assistance), and any federal, state or local rental assistance or housing subsidy, including Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, together with any requirement that comes with the program. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, misrepresent availability, delay an application or advertise a preference because of it. You may not ask about it, except to confirm the source, amount and expected duration of income to check that the applicant meets your nondiscriminatory standards. If you use a minimum-income test, apply it only to the tenant's share of the rent after any rental assistance or subsidy. Because program requirements are part of the protected source, refusing because of a voucher program's requirements is unlawful too. One exemption: if the building has three units or fewer and you live in one of them, you may refuse based on source of income. No lease statement is required.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law requiring you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has a fire sprinkler system or when it was last inspected. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a building and fire code question: the state Fire Safety Code applies to all structures unless specifically exempted, and for existing buildings the local fire official enforces it as the Uniform Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101) apply to existing structures. Those code regulations were not part of this search, so ask your local fire official what your building needs. If you mention sprinklers in a listing or the lease, describe them accurately.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Rentals
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires you to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in an existing rental home or apartment building; the sprinkler mandates written into the General Laws cover places of assembly such as nightclubs. Sprinkler requirements for housing come instead from the state Fire Safety Code, which applies to all structures unless specifically exempted and, for existing buildings, is enforced as NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 apply to existing structures, and from the building codes. If you change a building's use or type of occupancy (for example, converting a single-family house or commercial space into apartments), the building must meet the rehabilitation building and fire code for existing buildings, or new-construction rules where that code does not apply, which can bring sprinkler requirements with it. The code regulations were not part of this search: confirm your building's requirements with the local fire official before buying, converting or adding units.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness at the Property
bodyText: Rhode Island's rule on psychologically impacted property is written for sales. For land and buildings of one to four units, the fact or suspicion that a property is psychologically impacted is not a material fact requiring disclosure, and no claim arises against a seller or agent for not telling a buyer. Psychologically impacted includes an occupant who has or had, or is suspected of having, HIV, AIDS or another disease medical evidence shows is highly unlikely to spread through living in a home, and a property suspected at any time of being the site of a homicide, other felony or suicide. The statute names sellers and buyers, and no statute says whether you must tell a prospective tenant, so don't treat the sales rule as protection in a rental. The statute also never authorizes a false statement: if an applicant asks, answer truthfully or decline to answer, but never mislead. If a licensed broker handles your rental of a building with four or fewer units, the broker treats such facts as confidential information.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to give tenants a state-prepared statement, summary or bill of tenant rights, or to attach one to the lease. (Owners of federally insured or assisted developments must include a summary of tenants' rights in the notices and offers that law requires before prepaying the mortgage, not renewing a Section 8 contract or selling the development; those are event notices, not lease documents.) The Executive Office of Housing must publish a written guide to landlords' and tenants' rights and duties under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, in English and Spanish, update it at least every two years and post it on its website, but no law makes you hand it out. Giving tenants the link is a good practice, not a duty. The one state-prepared document you must hand over at the start of a tenancy is lead information: for target housing (generally pre-1978), before the tenant is bound, give the EPA pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home with the Rhode Island insert What You Should Know about the Rhode Island Lead Law.

title: Condominium Conversion and Tenant Purchase Rights
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statewide rent cap or just-cause law, so no notice about one belongs in your lease. Tenants do get notice and purchase rights in two situations. Condominium conversion: if units in your building will be sold as condominiums, each residential tenant and subtenant must get notice of the conversion, with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before having to vacate, or one year for a tenant aged 62 or older or one who has lived in the unit continuously for 10 years or more. During the notice period rent may not rise, the terms of the tenancy may not change, and the tenant cannot be made to leave except for nonpayment of rent, waste or disturbing other tenants; a lease also may not be ended against its own terms. A tenant may cancel the lease without penalty if all lease obligations have been met. Each tenant gets the first chance to buy the unit (60 days, or 180 days for the protected tenants), and if the tenant does not buy, for the next 180 days you may not offer the unit to anyone else at a better price or on better terms (the purchase right does not apply to a unit that will be used only for nonresidential purposes or whose converted boundaries do not substantially match the rented unit). You must pay reasonable moving costs within 50 miles to a tenant who is disabled or 62 or older. Missing the notice is a defense to an action for possession. These rules come from the Condominium Act; the older Condominium Ownership Act's conversion rules apply only to condominiums created before July 1, 1982. Federally assisted housing: an owner ending a Section 8 contract must give two years' notice to Rhode Island Housing, copy the tenant association and post it, and must first offer the development for sale, in this order, to the tenant association, Rhode Island Housing, the local housing authority and the city or town before a sale, lease, prepayment or condominium conversion that ends the assistance or its use restrictions. At least 90 days before prepaying the mortgage or not renewing a Section 8 contract, the owner must also give each assisted household a written notice of intent summarizing its rights, pay move-in help (up to $500) and relocation costs (up to $450), and offer a household in good standing at least a one-year lease extension (two years for certain households with a disabled or senior member or a child under 10) at a tenant share of no more than 30% of income, unless the owner records a covenant keeping the income restrictions.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law requiring a lease or notice telling tenants that a property is exempt from rent limits, just-cause eviction rules or tenant purchase rights, because the state has no general rent cap or just-cause law to be exempt from. The narrower rules that do exist (just cause after a foreclosure of a building with four or fewer units, and tenant notice and purchase rights on condominium conversion or on sale of federally assisted housing) carry no exemption notice either. Don't add a statement borrowed from another state's lease, such as California's 'not subject to the rent limits' notice: it cites law that does not apply in Rhode Island.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Notice
bodyText: Rhode Island has no truth-in-renting law: no statute requires your lease to carry a notice that it must comply with state law, warns tenants about unenforceable clauses, or delivers a state truth-in-renting statement. What Rhode Island does require is specific content. A written lease must list any fees beyond rent in the same section as the rent and say additional fees may apply (unless a state or federal subsidy for the tenant or unit requires a different lease format), say which utilities are included in rent and which the tenant pays, and state any renters-insurance requirement. If the lease passes real estate tax increases on to the tenant, the clause is void unless it limits the tenant to the unit's proportionate share, states the exact percentage, and promises a proportionate refund of any abatement. You must give the tenant your liability insurance declaration page with the written lease, disclose in writing who manages the property and who accepts notices for the owner, and for target housing include the lead warning statement and acknowledgment. A lease may not waive the security deposit rules or include the provisions the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act prohibits.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Rhode Island zoning law makes it easier to build and rent an accessory dwelling unit (ADU): a separate, complete living unit on the same lot as a legally established single-family or multi-family home, such as a detached cottage, a unit over a garage or an addition. One ADU per lot is allowed by right, through an administrative building permit only, if it is on an owner-occupied property as a reasonable accommodation for family members with disabilities, on a residential lot of at least 20,000 square feet, or inside the existing footprint of the home or an existing accessory structure. A city or town may not limit who rents the ADU by family relationship or age (unless a federal affordability subsidy requires it), require low- or moderate-income tenants outside inclusionary or comprehensive-permit projects, or revoke a legal ADU when the property or the occupancy changes hands. Condominium or homeowners association rules that conflict with these protections are void. One limit binds you: an ADU may not be offered or rented for tourist or transient use, meaning occupancy for less than 30 consecutive days, or through a hosting platform for such stays, so rent it as a regular residential tenancy of at least 30 consecutive days, not a short-term rental.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText:
Your lease cannot take away the tenant's fire and casualty rights or your duty to re-rent after abandonment, because both are in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and a lease may not make the tenant waive any right or remedy under that Act.

If fire or another casualty substantially impairs the tenant's use of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, getting back prepaid rent and the security deposit less the deductions the deposit statute allows, or, if staying is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value, counted from the date of the fire. The section has no exception for a fire the tenant caused, so plan on these rights applying either way; your remedy then is a damages claim against a tenant who caused it negligently or deliberately.

If a tenant abandons the unit, you must send the certified-letter notice and then make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental; if you don't, the lease is treated as ended when you learned of the abandonment.

A waiver clause is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' rent and attorney's fees.

title: Families With Children
bodyText: Rhode Island fair housing law protects families with children: anyone under 18 living with a parent, a legal custodian or the custodian's written designee, and anyone who is pregnant or securing custody of a child. You may not refuse to rent, ask about familial status, set different terms or fees, misrepresent availability or advertise a preference because a household has children. Exemptions are narrow: a two-unit building where you live in the other unit; an owner-occupied building of four units or fewer where a unit is already occupied by a senior or infirm person for whom children would be a demonstrated hardship; housing under a state or federal elderly program; housing solely for people 62 or older; and qualifying 55-or-older housing. You may apply reasonable occupancy limits set by state or local codes, by space and safety, to every household alike. No statute requires your lease to address children. Lead law adds a rule: you may not retaliate against a tenant, with or without a lease, for seeking lead-safe housing, including for a pregnant woman or a child under six.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Your lease may not authorize anyone, including you or your attorney, to confess judgment against the tenant on any claim arising out of the rental agreement, meaning a clause letting a court judgment be entered against the tenant without a contested case. Such a clause is unenforceable. If you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. Rhode Island court rules provide no confessed-judgment or confessed-ejectment procedure for residential tenancies, so a claim for unpaid rent or possession must go through the ordinary District Court process.

title: Deceptive Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: Rhode Island's Deceptive Trade Practices Act makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce unlawful, including any act that is unfair or deceptive to the consumer and any practice that misleads the public in a material respect. Trade and commerce covers advertising, offering, selling or distributing services and real or personal property, and a consumer who leases goods or services for household purposes and loses money may sue for actual damages or $500, whichever is greater, with possible triple damages and attorney's fees. The statute does not say expressly whether renting an apartment is covered, and we did not search case law, so assume the Act may apply to your advertising, fees and dealings with tenants. Since January 1, 2026, short-term lodging prices must be advertised as the federal junk-fee rule requires. The Act has no rule about blank spaces in a lease or giving the tenant a copy at signing. Plainly, don't misstate rent, fees, amenities or the condition of a unit.

title: Keeping Survivor Information Confidential
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, if a tenant or household member gives you written verification to end a lease early as a victim of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must keep that verification, the fact that the person is a victim, and their personal identifying information (such as address, Social Security number, email, phone number and birthdate) in strict confidence. Don't disclose any of it to any other person or entity unless the victim asks for and consents to the disclosure in writing, or another law requires it. You also may not refuse to rent to an applicant because they ended a lease this way or asked for a lock change, and a lease cannot waive these rules. Even before any termination, fair housing law bars asking applicants or tenants whether anyone in the household is or has been a domestic abuse victim. If a tenant is in the Secretary of State's Address Confidentiality Program, knowingly obtaining or disclosing their actual address without authority carries a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per disclosure. The District Court can order you to stop a violation.

title: No Employee Background-Check Mandate
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to run background checks on maintenance workers, property managers or other employees who have keys to or enter tenants' units. If you choose to screen, Rhode Island employment law (not landlord-tenant law) governs how and when an employer may ask about criminal records, and that law was not reviewed for this row. What landlord-tenant law does control is entry: whoever enters for you must follow the two-day notice and reasonable-time rules, and you remain responsible for how your staff use keys.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute written specifically against lease clauses that penalize a tenant because you served an eviction notice or filed an eviction case. Such a clause is still limited by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act or agree to pay your attorney's fees in a way the Act does not allow, and the Act allows fees in a nonpayment case only if the tenant received a five-day demand notice in the prior six months and the nonpayment was willful. A clause that does either is unenforceable, and knowingly using it lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. So don't add an eviction fee, notice fee or flat penalty for being sued; recover only what the Act and the court award.

title: No Liability Waivers or Indemnity for Your Liability
bodyText: Your lease may not excuse or limit any liability the law places on you as landlord, or make the tenant indemnify you for that liability or its costs. That covers clauses saying you are not responsible for injuries, property damage, repairs, security or acts of your employees, and hold-harmless or indemnity clauses that shift your own legal liability to the tenant. Such a clause is unenforceable, and knowingly using one lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees. What a lease may still do: hold the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, household or guests cause, require renters insurance if the lease says so, and leave you free to sue a tenant who negligently or deliberately causes a fire. Write those terms as the tenant's own responsibilities, not as a release of yours.

title: Fair Housing in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island's Fair Housing Practices Act protects more groups than federal law: race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income (including housing vouchers), veterans with an honorable or general discharge, servicemembers, country of ancestral origin, disability, age (adults 18 and over), familial status, and victims of domestic abuse or people who have sought a protective order. Treat homelessness (housing status) as protected too; it appears in the Act's definitions. You may not ask about these traits, refuse to rent, set different terms, misrepresent availability, delay an application, advertise a preference or retaliate against anyone who complains. Exemptions are narrow and class-by-class: families with children (owner-occupied two-unit buildings and senior housing), source of income (owner-occupied buildings of three units or fewer), religious organizations and private clubs, and choosing a roommate of a particular gender for a unit you will share. There is no general small-landlord exemption and none for advertising. A tenant may file with the Commission for Human Rights within one year; penalties reach $10,000 for a first violation and $50,000 for repeats, plus damages and attorney's fees, and either side may move the case to Superior Court, where a jury and punitive damages are available.

title: No Foreign-Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law restricting foreign governments, foreign adversaries or noncitizens from buying, owning or leasing real estate, and no lease-length rule tied to a tenant's nationality. State law says the opposite: aliens may take, hold, transfer and convey real estate and sue to recover possession on the same terms as U.S. citizens. So nothing in state law stops you from renting to, or buying from, a foreign national or foreign-owned company. Separately, you may not ask applicants or tenants about immigration or citizenship status (see the immigration-status rules).

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute written specifically about charging tenants for fines a city, town or the state imposes on you. But your lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for liability the law places on you, or the costs of that liability, and a fine for breaking your own legal duties (housing-code repairs, registration, smoke alarms, permits) is that kind of liability. A clause making the tenant reimburse such fines is unenforceable, and knowingly using it exposes you to actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees. Where the tenant caused the problem, for example by breaking the tenant's own housing-code duties or damaging the unit, you may recover your loss as damages for the tenant's breach, so write the lease in those terms. Some code citations, such as fire-code citations, can be issued to an occupant directly.

title: No Immigration or Citizenship Inquiries
bodyText: Since July 2, 2025, you and anyone acting for you may not make any inquiry about, or prompted by, the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, applicant or occupant of residential rental property, and may not require anyone to make a statement, representation or certification about their status. Don't base rental decisions on status either: you can't lawfully learn it by asking, and country of ancestral origin is a fair housing protected class. Remove citizenship, Social Security-only and immigration questions from applications and leases. You may still ask for information or documents needed to verify an applicant's income and financial qualifications, or to verify the identity of an applicant or occupant, and you may comply with any obligation under federal law (for example, a federal housing program's rules). Accept identity documents without treating them as proof of status: a Rhode Island driver privilege card or state ID may not be used as evidence of citizenship or immigration status. No city, town or housing agency may require you to collect or report status, and no Rhode Island law bars renting to someone because of their status.

title: Jury Waivers Not Offered
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute addresses a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease, and the library does not offer one. The state constitution keeps the right of trial by jury inviolate. An eviction or other landlord-tenant case starts in District Court, and any party may appeal within five days after judgment to Superior Court for a new trial on all questions of law and fact; there, a party must claim a jury under the court rules or the right is treated as waived.
