The Act's ban on waiving rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not plainly reach the jury right, which comes from the constitution, and whether a court would enforce a lease jury waiver signed before any dispute is a case-law question we did not research. If you want one, get legal advice and draft your own. From January 1, 2027, the five days expressly include weekends and holidays, and the party appealing pays a $75 filing fee instead of the old $50 attorney's fee and minimum costs.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require apartment owners, at any size of complex, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a key log or background-check employees who can get into units. A written practice is still sensible risk management: limit who holds master keys, record who checks keys out, and rekey when keys are lost or staff leave. Two rules already shape how keys are used. Anyone entering for you must follow the entry rules (consent not unreasonably withheld, at least two days' notice except in an emergency or where impracticable, at reasonable times). And since July 1, 2026, on a qualifying request from a tenant or household member facing a threat of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must within two business days make a good-faith effort to change the locks or let the tenant do so.

title: Penalty for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: If you deliberately use a lease containing terms you know Rhode Island prohibits, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and reasonable attorney's fees, on top of the term being unenforceable. The prohibited terms are those that make the tenant waive or give up rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, authorize a confession of judgment, make the tenant pay your attorney's fees in a way the Act does not allow, or excuse, limit or make the tenant indemnify you for liability the law places on you. Because the first category covers any right in the Act, a clause waiving deposit rules, casualty rights, entry notice or termination notice also counts. A real estate tax pass-through that leaves out the required statements is void but outside this penalty. A waiver of the survivor protections in effect since July 1, 2026 is void under its own section and, because those protections are part of the Act, is also a prohibited waiver that carries the penalty. Use the library's state-specific clauses instead of an out-of-state form.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, and no law requiring you, as a landlord, to answer police or child-protection investigators' requests for information about tenants or to give them access to a unit. But the reporting duties Rhode Island puts on every person bind you and your staff. Anyone who has reasonable cause to know or suspect that a child has been abused or neglected must pass that information to the Department of Children, Youth and Families within 24 hours, and a knowing failure is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to a year in jail, or both (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 40-11-3 and 40-11-6.1). Anyone who has reasonable cause to believe that a person 60 or older has been abused, neglected or exploited, or is self-neglecting, must report immediately to the Office of Healthy Aging, and failing to report abuse, neglect or exploitation carries a fine of up to $1,000 (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-66-8). Anyone who knows of a death that suggests a crime, violence, apparent suicide or a suspicious or unusual manner, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately notify the local police or the office of state medical examiners, and willfully failing to report it, or touching or moving the body or nearby items without the medical examiners' order, is a misdemeanor (R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-4-7). And anyone other than the victim who knows that a first-degree sexual assault is taking place in their presence must immediately notify the police, and knowingly failing to is a misdemeanor (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 11-37-3.1 and 11-37-3.3). The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act already gives you remedies for serious criminal conduct at the premises, and some cities and towns run their own nuisance or crime-free programs. One reporting duty applies only to short-term rentals: since January 1, 2026, every operator of a residential unit offered for tourist or transient use through a hosting platform must complete human trafficking awareness training within 180 days of first listing and every year after, and must adopt procedures for reporting suspected human trafficking to the National Human Trafficking Hotline or local police. For ordinary tenancies, respond to a warrant or subpoena as the law requires, and get advice before sharing tenant information informally.

title: What a Rhode Island Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Rhode Island has no single list of terms every lease must contain, does not require a written lease, and has no statute requiring you to hand the tenant a signed copy (do it anyway). What it does require is specific content. In a written lease: any fees beyond rent, listed in the same section as the rent with a statement that additional fees may apply (unless a subsidy program requires a different format); which utilities are included in rent and which the tenant pays; and any renters-insurance requirement. With an oral tenancy, give the fee list, the utility split and any insurance requirement in writing, and give 30 days' written notice before changing fees. A tenant may recover any fee you did not disclose this way. At or before the start of every tenancy, disclose in writing the name, address and number of the manager and of the owner or owner's agent for notices, and keep it current; give a copy of your liability insurance declaration page with the written lease. For target housing, include the lead warning statement and acknowledgment, even in oral leases. Any agreement for the tenant to do repairs must be in a signed writing. If the lease passes real estate tax increases on to the tenant, the clause must state the tenant's proportionate share, the exact percentage and a proportionate refund of any abatement, or it is void. From January 1, 2027, shoreline property needs a written shoreline access disclosure.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island sets no minimum type size for a residential lease, and no court rule or statute bars you from relying on a lease, or part of one, because the print is small. Type-size rules in Rhode Island law apply to other contracts, such as car-rental agreements, insurance premium finance agreements and home-solicitation and retail installment contracts. Print your lease clearly anyway: a tenant who can read the terms is less likely to dispute them, and the lease's required disclosures (fees in the rent section, the utility split, any renters-insurance requirement, the lead acknowledgment) only protect you if the tenant can see them.

title: Terms a Rhode Island Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's list of prohibited provisions is not the only limit on a Rhode Island lease. A lease may not: make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act; authorize a confession of judgment; make the tenant pay your attorney's fees beyond what the Act allows; excuse or limit your legal liability or make the tenant indemnify you for it; let you collect rent free of your repair and code duties; waive the security deposit rules; waive the survivor early-termination, no-refusal and lock-change protections in effect since July 1, 2026; give you a lien on the tenant's household goods or a right to seize property for rent; charge a convenience fee on rent unless you also accept a fee-free payment method; require a statement of immigration or citizenship status; pass on real estate tax increases without stating the tenant's proportional share, the exact percentage and a refund of any abatement; bar a tenant who stays within the state's possession and transfer limits from using cannabis by non-smoked, non-vaporized means or giving it away without payment; bar religious items, displayed out of sincere religious belief, on the entry door or door frame that total no more than 25 square inches (unless an item threatens health or safety or violates the law); or charge a tenant with a disability extra for a guide dog or other trained personal assistive animal (the tenant remains liable for damage it causes). Tenant repair or maintenance duties need a good-faith writing signed by both parties and adequate consideration, can never cover code compliance, and cannot reduce your duties to other tenants. Knowingly using a term the Act prohibits costs actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees, and a court may refuse to enforce any unconscionable term.

title: Questions You May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Rhode Island bars more than discrimination: you and your agents may not ask, in writing or orally, about an applicant's or tenant's race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital status, lawful source of income, veteran or servicemember status, country of ancestral origin, disability, age or familial status, or whether anyone in the household is or has been a domestic abuse victim or has sought a protective order. Since July 2, 2025, you also may not ask about immigration or citizenship status or require a statement about it. Questions you may ask: whether the applicant is 18 or older; questions confirming the source, amount and expected duration of income to apply your nondiscriminatory standards; questions verifying identity and financial qualifications; and age questions if the housing qualifies as 62-or-older or 55-or-older housing. Review application forms, screening scripts and online portals: a question about marital status, children, disability, benefits type or national origin can itself be a violation, even if you never use the answer.

title: No Senior Housing Staff Work Card
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require work cards or background checks for maintenance or management staff in private housing for people 55 or older, or in any other private rental housing. Rules that do require criminal records checks cover licensed health-care settings, such as long-term-care hospitals and personal care aides, and public housing authorities' elderly housing, not a private landlord's employees. If your community qualifies as 55-or-older or 62-or-older housing under fair housing law, that status turns on occupancy, facilities and published policies, not on staff screening. Screening staff who have keys to units of older residents is still prudent, following Rhode Island employment law.

title: No State Owner-Occupancy Rental Limit
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statewide law limiting the rental of homes in single-family zones to owners who live on the lot. State zoning law points the other way: households are a permitted use in every residential zoning district, and one accessory dwelling unit per lot is allowed by right in three situations, only one of which (an ADU built as a reasonable accommodation for family members with disabilities) requires the property to be owner-occupied. A city or town may not revoke a legally established ADU when the title or occupancy changes. Local zoning ordinances still govern use, density and short-term rentals, so check the town's rules before converting or renting a property. Separately, a 2025 state tax on certain non-owner-occupied residential property may apply to rented homes.

title: Hot Water Temperature
bodyText: Rhode Island sets a minimum, not a maximum, for hot water. The state housing code defines heated water as water heated to at least 120 degrees Fahrenheit, and every unit's kitchen sink, bathroom sink and tub or shower must supply an adequate amount of heated and unheated running water under pressure at all times; you may not rent a unit that falls short. Your landlord-tenant duty matches it: supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for it or the hot water comes from equipment in the tenant's exclusive control on the tenant's own utility connection. No statute requires you to set a water heater no higher than a stated temperature or to reset it before each new tenant. Set it at or a little above 120 degrees: too low breaks the code, and much higher risks scalding. Local codes may be stricter.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: Rhode Island has no law requiring you to install radiator covers when a tenant asks, or to attach a radiator-cover rider or notice to the lease. Your general duties still cover steam and hot-water heat: keep heating facilities in good and safe working order, and supply reasonable heat between October 1 and May 1 as the housing code requires. A hot, exposed radiator in a home with young children is a foreseeable injury risk, so consider offering covers on request. Local codes may say more.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute requiring window guards, window stops or other window-fall protection in rental housing, and no window-guard notice in the lease. The state housing code's window rules are about light, ventilation and screens: every habitable room needs a window or skylight to the outdoors, part of it openable, and screens are required in insect season. Rhode Island's building codes adopt the 2021 international building and residential codes, and the state's own amendments add no window-guard or window-stop rule. The model codes' provisions on window sill heights and opening limits for new construction weren't reviewed here, so ask your building official if you build, convert or replace windows. If young children live in an upper-floor unit, installing window stops or guards on request is a sensible safety step, as long as they don't block a required emergency exit.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Rhode Island protects tenants who organize: you may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization. If you act within six months after a protected complaint, the law presumes retaliation unless you produce evidence otherwise, and a tenant who proves retaliation gets the Act's retaliation remedies and a defense to eviction. You may still evict for unpaid rent or for a code violation the tenant's household caused. State law gives ordinary tenants no separate right to hold meetings in common areas, distribute literature door to door or invite organizers into the building, so apply your building rules on common areas and solicitation evenly and never single out organizing. In federally assisted developments, a tenant association that represents a majority of tenants receives notices and a first chance to buy the property before a sale or conversion that ends the assistance.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: You may not turn down an applicant who pays with a Housing Choice Voucher or other rental assistance because the program will inspect the unit, require a lease addendum or impose other program paperwork. Rhode Island defines a protected lawful source of income to include any federal, state or local rental assistance or housing subsidy, including Section 8 vouchers, and any requirement associated with the program, so refusing because of the inspection is treated as refusing because of the voucher. The one exemption: a building of three units or fewer where you live in one unit. Rhode Island has no statute on a tenant who refuses a subsidized-housing inspection; any such rule comes from the federal program and your program contract, and you still need to follow the state entry rules (consent not unreasonably withheld, at least two days' notice except in an emergency). If a unit fails inspection, the program's repair and payment rules apply.

title: Keeping Tenant Information Confidential
bodyText: Rhode Island has no general law listing what a landlord may not disclose about tenants or applicants, but several specific rules apply. Since July 1, 2026, if a tenant gives you verification to end a lease as a survivor of abuse, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, you must keep it, the victim status and the household's personal identifying information (address, Social Security number, email, phone, birthdate) strictly confidential, disclosing only on the victim's written request and consent or where the law requires. Knowingly obtaining or disclosing the actual address of someone in the state's Address Confidentiality Program without authority carries a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per disclosure. A real estate licensee working for you treats a client's finances, offers and motivations as confidential information. And if you keep Social Security, driver's license, financial account or health information, the state's Identity Theft Protection Act requires security, retention limits, secure destruction and breach notices (see the tenant-records rules). Outside these rules, share tenant information only as needed to run the tenancy, such as with a screening company, a collection agency or a court.

title: Screening Applicants in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island has no single tenant-screening act, but several rules shape screening. You may not charge an application fee. You may require an official state criminal background check and a credit check; if the applicant supplies one issued within 90 days you may not charge for it, and otherwise you may charge only the actual cost and must give the applicant a copy. A minimum-income test may count only the share of rent the tenant will pay after any voucher or subsidy. You may not ask about fair housing traits, domestic-abuse status or immigration status. Since July 1, 2026, you may not refuse an applicant because they ended an earlier lease as a survivor of abuse or asked a landlord to change locks. An applicant whose conviction was expunged may lawfully answer that they were never convicted. Rhode Island has no conditional-offer or look-back rule for criminal history, but if you deny housing to a holder of a certificate of recovery and re-entry based on a criminal records check, the law bars claims against you for that denial. Use one written standard for everyone, applied the same way.

title: Asbestos in the Building
bodyText: Rhode Island has no asbestos disclosure rule for leases, but the state asbestos law applies to rental buildings. If your building has friable (crumbling or easily damaged) asbestos, you must not let anyone be exposed to it where the exposure breaks the asbestos law, a Department of Health asbestos regulation, or an abatement plan the Department approved. Any occupant, including a tenant or the parent of a child living there, may ask the Department of Health in writing to inspect the building for friable asbestos or to enforce an abatement plan; the Department must answer within 45 days, and the complainant's name stays confidential. Removal or repair of friable asbestos is regulated work that follows the Department's rules and licensing. Before renovating, or if a tenant reports damaged pipe insulation, ceiling or floor material, have it assessed.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant law has no rule of its own on what happens when a tenant files for bankruptcy; a search of the Rhode Island General Laws and the 2025 and 2026 public laws found none. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act says general principles of law, including bankruptcy, supplement it, so federal bankruptcy law decides whether you can continue an eviction, collect past-due rent or enforce a lease term that ends the lease because of the bankruptcy. If a tenant tells you they have filed, stop collection and eviction steps and get advice on federal bankruptcy law before going further.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Rhode Island Leases: Why the Library Does Not Offer One
bodyText: Rhode Island's Arbitration Act makes a clearly written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable (R.I. Gen. Laws § 10-3-2(a)). In consumer arbitration, the right to a lawyer cannot be waived, and a drafting party that doesn't pay the arbitration fees within 30 days of the due date loses the right to arbitrate and faces court sanctions (§§ 10-3-22 to 10-3-25). The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is the problem. A rental agreement may not make the tenant waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Act (§ 34-18-17(a)(1)), and the Act places claims arising under it in the district or housing court (§ 34-18-9). If you deliberately use a lease containing terms you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent and attorney's fees (§ 34-18-17(b)). Whether an arbitration clause counts as such a waiver is unsettled. Federal arbitration law may override a rule that requires a courtroom, but because Rhode Island attaches a penalty to the lease term itself, the library does not offer an arbitration clause for Rhode Island.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Rhode Island follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (R.I. Gen. Laws § 6A-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (R.I. Gen. Laws § 6A-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Rhode Island's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-12). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Tenant Animals Left Behind or Without Care
bodyText:
Rhode Island's dog law treats as an "owner or keeper" anyone keeping, harboring or having charge or control of an animal, and anyone who lets a dog, cat, ferret or other domestic animal habitually be fed in their yard or premises (R.I. Gen. Laws § 4-13-1.2(8)). No set number of days applies. So if you take in and feed a pet a tenant left behind, you may take on the keeper's duties, including adequate feed, water and veterinary care for a dog (R.I. Gen. Laws § 4-13-42(b)). The cruelty law likewise treats as a guardian, with an owner's responsibilities, anyone who harbors or has control, custody or possession of an animal (R.I. Gen. Laws § 4-1-1(a)(4)).

A tenant who abandons an animal in a dwelling without providing for its care commits a crime (R.I. Gen. Laws § 4-1-26(a)). A pound or animal shelter treats an impounded animal as abandoned if the owner does not redeem it within 10 days (5 days if it wears no identification), and it may then be adopted (R.I. Gen. Laws § 4-1-26(b)).

Rhode Island has no landlord-tenant rule on pets or livestock left in a rental: nothing tells you to call animal control, hand animals to a shelter or care for them. You may enter without the tenant's consent only in an emergency, or during an absence of more than seven days if reasonably necessary to protect the property (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(b)).

The cautious course: if an animal appears abandoned or in distress, call the local animal control officer or police rather than keeping the animal yourself, document what you find, and put an optional caregiver clause in the lease so the tenant names someone you may let in. The library's optional clause `animal-care-access-ri` does this.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and none sets an age or condition test for carpet or paint charges. The deposit rule controls instead: you may keep from the deposit only unpaid accrued rent, reasonable cleaning expenses, reasonable trash disposal expenses, and physical damage beyond ordinary wear and tear caused by the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's statutory duties, all itemized in a written notice delivered with the balance within 20 days (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(b)). Ordinary wear and tear means deterioration from the tenant's normal, nonabusive living (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-11(11)). So the reasonable cost of cleaning carpets that actually need it can come out of the deposit as a cleaning expense, but worn, matted or faded carpet from normal use cannot be charged as damage. A lease may not waive the deposit rules (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(h)). Whether a court would enforce a flat or automatic professional-cleaning charge regardless of condition is case law. The cautious course: charge only the reasonable cost of cleaning the carpets need, keep the invoice and move-in and move-out photos, and itemize it.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Rhode Island Lease
bodyText: Rhode Island has no communal or native land system and no statute that makes a residential lease wait on a government officer's approval before it is valid; a lease binds when the parties sign it. The one tribal-land statute concerns the Narragansett settlement lands in Charlestown. The Narragansett Indian Land Management Corporation may make leases (R.I. Gen. Laws § 37-18-6(e)), but may not sell or otherwise alienate the land except by granting easements (R.I. Gen. Laws § 37-18-6(p)). Land it transfers to the federally recognized Narragansett Tribe keeps those restrictions and stays subject to Rhode Island and Charlestown civil and criminal law (R.I. Gen. Laws § 37-18-13). The statute names no officer who must approve a lease. Land held in trust by the federal government for a tribe is governed by federal law; if a property is on tribal land, get advice before using a standard lease.

title: No Energy Benchmarking or Tenant Usage-Data Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island's energy benchmarking law covers only state-owned, state-occupied buildings of at least 25,000 gross square feet, plus a voluntary benchmarking program for municipal and school buildings of that size (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-140-13(a)(2)-(3), (b), (d)). No statute requires a private residential owner to benchmark a building, gives you a right to a tenant's utility usage data, or provides for a lease clause releasing it. The energy office's general data-collection power reaches fuel wholesalers, resellers and large-storage users, not tenants (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-140-10). If you want usage data from an account in the tenant's name (for an efficiency program, an audit or your own tracking), ask the tenant for written consent and use the utility's own release form.

title: Who May Represent an LLC or Corporation Landlord in Court
bodyText: Evictions are heard in the District Court (or a housing court) (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-9). Only a member of the Rhode Island bar may practice law (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-27-5). Practicing law includes appearing as another person's representative before a court and preparing pleadings for a court case (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-27-2(1)), and "another person" includes partnerships, corporations and associations (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-27-1(b)). The District Court civil rules, which govern eviction cases, contain no rule letting an entity appear through a non-lawyer; they provide only for papers signed by an attorney of record or personally by a self-represented litigant (R.I. Dist. Ct. R. Civ. P. 11). In small claims, a court rule and a statute do speak to entities: a close corporation with assets under $1,000,000 may have an officer designate a representative by affidavit filed with the claim, LLCs and LLPs are treated as corporations for this purpose, every other plaintiff corporation must have a lawyer, and a defendant corporation must always have one (R.I. Gen. Laws § 10-16-3.1; R.I. Dist. Ct. Small Claims R. 3.02, 3.03). The owner or a partner may represent an unincorporated business there (R.I. Dist. Ct. Small Claims R. 3.02). An eviction is not a small claims case, so the small-claims exception does not reach it. Whether a member may appear for a single-member LLC in an eviction is case law. The cautious course: if your rental is owned by an LLC, corporation or partnership, hire a Rhode Island lawyer for eviction and other District Court civil cases; an individual owner may appear on their own behalf.

title: Hunting on Rented Farmland in Rhode Island
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute decides whether the landlord or the tenant of rented farmland holds the hunting or fishing rights, so the lease should say. The posted-land statute speaks only of the owner: it is an offense to enter posted land without the owner's permission to shoot, trap or fish, or to stay after being forbidden by the owner or the owner's authorized agent (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-44-4). Posting needs only conspicuous, legible signs (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-44-30). So if you want your farm tenant to decide who may hunt, name the tenant your authorized agent for that purpose in writing. A tenant in possession can still bar trespassers under the general willful-trespass law, which lets a person legally entitled to possession forbid entry (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-44-26(a)). A Rhode Island resident and immediate family may hunt without a license on land the resident owns or leases and lives on, if it is used only for agriculture and not for club shooting (R.I. Gen. Laws § 20-13-1). Put any hunting, fishing or trapping terms, and who gives permission, in the lease.

title: Telling Tenants About a Possible Foreclosure
bodyText: Rhode Island ties its foreclosure notice to mortgage delinquency, not to a foreclosure complaint. If you become 120 days delinquent on a mortgage on the property where the unit is, you must notify the tenant that the property may be subject to foreclosure, and until a foreclosure occurs the tenant must keep paying you rent under the lease (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(d)). The statute sets no form or timing beyond that, and it does not say expressly whether it reaches a new tenant who signs while you are already delinquent. The cautious course: give the notice in writing to current tenants as soon as you reach 120 days, and to any new tenant before signing, and keep a copy. Separately, the foreclosing lender must mail each bona fide tenant a notice of the scheduled sale, reminding them to keep paying rent and stating that it is not an eviction notice (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-27-7(a)). A tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant is not the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, it was at arm's length, and the rent is not substantially below market unless subsidized (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-27-7(b)).

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant may cure unpaid rent by tendering the full amount before you file suit (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(e)). After you file, the tenant may still cure by tendering all rent in arrears plus court costs at the hearing, but only if the tenant has not received a five-day demand notice from you in the six months before the case was filed (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-35(e)). After judgment there is no statutory right to redeem by paying. A stay of execution is conditioned on the tenant paying amounts equal to the rent as it would fall due, and accepting those payments neither waives your right to possession nor reinstates the tenancy (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-49). If the tenant misses them, the court, on your motion and proof of nonpayment, orders the execution issued, with no appeal (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-51). Accepting rent knowing of a default waives your right to end the tenancy for that breach unless you give written notice within 10 days, though accepting partial rent never waives the balance (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-41). Rhode Island has no separate forfeiture election for leases.

title: Which Code Editions Apply in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island's statutes generally do not freeze an outside safety code at a named edition; they leave the edition to rules. The state fire safety code is the National Fire Protection Association's Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101), with annexes, as updated or amended by the Fire Safety Code Board of Appeal and Review's rules (R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-28.1-2(a)). For existing buildings, the local fire authority applies the parts of those codes written for existing structures, consistent with the board's rules and decisions (R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-28.1-6(b)). The state building code is adopted by the Building Code Standards Committee using the International Residential Code for one- to three-family dwellings, the International Building Code for buildings with more than three units, and the International Energy Conservation Code, each with the committee's amendments (R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-27.3-100.1.5(b)). Electrical work must follow the latest edition of the National Electrical Code (R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-27.3-100.1.5(e)). The housing maintenance code, by contrast, is written into the statutes themselves and changes only by act of the legislature (R.I. Gen. Laws § 23-27.3-100.1.5.1(a)). So which edition governs your building depends on the board's and committee's current rules; check them, and ask the local building official or fire marshal before work or an inspection.

title: Which Repair Failures Trigger Tenant Remedies
bodyText: Rhode Island sorts your repair failures by seriousness only for some remedies. A tenant may end the lease for your noncompliance with the rental agreement, or for a failure of your maintenance duties materially affecting health and safety, by written notice giving you 20 days to fix it and a termination date at least 30 days out (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-28(a)). Damages and an injunction are available for any noncompliance with the lease or your maintenance duties, with no materiality test (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-28(b)). Repair and deduct covers failures of your code, habitability, facility, trash and water and heat duties whose reasonable cost of compliance is under $500 in total per year (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-30(a)). The statute does not define "materially" or list trivial defects that are excluded; that is case law. A tenant may not terminate, or repair at your expense, for a condition the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest caused deliberately or negligently (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 34-18-28(a)(3), 34-18-30(b)). If a local enforcing officer orders a dwelling repaired as unfit, rent to you is suspended and is paid into the municipal revolving fund instead (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-19(f)). Practical guidance: treat every written repair request as potentially serious, respond in writing and fix health and safety items first.

title: Your Repair Duties Can't Be Waived, Only Specific Tasks Shifted
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease cannot waive or modify your habitability duties. A lease term in which the tenant gives up rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is unenforceable, and knowingly using one lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' rent and attorney's fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b)). No lease, assignment, deed or security instrument may let anyone collect rent free of the duty to keep the unit fit and up to code (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-18). The one route is a good-faith agreement, in a writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling; it cannot cover work needed to meet the building and housing codes or reduce what you owe other tenants (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c)). The water, hot-water and heat duties carry their own built-in exceptions rather than a waiver: they do not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for them, or where the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct utility connection (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(6)). There is no rule letting a lease waive the water supply where there is no well or utility water. The housing code also lets a written agreement with the occupant decide who puts up screens and storm doors and windows (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-6(g)).

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: When you breach the lease or your maintenance duties, a Rhode Island tenant has a menu of remedies. Termination: for a breach of the lease, or of your maintenance duties materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may give written notice ending the lease at least 30 days later unless you fix the breach within 20 days (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-28(a)). Damages and an injunction, plus attorney's fees if your breach was willful (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-28(b)). Repair and deduct for repairs costing under $500 a year, after written notice and 20 days (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-30(a)). Heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service: buy it and deduct, recover lost rental value, or move to substitute housing rent-free, plus attorney's fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-31(a)-(b)). A counterclaim in a rent or nonpayment case, with rent paid into court (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-32(a)). Lead has its own rent escrow: whenever the unit fails the lead risk-reduction rules (including lacking a valid certificate of conformance) or a licensed inspector finds lead hazards, the tenant may petition the District Court to pay rent into the court registry, released to you only when you comply (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-128.1-14(a), (c)). You may not evict, end the tenancy, raise the rent or cut services because a tenant in good faith uses that remedy (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-128.1-14(e)). The lead law also allows a court order to compel compliance with costs and fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-128.1-10(b)), and damages that may be doubled or tripled (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-128.1-11(c)). And if a local officer orders an unfit dwelling repaired, rent is suspended and paid into the municipal fund (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-19(f)).

title: Recording a Rhode Island Lease
bodyText: Rhode Island never requires you to record an ordinary residential lease, and recording does not change any right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A lease for one year or less is valid even if oral (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-11-1). A lease for longer than one year is a conveyance that must be in writing, signed, acknowledged, delivered and recorded in the land records of the city or town where the property is, but even unrecorded it binds you and the tenant, your heirs, and anyone who takes with notice of it (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-11-1). Instead of the whole lease, you may record a memorandum naming the parties, describing the property and stating the duration, including renewal and purchase options (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-11-1). Recording gives everyone constructive notice of the lease (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 34-13-1(7), 34-13-2). Rhode Island has no special rule about leases to relatives. Practical guidance: recording matters only for leases longer than a year, or leases with an option to purchase or right of first refusal, where you or the tenant want the lease to bind a later buyer or lender.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages: Ten Years
bodyText: Rhode Island has a long general deadline: unless a statute provides otherwise, every civil action must be started within 10 years after the claim accrues (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-1-13(a)). That covers a suit for unpaid rent or for damage to the unit under an ordinary lease. A contract under seal gets 20 years (R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-1-17). The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets no shorter deadline of its own for a landlord's claim against a former tenant. No Rhode Island statute says whether a partial payment or a written acknowledgment restarts the period; that is case law. Practical guidance: don't wait. Evidence and the tenant's whereabouts fade long before 10 years, so sue for any balance beyond the deposit promptly after the itemized deposit notice, and keep the lease, ledger and move-out records at least that long.

title: Shifting Chores and Repairs to the Tenant
bodyText: Rhode Island lets you shift specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling to a tenant of any dwelling unit, but only by a good-faith agreement in a writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, and only for work that is not needed to bring the unit up to the building and housing codes and that does not reduce what you owe other tenants (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c)). The statute asks for adequate consideration, not specifically a rent reduction, and for specified work. A conspicuous lease clause signed by both parties can be the writing if it lists the tasks and states what the tenant gets for doing them. The housing code itself assigns some chores: occupants of one-, two- and three-family dwellings furnish their own refuse containers (owners of four or more units must supply them) (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-6(f)); a written owner-occupant agreement may decide who hangs screens and storm doors and windows (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-6(g)); and the occupant of a single-unit dwelling handles extermination unless the infestation comes from your failure to keep the building pest-proof (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-6(i)). Any other shift of your duties is an unenforceable waiver (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(1)).

title: Rights a Rhode Island Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: A Rhode Island lease may not have the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, confess judgment, pay your attorney's fees beyond what the Act allows, or excuse, limit or indemnify you for your legal liability; such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using one costs actual damages plus up to three months' rent and attorney's fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17). No lease, assignment, deed or security instrument may let anyone collect rent free of your repair and code duties (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-18). The deposit rules cannot be waived (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(h)), and a waiver of the survivor early-termination, no-refusal and lock-change protections is void (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-67). A separate non-waiver rule reaches a sale-and-lease-back of a home in foreclosure: when a foreclosure purchaser (someone acting as acquirer in more than four such deals in 24 months) buys a homeowner's home and leases it back, any waiver of the protections is void except a narrow handwritten waiver of the five-day cancellation right (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 5-80-1(b)-(c), 5-80-6). The purchaser may not use unfair or commercially unreasonable lease terms (R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-80-8(3)). Waivers of the foreclosure-consultant law are also void (R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-79-5). If you buy a home from an owner in foreclosure and rent it back, get legal advice first.

title: No Plain-Language Rule for Rhode Island Leases
bodyText: Rhode Island has no plain-language, readability, section-captioning or front-page-statement law for residential leases, and no consumer-contract statute with a dollar ceiling that pulls leases in. The plain-language rules it does have are for other contracts, such as home heating oil price plans (R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-82-1(a)). The Deceptive Trade Practices Act reaches the advertising, offering and sale of services and real property (R.I. Gen. Laws § 6-13.1-1(5)), so misleading lease terms or advertising can still cause trouble (see the consumer protection row). The limits that do reach a lease are its prohibited terms: no waiver of the Act's rights or remedies, no confession of judgment, no attorney's fees beyond the Act and no exculpation or indemnity for your own liability, on pain of up to three months' rent plus fees if you knowingly use them (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17). Write the lease plainly anyway, with the fees in the rent section and the utility split stated, since those disclosures must be clear to work.

title: Rent Cannot Be Collected Free of the Repair Duty
bodyText: Rhode Island keeps the uniform act's rule: no rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may let anyone receive rent free of the duty to comply with your maintenance obligations (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-18). So an assignment of rents to a lender, a master lease or a management contract cannot carve out the repair duty for whoever collects the rent. A person who rents the unit for you without giving the tenant the required written names and addresses of the manager and owner becomes an agent of each landlord for performing your duties and for spending or making available for that purpose all rent collected (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(c)(2)). If you sell in good faith to a bona fide purchaser, you are relieved of liability only for events after written notice to the tenant naming the buyer and certifying compliance with the housing code's sale rules (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-23(a)). A buyer of four or fewer units, other than a third-party bona fide purchaser, takes subject to the same duties toward the tenant (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-23(c)). Whoever holds your interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-19(g)).

title: Fees Must Be Listed in the Lease
bodyText: If any fee beyond rent applies to renting the unit, a Rhode Island lease must disclose those fees in the same section as the rent and say that additional fees may apply (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(1)). That placement rule does not apply where the tenant or unit receives a state or federal subsidy requiring a different lease format (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(1)). With no written lease, give the tenant a written list of all fees beyond rent, and disclose any change in required fees in writing at least 30 days before it takes effect (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(2)). The lease must also say which utility costs are in the rent and which the tenant pays, and state any renters-insurance requirement (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3)-(4)). If you don't, the tenant may recover the fees paid that were not disclosed as required (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(5)). You may not charge a convenience fee on a rent payment unless you also accept a fee-free way to pay (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-61). You may not charge any rental application fee; you may charge only the actual cost of a background check or credit report the applicant does not supply, and must give the applicant a copy (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-59(a), (b)(2)). Rhode Island has no cap on markups for third-party-billed services, no ban on common-area maintenance fees, no charge rule for partial payments, and no all-in "total monthly payment" label.

title: State Landlord-Tenant Guide: Available, Not Required
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to hand tenants a state-published rights and responsibilities guide, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one, before signing or at renewal. The Secretary of Housing must create a written consumer guide to landlords' and tenants' rights and duties under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, update it at least every two years, and post it on the Executive Office of Housing's website in English and Spanish (R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-167-5(a)(8)). No statute makes you distribute it. The Fair Housing Practices Act contains no brochure or poster duty for landlords. Giving tenants the link to the state guide is good practice. The one state-prepared document you must hand over is lead information for pre-1978 housing (see the lead rows).

title: Shorter Notice for Showings: Ask Each Time
bodyText: A Rhode Island tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, mortgagees or tenants (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(a)). Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give at least two days' notice of your intent to enter, and enter only at reasonable times (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-26(c)). Nothing in the statute lets a tenant waive or shorten that notice in advance, whether for prospective tenants or buyers, and a lease term in which the tenant waives a right under the Act is unenforceable; knowingly using one exposes you to up to three months' rent plus attorney's fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-17(a)(1), (b)). Because the scheme rests on consent, a tenant may agree to a particular showing on shorter notice at the time; keep that voluntary and get it in writing (a text or email). Abusing access, or repeated harassing demands for entry, lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the lease, with damages and attorney's fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-45).

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Rhode Island Lease
bodyText: No Rhode Island statute requires a residential lease to state that the property lies in a fire, water, sewer or other special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge a district's charges, plans or restrictions. The disclosures the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does require are the names and addresses of the manager and the owner or agent for notices (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(a)), the mortgage-delinquency notice (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(d)), the shoreline access disclosure for shoreline property (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-20(e)), and the fees, utilities and renters-insurance disclosures (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)). If a district bills for water, sewer or other services, say in the lease which of those charges are in the rent and which the tenant pays, since that disclosure is required for every utility cost (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3)).

title: Stove and Refrigerator Requirements
bodyText:
Rhode Island's housing code requires every dwelling unit's kitchen to have a stove or similar cooking device and a refrigerator or similar device that keeps food between 32°F and 50°F, properly installed with all connections for safe, sanitary and efficient operation (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-7(1)(iii)). The stove and refrigerator need not be installed while the unit is unoccupied if the incoming occupant is expected to provide them, as long as you provide enough space and adequate connections (R.I. Gen. Laws § 45-24.3-7(1)(iii)).

You must comply with the housing code and keep in good and safe working order every appliance you supply or are required to supply (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(1), (4)). So you may let the tenant bring their own stove and refrigerator, but say so in the lease (the appliances-excluded clause does this), and any appliance you supply is yours to maintain. Rhode Island has no recall-replacement rule and no required tenant acknowledgment for a tenant-supplied refrigerator.

title: Renting to Students in Rhode Island
bodyText: Rhode Island has no student-housing license, disclosure or lease rule. Its student-housing rule is an exclusion from the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: unless the parties expressly agree to be governed by it, the Act does not cover residence at a public or private institution that is incidental to providing educational (or medical, counseling, religious or similar) services, or a member's occupancy in the part of a building operated for a fraternal or social organization (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-8(1), (3)). So a college-run residence hall and a fraternity or sorority house operated by the organization fall outside the Act, but a privately owned house or apartment rented to students is an ordinary tenancy covered by every rule in this library. One rule matters in shore towns: a written seasonal lease running no earlier than September 1 to no later than June 1, with no renewal, lets you file for eviction without a cure notice if the tenant is charged with violating a municipal ordinance or breaks the lease's occupancy, noise or disturbance terms (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-36(f)).

title: Housing Your Employees
bodyText: Rhode Island's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not cover occupancy by a paid employee of a landlord whose right to occupy depends on employment substantially for services, maintenance or repair of premises with more than eleven units, unless the parties expressly agree to be governed by it (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-8(5)). Every other employee you house, such as a farmhand, a caretaker of a smaller building or an employee of your other business who pays rent, is an ordinary tenant under the Act. Rhode Island has no statute requiring a signed employee-housing disclosure, an offer of a rental agreement when the job ends, or visitor access to employer housing. The cautious course: put the housing terms in a written agreement separate from the employment terms, saying whether the Act applies, what happens to the housing if the job ends, and how much notice you will give. Never remove an employee-occupant by self-help; use a court process.

title: Tenant-Performed Repairs by Written Agreement
bodyText: Rhode Island has one tenant-repair subsection, and it reaches every dwelling unit, not only single-family homes: you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, but only if the agreement is made in good faith, is in a writing signed by both of you, is supported by adequate consideration, does not cover work needed to meet the building and housing codes, and does not reduce your obligations to other tenants (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(c)). Your core duties themselves cannot be waived (R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 34-18-17(a)(1), 34-18-18). If the tenant breaches the tenant's own maintenance duties in a way that materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, and doesn't fix it within 20 days of your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, have the work done skillfully, and bill the actual and reasonable cost as rent on the next rent date, or for immediate payment if the tenancy has ended (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-39). List the tasks specifically and state what the tenant receives for them.

title: Changing Lease Terms Mid-Tenancy
bodyText: Rhode Island sets different notice periods depending on what you change. Rent: give written notice at least 60 days before an increase takes effect, or 120 days for a month-to-month tenant over 62 (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-16.1(a)-(b)). Fees: disclose any change in required fees in writing at least 30 days before it takes effect (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(2)); that sentence sits in the paragraph for tenancies without a written lease, but follow it for every tenancy. So raising a fee the lease already provides needs a shorter notice than a rent increase, unless the charge is really rent; when in doubt, give 60 days. Rules: a rule adopted after the lease is signed that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain is not valid without the tenant's written consent (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-25(b)). Any other term: no statute lets you change it by notice during a tenancy. In a periodic tenancy you may end the tenancy by the statutory notice, 30 days for month-to-month (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-37(b)), and offer a new agreement on new terms; during a fixed term, changes need the tenant's signed agreement. An increase or change in retaliation for a tenant's complaint is prohibited (see the retaliation row).

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Rhode Island's willful-trespass law lets you keep a non-tenant out of parking lots, hallways and other parts of the property you control. A person who willfully trespasses, or who has no legitimate purpose there and stays on the land or the premises of a home after being forbidden by the owner, the owner's authorized agent or a person legally entitled to possession, faces up to a $1,000 fine, a year in jail, or both (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-44-26(a)). So give the person a written no-trespass notice signed by you or your manager, keep a copy, and tell the police. The law does not apply to tenants or occupants who rightfully entered at the start of their tenancy or occupancy and stayed after it ended or is said to have ended; you recover possession from them only through a civil case (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-44-26(b)). A tenant is legally entitled to possession of the unit, so a person the tenant invites into the unit is the tenant's guest; enforce a ban there through the lease, not by trespass. Posting land needs only conspicuous, legible signs (R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-44-30).

title: Court Can Refuse to Enforce an Unconscionable Lease Term
bodyText: If a Rhode Island court finds as a matter of law that a lease or any term of it was unconscionable when made, it may refuse to enforce the lease, enforce the rest without the unconscionable term, or limit the term to avoid an unconscionable result (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-13(a)(1)). The same applies to a settlement in which a party gives up a claim or right under the Act or the lease (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-13(a)(2)). When unconscionability is raised, by a party or by the court itself, both sides get a reasonable chance to present evidence of the lease's setting, purpose and effect (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-13(b)). The test is unconscionable "when made": Rhode Island has no statute letting a court revise or end a lease because it later became excessively burdensome. Practical guidance: keep terms reasonable and explain unusual ones to the tenant before signing, since the court judges the term in its setting.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Rhode Island)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Rhode Island property law does not use, so the civil-law rules on leases by a usufructuary don't apply. The closest Rhode Island interest is a life estate, such as a parent who deeded the house to the children but kept the right to live there for life. No Rhode Island statute says what happens to a residential lease signed by a life tenant when the life estate ends; that is case law. Two statutes touch the edges. A grantor who reserves a life estate with enhanced powers may sell, convey, mortgage or otherwise dispose of the property during life without the remainder holders, and a recorded conveyance under those powers passes title free of their interest (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-4-2.1). And when a reversion merges into another estate, its new holder keeps the same remedies against the lessee for rent and covenants (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-4-12). The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder holders sign the lease or agree in writing that it will continue if your life estate ends first.

title: Utilities You Pay
bodyText:
Every Rhode Island lease must say which utility costs are included in the rent and which are the tenant's responsibility, and a tenant may recover fees paid that were not disclosed as required (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3), (5)).

Once the lease or the law makes a utility yours, Rhode Island holds you to it. You must supply running water and reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat from October 1 to May 1, unless the building isn't required by law to be equipped for them or the heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control on a direct utility connection (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-22(a)(6)).

If, contrary to the lease or that duty, you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, the tenant may, after reasonable notice, buy the service and deduct the cost from rent, recover the lost rental value, or move to substitute housing and owe no rent meanwhile, plus attorney's fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-31).

If you willfully interrupt or cause the interruption of an essential service, including by letting an account in your name be cut off, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to three months' rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-34). Rhode Island has no statute letting a tenant take over your utility account and deduct the payments; pay included utilities on time.

title: No Utility Bill History or Disclosure Attachment Required
bodyText: Rhode Island does not require you to give a prospective tenant past heating, cooling or other utility bills or energy-use data for the unit, or to attach a utility disclosure form to the lease. The only utility disclosure is the lease statement of which utility costs are included in the rent and which the tenant pays (with no written lease, give it in writing) (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3)). If you don't make it, the tenant may recover undisclosed fees paid (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(5)). Apartment houses of more than ten units begun after July 1, 1977 may not use master meters for electricity, so each unit has its own meter (R.I. Gen. Laws § 39-3-7.1). Sharing past bills on request is a good practice, not a duty.

title: No Submetering Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Rhode Island has no statute setting a lease disclosure, billing formula, fee cap or type-size rule for submetered or allocated utility billing. The general lease rules carry the load: the lease must say which utility costs are in the rent and which the tenant pays (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(3)), and any charge beyond rent, such as a submeter or allocation charge, must be listed in the same section as the rent with a statement that additional fees may apply (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(1)). A tenant may recover fees you didn't disclose that way (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-15(a)(5)). Apartment houses of more than ten units begun after July 1, 1977 may not use master meters for electricity, and each unit must have its own meter (R.I. Gen. Laws § 39-3-7.1). You may never interrupt a utility to collect a charge (R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18-34).
